title: Ciganda's late sparkle lifts Europe on dramatic opening day of Solheim Cup
description: Carlota Ciganda steals the show after Europe's top pairing of Charley Hull and Lottie Woad fail to ignite on day one of the Solheim Cup against the United States.
fullText:
As Solheim Cup rivalries were renewed for the 20th time, Carlota Ciganda once again stole the show after Europe's top pairing of Charley Hull and Lottie Woad failed to ignite against the United States at Bernardus Golf Club in the Netherlands.

The 36-year-old Spaniard, who is the oldest player on show this weekend, let out a roar of pure emotion after holing a 15-foot putt to earn Europe what had seemed an unlikely half point in the final fourball match of the day to ensure honours are even at 4-4 heading into Saturday.

Ciganda's celebration evoked memories of the nerve-shredding finale at Finca Cortesin in 2023, when her putt allowed Europe to retain the trophy with a 14-14 tie.

And once again Nelly Korda, beaten by Ciganda in Spain three years ago, was on the receiving end.

The world number one and her playing partner Lauren Coughlin both left match-winning putts short to allow Ciganda, who had crucially won the 16th hole with an eagle, to deliver a stunning reprieve for Anna Nordqvist's team.

"I love this week. I just love playing for the team, for my team-mates. We fought hard and we got half a point, which is important," said Ciganda, who is playing in her eighth Solheim Cup.

"It gives us big momentum and hopefully we can take that into and win both [of Saturday's] morning and afternoon sessions."

European hopes of parity had begun to fade into the shadows of the evening sunshine, with Angela Stanford's visitors seemingly assuming control of the biggest team competition in women's golf.

It proved to be a hard-fought opening day between Europe and a US team looking to retain the trophy following their 15½-12½ victory in Virginia two years ago.

However, despite Ciganda's heroics, there was also a sense of what might have been for the hosts, who found themselves 6-2 behind at this stage two years ago at the Robert Trent Jones Golf Club.

History has shown a good start to be essential in this competition, with the team holding the advantage after the opening day taking home the trophy 14 out of 19 times.

And the decision to send out Hull and Woad first in both the morning foursomes and the afternoon fourballs failed to deliver the impetus Europe's captain Nordqvist would have hoped for.

When Hull and rookie Woad emerged on the raucous opening tee with daylight barely breaking through at 06:40 BST, they did so as the two highest-ranked players in the European side at eight and seven respectively.

Yet despite winning the opening hole, Nordqvist's gamble never looked like paying off against the formidable pairing of Korda and Allisen Corpuz.

The American duo won all four of their foursomes matches across the previous two editions of this contest and became the first to make it five on the spin with a comfortable 4&3 victory.

Disappointingly for Europe, Hull and Woad then let a three-hole advantage slip on the back nine on Friday afternoon against Yealimi Noh and Angel Yin, who was playing only her third competitive round since June.

They did at least scramble a half point despite loud music distracting Woad and Noh as they lined up their final putts.

In contrast Europe's three other debutants, Julia Lopez Ramirez, Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud, delivered in style.

England's Rhodes and France's Nadaud produced a superb performance to defeat Corpuz and Auston Kim 2&1, while the big-hitting Lopez Ramirez teamed up with her compatriot Ciganda in that final match against Korda and Lauren Coughlin.

"There's another 36 holes [on Saturday], so not every player's going to play five matches," said Nordqvist of her plans.

"Sometimes you've got to sit out someone, and for me, it was important to play all 12 players [on Friday], and the way the pairings worked out, that's how I had to play it."

During the build-up Nordqvist and Stanford both spoke of using the Solheim Cup as an advertisement for women's golf.

And the levels of skill, drama and grit on display only served to underline those comments, with the American players also poignantly wearing custom pins to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

"I just told them that I was proud of them again," said Stanford after the conclusion of play.

"We took a big swing from them. When you send Charley and Lottie out first, both sessions, we took some of their best body blows today.

"I'm excited because I feel like we're a heavyweight fighter. We fight with our mentality and we're just going to see how long we can last, and I feel pretty good about how long we can go."

Korda in particular set the tone early on Friday with her fifth win with Corpuz, equalling the points record for pairings set by Europe's Alison Nicholas and Laura Davies.

The US pairing of Alison Lee and Coughlin were always in control against Nanna Koerstz Madsen and Celine Boutier, taking their foursomes match 3&2 as the US opened a 2-0 lead.

An out of sorts Koerstz Madsen, who talked to her coach between sessions about her swing, and Boutier were also later on the end of a 5&3 demolition in an encounter that marked Megan Khang's sixth consecutive win in Solheim matches and her eighth in the past nine - this time alongside the metronomic Alison Lee.

Europe's fightback in the opening session was initiated by Swedish duo Maja Stark and Linn Grant who defeated Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho 3&2.

Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit followed that up by holding their nerve to defeat Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan in another match that went down the 18th.

On Saturday, eight more points will be available across the foursomes (alternate shot) and fourballs formats, before the singles on Sunday, which will involve all 12 players on each team.

Europe require 14½ points to regain the cup, while US need 14 points to retain it.

title: Benn defies concerns to make weight for Garcia bout
description: Conor Benn and Ryan Garcia both comfortably make the welterweight limit for their WBC title fight despite concerns at how they would fare on the scales.
fullText:
Conor Benn and Ryan Garcia both comfortably made the welterweight limit for their WBC title fight despite concerns at how they would fare on the scales.

Briton Benn, 29, weighed in at 10st 6lb (66kg) for Saturday's bout - half a pound heavier than the champion.

The official weigh-in took place behind closed doors at the UFC Apex on Friday, in front of about 50 members of the media, before a ceremonial event later in the day which will be open to the public.

Garcia has won 25 of his 28 professional contests, including 20 knockout victories, with two defeats and one no-contest. Benn has 25 wins - 14 by knockout - and one loss, and is fighting for his first world title.

American Garcia, 28, won the WBC belt with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making his first defence against Benn.

Eggs, insults & a champion with a fake beard - Garcia and Benn face off

Why Nigel Benn can't walk away from Conor

Benn does not deserve world title shot - Garcia

Much of the build-up this week has centred on how Benn would cope with returning to the 10st 7lb welterweight limit for the first time in more than four years.

His two fights against Chris Eubank Jr were both at middleweight, with Benn weighing 11st 2lb (71kg) for the first and 11st 5lb (72kg) for the rematch. For his win over Regis Prograis in April, Benn weighed 10st 10lb (69kg).

He has already said he will vacate the title and move back up in weight if he beats Garcia.

Benn had looked increasingly gaunt and drawn during fight week and told BBC Sport the cut had taken him to the "pits of hell".

But Benn smiled as his weight was announced and looked in good shape, surprising several observers who had expected the effects of the cut to be far more visible.

A handful of undercard fighters weighed in after Benn while Garcia was still nowhere to be seen, prompting questions about whether the Californian was having difficulties making the limit.

Garcia has had problems on the scales before. He weighed more than three pounds over the light-welterweight limit before his fight against Devin Haney in 2024.

There was no such drama this time. Garcia sprinted towards the scales about 10 minutes after Benn and also looked at ease as he comfortably made weight.

The weight is particularly significant because of the contrasting styles.

Benn relies heavily on aggression, explosiveness and sustained pressure, while Garcia is a fast and dangerous counter-puncher who is comfortable catching opponents as they come forward.

Any draining effects of the cut could therefore leave Benn more vulnerable to Garcia's speed and powerful left hook, while also raising questions over whether the Briton can maintain his usual intensity over 12 rounds.

With no rehydration clause in place, Benn said he could weigh as much as 12st 7lb (80kg) by the time he steps into the ring on Saturday.

He is still an underdog against Garcia - a fighter with greater amateur pedigree and a more accomplished professional resume - but Benn's size and physical pressure could become one of his biggest advantages.

Outgoing Rep Chip Roy says the GOP has already 'delivered significantly,' but must 'finish the job'
description: Outgoing House Republican Chip Roy of Texas said that while Republicans have "delivered significantly," they still must "finish the job."
fullText:
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas — who lost the Lone Star State GOP attorney general primary runoff in May and will depart the U.S. House of Representatives when his current term expires — said Republicans have "delivered significantly" but "need to finish the job."

"Well, we've done so much that frankly, it kinda gets lost in a lot of the noise," Roy told Fox News Digital during an interview on Wednesday, pointing to issues such as tax provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump last year.

The Texan pointed to the nation's border as the "biggest example" of Republicans' achievements, saying that "we've literally shut down the flow across the border" through enforcing the law.

He also pointed to the passage of the "Laken Riley Act," a measure named after the 22-year-old woman murdered in 2024 by Jose Ibarra, a man who, according to a 2024 statement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), had previously been "arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)" after illegally entering the U.S., but was "paroled and released for further processing."

Roy said Republicans "need to unite with a singular vision about where we wanna take the country if we wanna be... rewarded in November... and then frankly looking ahead to 2028."

Texas Maga Battle Ends With Middleton Victory As Chip Roy Falls Short In Ag Race

"Have we done everything we should do? No," Roy said, claiming that "Congress has fallen short" regarding some of what they "should do."

But he still believes the GOP could potentially retain their majorities in both congressional chambers during the midterms.

"I think right now Republicans are staring at barely holding onto the Senate and slightly losing the House, but I still think we can win the House," he said.

The House is now only scheduled to work for several days next week before a lengthy break until after the Nov. 3 elections. Roy indicated that Republicans should get back to work after the midterms "to do our part to finish the job."

"Obviously I'm not campaigning. So I'm thinking a lot about what we could do with another reconciliation package or what we might be able to do in the lame duck or in January, when I'm not in office," he noted.

Fentanyl Deaths Could Now Cost Drug Dealers Their Lives Under New Gop Proposal

In a Sunday post on X, Roy wrote, "Government does not fund anything. It takes money from people under force of law and distributes it to other people very inefficiently and usually tyrannically. Child care is unaffordable because government (& corporate cronyism) has made life unaffordable. Stay out."

The New York Times reported last week that the Trump administration is moving to enable some married people with a stay-at-home parent situation to receive a childcare subsidy from a federal program that was meant to help parents who work.

The proposal "creates the option for a new category of care, parent-based child care, that will allow one married parent to receive C.C.D.F. [Child Care and Development Fund] assistance to care for their own child, while a spouse works at least 35 hours per week," the outlet reported, citing a draft document.

Roy said during the interview on Wednesday, "I just don't believe that it's good for the human soul to have the government coming in with a grant and making you dependent on government. I just don't philosophically think that that's freedom. I think freedom, non-dependence, independence is what makes America great."

A White House official said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Thursday that the Trump administration "has not announced any such proposal. Until and unless it does, any discussion about potential policies is baseless speculation."

Chip Roy Fields Proposal To Block Pay And Power For Longtime Lawmakers

As for whether he has any interest in running for office again, Roy said the matter is "up to God" and to Texans, adding that he has "a calling for service" and his current focus is on attempting to "solve the big problems for" Americans.

America built a fortress after 9/11. Then the threat started hiding in plain sight
description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, lone actors radicalized online have replaced al Qaeda's complex plots as the greatest terrorism threat to the homeland.
fullText:
On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Javed Ali drove past the Pentagon on his way to work in northern Virginia.

Roughly half an hour later, American Airlines Flight 77 slammed into the building.

From his office in Falls Church, Ali could see smoke rising from the Pentagon. A year later, in a turn that captured how dramatically the country had changed, he was walking into the still-damaged building himself — now working in the Defense Intelligence Agency's counterterrorism office.

Trump Confirms Pentagon Plans For 25Th Anniversary Of 9/11 Attacks, Disputes Report On Ground Zero Absence

"It was a very eerie and odd and surreal moment in my career," Ali told Fox News Digital.

Ali's career would eventually take him from the DIA to the newly created Department of Homeland Security and later the FBI, giving him a front-row seat to the enormous national security architecture America constructed after the deadliest foreign attack on U.S. soil.

Twenty-five years later, that architecture presents something of a paradox.

But success against the threat of 2001 did not eliminate terrorism. It helped change it.

American Youth Radicalized Online, Busted In Suspected Terror Plots After Hating Country On Social Media

Today's most difficult threats increasingly involve individuals radicalized online, small cells with little warning signature, foreign terrorist organizations seeking to inspire attacks from afar, and an expanding layer of cyber and state-sponsored threats capable of reaching deep inside the United States without hijacking an airplane.

The question 25 years after 9/11, therefore, is not simply whether Americans are safer.

They are safer from one kind of attack — while increasingly exposed to others.

An Ai Cyberattack Could Turn Off America's Lights Before Washington Even Understands Why

The scale of the American response was extraordinary.

Just over two months after the attacks, President George W. Bush signed legislation creating the Transportation Security Administration. TSA says its creation amounted to the largest civilian undertaking in U.S. government history at the time, with the federal government rapidly assuming responsibility for airport passenger and baggage screening.

The following year, Congress created the Department of Homeland Security, combining all or part of 22 federal agencies and offices. DHS began operating in March 2003 and today employs more than 260,000 people across missions ranging from border and aviation security to cybersecurity, intelligence and emergency response.

The changes went far beyond new agencies.

The 9/11 Commission found that the pre-attack breakdown was deeper than the familiar failure to "connect the dots." Responsibility had been scattered across agencies, information was not consistently shared, and no single entity was empowered to integrate intelligence and drive joint action across the foreign-domestic divide. The commission concluded that "responsibility and accountability were diffuse."

Washington spent the next two decades trying to close those gaps.

Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that post-9/11 wars and related obligations have cost roughly $8 trillion. It estimates that more than $1.1 trillion has been spent on homeland security efforts to prevent and counterterrorism inside the United States since DHS was created.

Ali said it can be easy, with 25 years of hindsight, to forget how persistent the original threat remained.

Even after the United States invaded Afghanistan, killed or captured senior al Qaeda figures and put the organization under extraordinary pressure, the group continued attempting to find ways back into the homeland.

During Ali's years at DHS, he said officials repeatedly confronted plots involving al Qaeda and its affiliates, including a 2006 plot originating in Britain to bomb transatlantic airliners traveling to North America.

Usama bin Laden was killed by U.S. forces in Pakistan in May 2011. But rather than marking the end of the era of jihadist terrorism, the following years produced a new and in some ways more difficult challenge.

ISIS grew out of al Qaeda in Iraq, expanded rapidly amid the wars in Iraq and Syria and declared a self-described caliphate in June 2014. At its height, the group controlled vast territory and millions of people in Iraq and Syria while encouraging or directing attacks far beyond its borders. The State Department reported that ISIS had emerged from al Qaeda in Iraq and expanded dramatically during 2013 and 2014.

For U.S. counterterrorism officials, Ali said, the center of gravity increasingly shifted from identifying trained operatives sent by an organized group to finding individuals who might be radicalizing inside Western countries.

Then came another shift: attacks by lone offenders across different ideologies, often with no direct operational relationship to an organization overseas.

"Mostly lone actors, lone offenders, not tied to groups overseas, not traveling overseas, and not being directed by people overseas," said Ali, now an associate professor of practice at the University of Michigan's Ford School of Public Policy.

Dhs Chief Announces Changes To Its Seal To Reflect That Department Is 'At War Every Single Day'

The transformation is now reflected in the government's own threat assessments.

The 2026 Annual Threat Assessment from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said setbacks to the ability of Islamist terrorist groups to conduct "large-scale complex attacks" have pushed them toward information operations and propaganda designed to inspire or enable people in or with access to Western countries.

The assessment said there were at least three Islamist terrorist attacks in the United States in 2025 and that law enforcement disrupted at least 15 U.S.-based Islamist terrorist plotters that year. Roughly half of those disrupted plotters had some online contact with Islamist terrorists or were inspired by foreign terrorist organizations, according to the assessment.

The vulnerability was demonstrated on New Year's Day 2025, when Shamsud-Din Jabbar, a U.S. citizen from Texas, drove a pickup truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street in New Orleans, killing 14 people. The FBI described the attack as an act of terrorism and said Jabbar had become increasingly isolated before adopting extremist views.

In the days after that attack, the FBI said lone actors and small cells who radicalize online had posed the greatest terrorism threat to the homeland in recent years precisely because they can be so difficult to detect and disrupt.

That presents almost the inverse of the 9/11 problem.

The 9/11 plot required 19 hijackers, overseas leadership, financing, international travel, flight training and years of planning. The challenge for investigators was collecting pieces of information held across different agencies and assembling them quickly enough.

A lone actor may offer far fewer pieces to collect in the first place.

Ali said many recent attackers or alleged plotters had not previously come onto the radar of the FBI or local law enforcement, leaving authorities with the extraordinarily difficult task of identifying people who may not commit an obvious crime until they move toward violence.

"So yes, we are safer from a certain type of threat," Ali said, "but again, we are not immune from terrorism, and other types of threats are much more difficult to identify or stop."

Kash Patel Reveals The Chilling Holiday Terror Plots Fbi Federal Agents Quietly Stopped

That changing threat has also fueled a broader debate over whether the institutions created after 9/11 became too large, too expensive or too focused on the dangers of the previous era.

Morgan Murphy, who served as press secretary to the secretary of Defense during the first Trump administration and later worked in the Trump White House, argues that Washington built too much bureaucracy around the 9/11 threat while other vulnerabilities grew.

"TSA agents still pat down grandma and gum up travel while Beijing wires our living rooms with cheap TVs and selfie sticks through the supply chain handed to them by Clinton, Bush, Obama and Biden," Murphy said. "We spent two decades frisking American passengers while our adversaries plugged themselves into our homes and businesses."

"The genius of America after Pearl Harbor was that we built to fight. After 9/11, we built to process," Murphy told Fox News Digital, "Real security means sovereignty at home and lethality abroad — a sealed border, an untangled supply chain, and enemies who fear us."

Theo Wold, who served as acting assistant attorney general in the Justice Department's Office of Legal Policy and as deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy during the first Trump administration, offered a similar critique, arguing that post-9/11 Washington relied too heavily on large bureaucracies, expansive government authorities and wars in the Middle East.

"George W. Bush and the D.C. governing elite responded to 9/11 the way their politics demanded: create large, unwieldy bureaucracy, push for special legal authorities with limited oversight and activate ground wars in the Middle East," Wold told Fox News Digital.

"Those wars didn't make us safer, the legal authorities were wielded against Americans, and the bureaucracy is full of waste and has proven nearly unworkable," he said.

Wold argued that the lesson from the past quarter-century should be a more narrowly targeted national-security model.

"Now we know better. Americans are safest when we are nimble and focus ruthlessly on targeting real enemies," he said.

The challenge now extends beyond terrorism.

The 2026 intelligence assessment warns that China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and non-state ransomware groups continue seeking access to U.S. government networks and private critical infrastructure for espionage, financial gain and possible future disruption. It also warns that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyber capabilities and that several state adversaries are developing missile systems capable of threatening the homeland.

The security landscape that began with al Qaeda operatives training to fly passenger jets has therefore expanded into something far less geographically defined: terrorist propaganda transmitted to an individual's phone, malicious code inserted into a computer network, attacks on critical infrastructure and state adversaries capable of reaching Americans from thousands of miles away.

For Ali, however, the evolution of the threat should not lead Washington to conclude that the original threat has vanished.

One of the central lessons of the years before Sept. 11, he said, was that emerging terrorist organizations have to be confronted before they have the time and space to develop operational capability.

"When these terrorist threats start to emerge, whether it's overseas or here, you have to put pressure on them before they gather momentum to carry out operations," Ali said.

The danger, he argued, would be allowing counterterrorism to fall so far down Washington's list of priorities that the country begins recreating the complacency that existed before 9/11.

"Terrorism as a tactic is probably never going to be defeated," Ali said.

Twenty-five years after he watched smoke rise from the Pentagon, Ali's answer to whether America is safer reflects the contradiction at the heart of the post-9/11 era.

The United States built a massive system to prevent the next 9/11.

It appears to have made another 9/11 far harder to execute.

The harder question now is whether that system can recognize the attack that doesn't look anything like it.

Saudi Arabia tells Trump now is the time for military action as Iran-backed Houthis advance
description: Houthi forces seized Perim island and key positions along Yemen's Bab al-Mandab Strait as Saudi Arabia urged Trump to take direct military action.
fullText:
Saudi Arabia is urging Washington to take direct military action against Iran-backed Houthis, Fox News Digital learned after the terrorist group seized key positions along Yemen's Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday.

The dramatic strengthening of Houthi's positioning along the coastline of Yemen is in one of the world's most important shipping choke points — a narrow passage that links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, which has been used as a bypass as the Iran war continues to severely disrupt shipping, especially of oil, through the Strait of Hormuz.

The rapid advance on Friday triggered urgent discussions at the highest levels in Riyadh and Washington, and a source familiar with the matter tells Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis.

New Risk For U.s. Consumers As Iran-backed Attacks Threaten A Second Major Oil Chokepoint

The Houthis reached the strategic island of Mayyun, also known as Perim, after Yemeni government forces withdrew and also took the mainland coastal town of Dhubab, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Friday.

Fox News Digital independently confirmed key elements of an Axios report with a source familiar with the matter, who said the crown prince spoke with Trump a few times over the past 24 hours about the escalating situation in Yemen.

The U.S. does not want to take direct military action for now, but Trump told bin Salman that Washington would assist Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting support, according to the source.

The source also confirmed that U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to Saudi Arabia for coordination talks.

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the calls or whether additional U.S. military action is under consideration.

Iran's Biggest Weapon Against The U.s. May Be Slipping Away, Experts Say

The convergence raises the prospect of simultaneous pressure on two of the world's most consequential maritime arteries: Iran disrupting traffic through Hormuz while its Houthi allies strengthen their position around Bab al-Mandab.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the shift reflects Tehran's effort to recover leverage as pressure around Hormuz changes.

"Trump's success in pushing back on Iran's maritime threat in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf has made the regime lose the maritime leverage it had, and now it is looking to double down on the Houthis who have proven to be able to impact Red Sea shipping and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the past," Ben Taleblu said.

"As Tehran loses leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, it is trying to wield a knife and a handshake at once: diplomacy with Arab states and a knife in the back via the Houthi offensive," he added.

Iran Calls On Houthis To Prepare To Cut Off Red Sea Gateway — Can The Terror Group Do It?

The latest advance follows the Houthis' capture Thursday of the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, which was previously held by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Former U.S. special envoy for Yemen Timothy Lenderking said Friday that the Houthis had spent the years since the 2022 U.N.-brokered truce rebuilding their military strength and are now exploiting the broader Iran conflict to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia.

Speaking during an on-the-record Middle East Institute virtual briefing, Lenderking said the April 2022 truce largely put Yemen's civil war on pause but also "did allow the Houthis to regroup, retrain, refit, restock."

"They're extremely entrepreneurial. They use every opportunity to build their capability, to test their capabilities, such that they are now the most lethal non-state actor in the entire Middle East," Lenderking said.

Lenderking traced the latest round of escalation in part to Iranian Mahan Air flights into Sanaa earlier this summer, which he said brought personnel and equipment intended to support the Houthi war effort, adding that the personnel were from Iran and were "probably IRGC members."

Iran-backed Houthi Threat In Red Sea Could Lead To Major U.s. Policy Shift, Analysts Say

Lenderking said the Houthis are now taking advantage of the wider conflict with Iran to increase their leverage over Riyadh.

"They've seized this opportunity, bringing these various lines of effort together, to put a great deal of pressure on the Yemen government and the Saudis specifically," he said.

On Thursday, a senior Trump administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

The stakes extend well beyond Yemen.

The Bab al-Mandab is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. About 7% of global oil output passed through the strait in June, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Disruption can force ships to reroute around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding significant time and cost to voyages.

Expert Warns Of 'General Escalation' Of Fighting If Houthis Resume Red Sea Campaign

Ben Taleblu said the speed of the Houthi advance exposed vulnerabilities in the Saudi-led effort to contain the group.

"The U.S. should help the Saudis stymie the Houthi advance," he said. "The inability of the Saudis to prevent the Houthis from taking the strategic port city of Mocha, for example, does not bode well for what may come."

Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the danger extends beyond the territory captured. Retreating government forces, he said, left behind military equipment that could strengthen the Houthis on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."

The developments mark a dramatic reversal from the relative calm that followed the 2022 truce and leave Washington and its regional allies confronting a growing question: whether the Houthi advance can be contained without opening another direct U.S. military front as American forces remain focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Federal appeals court says clean drinking water is not a constitutional right
description: The ruling followed a lawsuit filed in 2022 by residents in Jackson, Mississippi, over the city's lead-contaminated water system.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Clean drinking water is not a guaranteed right under the U.S. Constitution, a federal appeals court ruled.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit — in a 10-5 ruling — said the alleged contamination in Jackson, Miss., did not violate rights protected by the 14th Amendment.

"The Constitution does not provide redress for every governmental wrongdoing," Circuit Judge Kurt Engelhardt wrote.

The ruling followed a lawsuit filed by residents over the city's lead-contaminated water system. The lawsuit, launched in 2022 by Priscilla Sterling, Raine Becker, Shawn Miller and John Bennett, argued that the city knowingly allowed residents to drink unsafe water.

The complaint against Jackson claimed that testing conducted by the state's health department between 2010 and 2013 revealed increased levels of lead in the water.

"We are skeptical that the right to not be harmed by lead-contaminated water fits within the right to bodily integrity, and Plaintiffs point us to no historical tradition or Supreme Court precedent convincing us," Engelhardt added.

The judge also noted that the city's mismanagement, which residents blame for their lead exposure, falls outside the constitutional protection.

"It is undisputed that the Constitution does not guarantee clean water," the court said.

It also found no constitutional right to truthful information from government officials during a public health crisis.

title: AOC’s ‘modern-day lynchings’ claim torn to shreds online as Black hanging case findings tell a different story
description: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ayanna Pressley demand DOJ and FBI investigate Black hanging deaths, alleging racial terror and modern-day lynchings.
fullText:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., warned Friday of "racial terror" and "widespread modern-day lynchings" in the U.S. as she joined dozens of Democrats demanding that the DOJ and FBI investigate hanging deaths of Black Americans.

Multiple official findings in several recent cases show that law enforcement or medical examiners ruled the deaths suicides, while at least one very recent death remains under a homicide investigation.

AOC alleges there is systemic racial bias at the agencies, while fellow progressive lawmaker Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., called the hangings a "national crisis" in a letter to the agencies that she spearheaded.

Ms Rachel Speaks Out On Black Hanging Cases As Raleigh Death Is Declared Suicide

"This year, there have already been 10 reported hangings of Black people in the U.S. I'm proud to have signed onto Rep. Pressley's letter to address these widespread modern-day lynchings and put a stop to this racial terror," Ocasio-Cortez wrote on X in support of the call.

Pressley warned in her letter that "Black folks are being found hanged in America" and insisted: "We cannot stand by while strange fruit hangs from trees across the country."

The letter, addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, was signed by Pressley, Ocasio-Cortez and about 50 Democrats. They demanded a "thorough, transparent, and comprehensive federal investigation into every hanging death of a Black individual across the United States," arguing that federal agencies have failed for decades to adequately investigate such deaths.

Family Identifies Young Woman Found Fatally Shot In Home Owned By Rep Ayanna Pressley's Husband

One 2026 case involved the death of a 21-year-old Atlanta man who had gone missing. He was later found hanging from a tree in a Cobb County park, where officials ruled out foul play and deemed the death a suicide, according to Atlanta's NBC affiliate.

Another 2026 case involved Delta State University student Demartravion Reed in Mississippi. Officials "determined the cause of death to be a hanging and the manner of death as suicide."

At the time, the case reopened old memories of the murder of Emmett Till, according to reports. Till was a Black teen kidnapped and murdered by White men not far from the site after he was falsely accused of flirting with a White woman in 1955.

15-Year-old Black Teen's Murder Reveals The Ugly Truth About White Guilt In America

A Grio report on Pressley's letter also referenced the hanging deaths of a 58-year-old man in Albany, N.Y., and a 39-year-old man in Brookfield, Wisconsin.

The Albany Police Department said Earl Smith's death was "ruled a suicide" and investigators found "no evidence" of criminal activity.

"The Albany Police Department is aware of concerns posted on social media suggesting that criminal activity was involved with this incident, which has understandably caused public concern," the department said.

A preliminary investigation of the Wisconsin man's death also indicated suicide, according to Brookfield's police chief cited by the Waukesha County Freeman.

At least one case remains under homicide investigation, according to reports.

Tasia Fortune was found hanging outside an abandoned house in Jackson, Mississippi, CNN reported Thursday. Authorities later questioned Terence Bernard Anderson, the father of one of her children, and arrested him on unrelated weapons charges, according to several reports.

Aoc Slams 'Oppressed' Trump States While Touting Nyc Services Despite $5B Deficit And Transit Crime Spike

The lawmakers' characterization also drew criticism on social media.

"Those community notes are stacking up," one critic said, as X's crowdsourced correction indicator included several wire reports and media links disputing Ocasio-Cortez' claims.

"There should be some sort of penalty for willfully lying on social media, especially for a politician," another claimed.

Former Energy Department official Matt Van Swol posted to X, "In the last 'lynching' of a Black woman, the media conveniently left out the prime suspect in the case was her Black boyfriend. Zero White people are lynching Black people in America today."

Watch: Squad Democrat Speaks Out After Teen Found Shot Dead At Husband's Boston Property

Former Senate staffer Matt Whitlock added that "every death is a tragedy, but what do you think 'widespread' means if only one of these was actually a homicide. Not sure you've landed the point about 'racial terror' with this."

X's crowdsourced Community Notes feature also pointed readers to law-enforcement and medical-examiner findings in several of the cases, stating that most high-profile hanging deaths it identified in 2025 and 2026 had been ruled suicides and that one remained under homicide investigation.

When reached for comment, Pressley spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez directed Fox News Digital back to the lawmakers' letter to Blanche and Patel, specifically a line reminding them that "Congress enacted the Emmett Till Antilynching Act in 2022 to ensure the DOJ and FBI are empowered to fully investigate suspicious deaths and hold individuals accountable."

Fox News Digital reached out to Ocasio-Cortez, the DOJ and the FBI for comment.

title: Hillary Clinton: 'I hate' Trump and Netanyahu's governments but love America and Israel
description: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton told "Morning Joe" she hates the policies of President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but loves Israel and America.
fullText:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said she hated the governments and policies of President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but said she loved America and Israel during an interview Thursday.

"I have said repeatedly I love Israel and I hate Netanyahu's government and his policies. I love America, and I hate Trump's government and policies. I think it's bad, in the first case for Israel, what's happening, and I think it's really bad for the United States, what's happening," Clinton told MS NOW's "Morning Joe."

Clinton spoke to the MS NOW panel about Israel and achieving peace in the Middle East.

Hillary Clinton Breaks With Democratic Critics By Backing Trump's Gaza Plan As The 'Only Game In Town'

"I think we've got to be very clear, the messages we send, hopefully the Israeli people, especially after this bombshell that came out in the Israeli press, where Netanyahu had been literally called by Sheikh Mohammed, MBZ, from UAE, and warned that Hamas was planning something," Clinton said.

"And either he didn't believe it or he, it's horrible to say, he wanted to see what they could plan so that then he could come down hard, and it would enhance his position."

"I don't know what his thinking was, but the bottom line, talk about a failure of imagination. This was a failure of leadership," she continued. "This was a failure of protecting the people of Israel. He's been told what was going to happen. So, if the Israelis want to vote for that again, then I think the United States has to take a very tough position."

title: Oakland schools in hot seat over 'students of color' program while taking millions in federal funding
description: Defending Education filed a Title VI complaint alleging Oakland Unified School District's Latinx mentoring program excludes White students.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX — The Oakland Unified School District (OUSD) is in the hot seat over a federally funded "Latinx Mentoring and Achievement Program" that allegedly excludes White students from receiving academic support, mentorship and cash incentives.

Defending Education (DE), a national educational rights group, filed a federal civil rights complaint against the district alleging that its Latino Men & Boys (LMB) and Latina Mentoring & Achievement (LMA) programs violate Title VI and Title IX of the Civil Rights Act.

"The Supreme Court has recognized only two compelling interests that permit resort to race-based government action: first, 'remediating specific identified instances of past discrimination that violated the Constitution or a statute,' and second, 'avoiding imminent and serious risks to human safety in prisons, such as a race riot,'" the complaint, sent exclusively to Fox News Digital, states.

California County Approves Reparations Plan As Neighboring School District 'Black Thriving' Effort Stalls

The initiative, nationally recognized by The Obama Foundation, is listed under OUSD's "Community Partners" webpage and operates in conjunction with The Unity Council — an Oakland-based organization that claims to promote "social equity and enhancing quality of life by creating vibrant communities where everyone can work, learn, and thrive."

According to The Unity Council's website, the initiatives "are school-based, culturally rooted programs located in selected schools in the Oakland Unified School District." The original LMB program was later expanded to create the LMA program following initial outreach.

"The programs work with Latinx youth ages 12–18 and their families and schools to improve outcomes in mental and physical health, education, and career planning," The Unity Council's site states. "The program significantly increases graduation rates for Latinx youth in Oakland schools and promotes healthy lifestyles, academic focus and leadership development. The program is available for male-identified, female-identified, and non-binary youth."

Erika Kirk Urges Conservative Students Not To Back Down In First School Year Since Charlie's Assassination

However, PDE's civil rights complaint alleges that because OUSD receives millions in federal financial assistance, offering racially exclusive perks through third-party partners breaches federal nondiscrimination laws.

The complaint further details that the LMB initiative grants direct financial payouts to participating students.

"During the 2024-2025 school year, the Unity Council distributed roughly $3,000 in 'milestones and stipends' to minority students through the LMB program," the complaint states. "This is important because the LMB program discriminates against students based on race. For example, OUSD's 2022-2023 service agreement with the Unity Council says that the LMB program is offered to 'Latino males and other students of color' and their families. OUSD's 2024-2025 service agreement likewise states that the LMB program is meant for 'approximately two hundred Latino young men and their families.'"

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

"In other words, OUSD pays the Unity Council to run a program that gives tutoring, mentoring, health and wellness programs, and even cash to male minority students — specifically male Latino students," PDE argues in its filing. "But the LMB program does not include White students. Nor does OUSD offer any other similar support program for White OUSD students. Because the program denies these benefits to White students, it discriminates against these students on the basis of race."

Neither OUSD nor The Unity Council immediately responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment regarding the federal complaint.

"Oakland Unified School District has forgotten that ours is a colorblind Constitution. In a ham-fisted attempt to guarantee student 'equity' outcomes, Oakland USD has sponsored a multitude of programs geared toward only one race or sex in violation of federal law," said Sarah Parshall Perry, vice president and legal fellow at Defending Education.

Perry went on to say, "Cash stipends, tutoring assistance, wellness programs, and food and housing benefits for only one group of students, to the exclusion of others, are just the tip of the iceberg in one of California's largest school districts. Discriminating on the basis of race or sex — even when classified as a benign 'diversity' effort — is illegal. This Administration has made that abundantly clear, but it seems Oakland is due for a refresher."

title: Trump Wants Voters to Pretend He’s on the Ballot
description: Chris...
fullText:
But Republican midterm candidates are hoping everyone forgets he exists.

The balance of commentary on the GOP’s midterm pep rally in Dallas has focused on President Donald Trump’s outlandish and unlikely scheme to bribe voters with a $5,000 payoff should the Republicans prevail in the midterms. That’s understandable, since Trump’s scheme is brazenly illegal—as was the case when Elon Musk promised a similarly sleazy $1 million “lottery” windfall to right-leaning voters in Wisconsin’s 2025 balloting for state Supreme Court justices. (The only material difference here is that Musk was in a position to deliver the promised bribe, while Trump very much is not.)

Yet such rank corruption is increasingly the Republican Party’s business model—which is why the mini-convention also featured blaring violations of the Hatch Act, with both Attorney General Todd Blanche and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent electioneering for the GOP in a register only marginally less corrupt than their boss’s spectacle of transactional grift. (In Bessent’s case, the bond markets reacted with an alacrity that our judicial system now conspicuously lacks.) Until we regain a viable system of genuine constitutional oversight, the most urgent question before our flailing political order is whether Trump’s pitch to voters is likely to work. By this, I don’t mean the president’s bribery ploy but the political appeal he also made in Dallas: “Pretend that I’m on the ballot” in November’s midterm elections.

Sure, that’s a predictable come-on from a chief executive who sees all the basic operations of government as an extension of his own ego. At the same time, it’s a likely recipe to kill off any Republican prospects for keeping the party’s present governing trifecta intact. Trump is a stunningly unpopular president, reaching a nadir of approval in the low to mid 30s just last week. That’s why a strong contingent of vulnerable GOP candidates running in swing states were no shows to what Republicans were calling Dallas’s “Trump-a-palooza.” It’s also why a growing number of similarly situated Republican hopefuls have been scrubbing either the person of Trump or key elements of his governing agenda from their campaign websites. Pretending that Trump is on the ballot is pretty much the last thing they want to do.

The strategy behind making the GOP midterms a referendum on Trump is a revival of the one that won him the 2024 election: target “low propensity” voters otherwise tuned out of politics with sops to their short-term self-interest. This is what yielded such pseudopopulist proposals as the cynically sunsetted “no tax on tips” revenue policy and deductions of interest on auto loans; it’s also the clear logic behind the $5,000 bribery scheme (which, like so many other gruesome features of our late-stage oligarchy, was previewed in Idiocracy).

But the glaring problem with continuing to flog the low-propensity strategy is that midterm cycles simply don’t work that way: They run mostly on motivated base voters, who are paying very close attention to politics. (On top of which, of course, midterm balloting almost always favors the party that’s out of power in the Oval Office.)

What’s more, there’s strong evidence that even the low-propensity voters whom the 2024 Trump campaign successfully recruited are experiencing serious buyer’s remorse. Pollster G. Elliott Morris has distilled the findings from eight months’ worth of surveys tracking the positions of voters on the issues most important to them with their support for a major-party presidential candidate in 2024. His key takeaway is very bad news for the promoters of the Dallas convention and the strategy behind it: “voters who are less likely to turn out to vote are actually much less approving of Trump overall and on key issues.” A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released at the end of August found that 15 percent of respondents who voted for Trump in 2024 said that they might or would vote differently if given the choice again; 6 percent said they regretted voting altogether. Only 58 percent of Trump voters in the survey said they were very confident they’d make the right choice in 2024—a marked drop-off from the 74 percent saying as much in April 2025. (The segment of voters sorry that they’d voted at all, meanwhile, was just 1 percent back then.)

These dynamics supply a whole bevy of reasons why the GOP should be urging voters to pay no attention to the bloated, bellicose orange man behind the curtain. Yet after spending the past decade transforming the Republican Party into an authoritarian cult of personality, there’s no other clear path before them. If party strategists were to plow ahead without trying to marshal a new model army of low-propensity voters, things would look considerably worse for them: Morris’s polls show a clear leftward shift in the likely 2026 electorate—together with nearly every midterm survey of the generic Republican and Democratic ballots. Indeed, a recent Gallup poll found that 49 percent of likely 2026 voters identify as Democrats, with just 39 percent aligning with the GOP—the largest such margin since 2008, when Democrats last secured a supermajority in Congress, along with the White House. Half of self-identified independent voters—the swing constituency in many past midterm cycles—now say they lean Democratic.

Even the MAGA movement’s quasi-mythic hold on white working-class voters is eroding. Prior to the 2018 blue-wave midterms, voters in this prime Trump electoral stronghold supported his economic program by margins of 30 percent and more; now, they disapprove of his handling of the economy by a 14-to-30 percent margin. It’s far from clear how Republicans intend to reverse these trends in a two-month span, but one surefire way to make them worse is to continue acting like Donald Trump is on the ballot.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel

title: 49ers Week 1 overreactions: San Francisco is bigger Super Bowl threat than Rams, Seahawks
description: The San Francisco 49ers asserted themselves as contenders in the NFC during their season opener. San Francisco dominated Los Angeles in a 27-7 victory in front of an international crowd at Melbourne Cricket Ground.
