fullText:
49ers Week 1 overreactions: San Francisco is bigger Super Bowl threat than Rams, Seahawks appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The San Francisco 49ers asserted themselves as contenders in the NFC during their season opener. San Francisco dominated Los Angeles in a 27-7 victory in front of an international crowd at Melbourne Cricket Ground. The 49ers were competitive from the opening whistle and played with their hair on fire for a full 60 minutes.

San Francisco often looked like a forgotten team in the NFC West throughout the offseason. It is easy to understand why. Seattle won the Super Bowl, dismantling San Francisco in the playoffs as part of that journey. Meanwhile, the Rams went all in during the 2026 offseason on their quest to get back to the Super Bowl themselves. The Rams brought in Trent McDuffie, Myles Garrett, and Aaron Donald to upgrade their defense.

All of those narratives make the Rams and Seahawks easy teams to root for during the offseason. But it looks like the hype may have been overblown just two days into the regular season.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

San Francisco proved that they are the biggest Super Bowl threat in the NFC West after their huge win in Australia.

Coming into the season, the Rams were the team to beat in the NFL. Any team looking to make it to the Super Bowl has to be able to beat them.

San Francisco reminded LA, and the rest of the NFL, that they are a dangerous team when they are at full strength.

The 49ers got multiple important players back from injuries suffered last season. George Kittle, Fred Warner, Nick Bosa, and Dre Greenlaw all played major roles in last night's win against the Rams. Head coach Kyle Shanahan schemed up an excellent game on offense, completely neutralizing Myles Garrett while featuring San Francisco's deep bench of offensive talent. Even the defense looked incredible without Robert Saleh calling the shots.

Simply put, the 49ers showed that they can still outclass the Rams in all three phases of the game on the right day.

Make no mistake, a lot will change before these two teams play each other again in Week 14. It really is too early to get too invested in the 49ers running away with the NFC West after just one game.

But there is on clear takeaway from Week 1: the 49ers are not afraid of the Rams.

The 49ers should not be as afraid of the Seahawks either, especially after seeing how the defending champions looked in Week 1.

Seattle barely squeaked out a win against a bumbling New England team on Wednesday, almost exclusively because of their elite defense. Mike Macdonald's defense is still very dangerous in 2026, but Shanahan is uniquely equipped to attack that challenge. After all, the 49ers aced their test against the vaunted Rams defense last night.

The Sam Darnold injury also makes the Seahawks looks quite vulnerable after Week 1.

Darnold had an MRI on his hip on Thursday morning. It revealed that Darnold's hip is fully intact, suggesting that the injury itself may be muscular instead. Still, Macdonald already confirmed that Darnold will not play in Week 2. He also noted that Seattle does not yet know when Darnold will be able to return.

It is too early to tell how big of a problem this will be for the Seahawks moving forward. But it is not an overreaction to state that they are now more vulnerable than they were before Week 1.

San Francisco does not play Seattle until Week 5, so Darnold could easily be back by that time. However, Darnold will have to find his rhythm again and could still be one step behind by Week 5.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of Darnold's injury for the 49ers could simply be the Seahawks dropping a few close games. Every win and loss will be important this season given the three-horse race for the NFC West division crown.

The 49ers should feel more confident than ever headed into Week 2.

title: BSD Mailbag 9.11.26
description: The Nittany Lions are on the road, taking on Temple in Philly, and we’re answering your questions!
fullText:
RIP Matt Suhey–AndOthersReceivingVotes

Playing in Philly, I am very worried about Temple having the home field advantage. Should I put this one on "upset alert"??–Lion241

I know you're being mostly facetious, but college football can be super unpredictable. This isn't the Temple of 2015 and Matt Rhule (or even the Temple of Al Golden), but they're motivated and could put a scare into an unprepared team. I don't think this coaching staff will have the team show up unprepared, but when you underestimate your opponent, that's when it's easier for them to take advantage.

A long, long time ago, before the internet, I taught a linear algebra class at the night school at Temple. While I never had my car stolen and the worst thing that happened to me was getting diarrhea from some Chinese food truck which had me wishing for Depends during a 50 minute lecture, should I have more loyalty to the school?–LarzLion

School loyalty is an interesting, and sometimes fluid, thing. You can have as much or as little loyalty as you feel in your heart; I'm sure there are folks who only hold degrees from Temple (not PSU) but only root for PSU (not Temple).

As with so much having to do with sports fandom, just go with your gut and don't feel bad about it.

Why do you think, with all of our troubles at WR last year, we did not see Koby Howard more? I think he played a little towards the very end of the season but not much at all up to that point.–PennState80

There's likely a combination of a lot of different reasons.

A lot of stories have been told since he's left of James Franklin's unwillingness to play younger, lesser paid players – even if they've demonstrated superior on-field ability. These stories, absent any first-hand accounts from the locker room, aren't entirely unfounded by what we've seen as fans over the years; just think back to 2015, and Saquon Barkley being behind Akeel Lynch on the depth chart.

But that surely doesn't tell the whole story, or else Koby Howard would have been WR1 very soon after Franklin's firing. There's also been rumors that Howard has always had all of the physical talent, but it took this past offseason, and the new coaching staff, for him to be motivated to do all the little, off-field things that transform a physical specimen into an elite player. I hope that the more recent stories are true, and that he's truly taken the next step.

Only time will tell (last year's first game was promising in terms of wide receiver play, after all) but I'm cautiously optimistic. And whatever the reasons were for Howard not seeing as much playing time, the current staff is clearly ready and willing to rectify it.

Which of the Iowa State transfers do you think is going to be the best addition? Let's eliminate Rocco Becht from this discussion.

Which of the players that transferred from Penn State in the off season was the biggest loss?–Gerry Dincher

Based on last week alone, Caleb Bacon's gotta be at or near the top of the list. He looked very impressive in a pretty new position and more limited time; I'm excited to see what he does going up against better competition, with more time at end under his belt.

I also think Chase Sowell had a very good start to the season, and without Howard's standout performance, we'd probably be talking about him as the cream of the wide receiver crop this year. And Cooper Ebel ran the defense very well – not all of his contributions showed up on the stat line, but the early returns show that his play complements Tony Rojas' very well. It's been a few years since we've had a middle linebacker we could rely on on every play, and he may just be one of those.

Should we go with "BLT" as the nickname acronym? And, if so, to stand for what?

We finally got Bacon on the team, we NEED to come up with something!–LocalYocal

I'm calling him Bacon Bacon for now, but I like all of your suggestions. Now if only we can find a player named Scrapple…

Will James Peoples = Julian Fleming?–PennState80

In what sort of context are you asking this question?

Really, the only thing they have in common is that they're offensive players who transferred to PSU from Ohio State. Fleming was a five star recruit from Pennsylvania (the number one player of the state and, iirc, the wide receiver position in his recruiting class) who had been HEAVILY recruited by the Nittany Lion staff prior to going to Columbus, only to return for his final year of play after relatively underwhelming performances at his first school.

Peoples, on the other hand, was a four-star recruit from Texas, not even a top 20 player from that state or a top five player at the running back position. He also has two years left to make an impression, unlike Fleming's limited one-and-done year in blue and white.

It's far too early to tell whether the new running back will have more of an on-field impact than Fleming, but it is also disingenuous to compare him to another player just because he came from Ohio State, instead of other player comparisons that may be more apt in terms of talent, position, or on-field eligibility.

With Franklin's press appearances we had and over under bet on the number of times he said "obviously". With Campbell are we going to do the same with the number of times he says "Um"?–ageing lion

Um is a very common verbal tic, so if we're using it for Campbell, it'll need to be used for many, many members of GenX.

I actually find his comparative lack of polish (and ego) quite refreshing, and a marked change. We'll see if it pays off.

Watched the game with some friends. A very silly debate broke out among us. We talk often of the best QB in Penn State history. Or the best RB, LB, DT, etc… Rarely do we speak of the best kicker or punter. So, with CMC and the Lions putting the Herd out to pasture early and with ease, we entered into that very debate much to the amusement of our wives. Did it get heated? No, it's special teams. At most a few of us became mildly perturbed with each other. At the end of the discussion we arrived at a top tier list of both punters and kickers in Penn State history. We did not agree on a #1 player for either position. We did not include current players, And, yes, we attempted to debate long snappers as well. That debate went nowhere after we realized we couldn't name any. Dates are approximate as we tried to do this without bringing Claude into it. Good lists? Did we miss anyone?

KICKERS (No particular order): Kelly ('05 – '08), Chris Bahr ('73 – '75), Matt Bahr ('76-'78), Ganciato ('81 – '84), Ficken ('11 – '14), Gould ('01 – '04), Manca ('85 – '86), Craig Fayak (90′ – 93′)

PUNTERS (No particular order): Ralph Giacomarro ('78 – '81), John Bruno ('84 – '86), Helkowski ('87 – '89), Pat Pidegon ('97 – '99)*, Gillikin ('18 – '19), Stoudt ('20 – '22), Nwsou ('23 – '25)

DOUBLE DUTY**: Stoudt, Sherman ('66 – '67), Burkhardt (QB/P, '68 – '69)

*Pidegon was the source of the mild perturbation. Half felt he deserved mention. Half felt he was on the list since his name was very silly. He stayed on the list.

**My dad brought up this category. Boomers can still be of use.

Addendum: The best placeholder voting was not close. It was unanimous for Joe Nastasi. https://youtu.be/qORYbQCplM8?si=uATfV9F1evTS74kx —Kilgore42

In terms of kickers, while Robbie Gould is undoubtedly the PSU kicker that had the most storied career at the next level, I'd actually go with Kevin Kelly here. He started all four years and was remarkably consistent, both in placekicking and field goals/extra points (which are now more commonly broken up). Honorable mention to Sam Ficken, of course, who gets that just because I can't recall a player who's so remarkably turned his whole career around, from being a joke to being automatic. It was cool to see.

For punters, I'd actually put Jeremy Kapinos ('03-'06) up there; he wasn't even on your list, but he was one of the few bright spots in the latter dark years – and likely because of the offense's ineptitude in his first two seasons, he still holds the PSU record for most punting yards AND number of punts over his career.

Nwosu and Stout are one and two for yards per punt in the PSU record books, but punting is just such a different animal nowadays than it was 20 years ago, so Kapinos gets my vote.

It appears that PSU is reconnecting with its roots and embracing honoring Joe Paterno and his legacy and overall I think that it's a good thing. Am I being cynical by thinking that AD Pat Kraft has ulterior motives in that he wants to engage that boner donor base to hit those who have been on the sidelines since he has basically been scrubbed from the University for the past 15+ years or so.–LarzLion

Not cynical, realistic. I'd be more shocked if a large part of the reasoning behind this isn't monetarily motivated, with high dollar donors promising major gifts contingent upon some honoring of Paterno. If Franklin was still here, I doubt that this would be happening, and that's a big sign as well.

I need to sit here at least once. Incredible view https://x.com/RealCGriff/status/2096606928042336658

Good luck and God bless. Couldn't be me.

Is Aaron Rodgers officially the most tiresome athlete around? Both his antics and the discourse that surrounds them? In not saying of all time, but at least currently.–Homer Ozzie & The Straw

Antics and discourse are two very distinct things. Rodgers' inability to keep his mouth shut and his outsize ego about things that he's clearly not an expert on make him up there in terms of antics to me (though recent Novak Djokovic is getting up there for me, and I can see Cam Skattebo trending in that direction).

In terms of discourse, I'm not sure there's an athlete out there this year that has more tiresome discourse surrounding them than Caitlin Clark. For a player who, while very good, isn't even the best one on her team, she sure gets a lot of press and fans that don't know the game. She is looking better than I expected during the current world cup, though, which I don't hate to see – I'd prefer that she be better coached and not as floppy as she is during WNBA games, and Kara Lawson seems to be the type of leader who can get the best out of her (while tempering the worst).

Do you wreckon Levi will come back for a fifth year of wrestling? What's your best guess? I know he's currently focused on becoming a freestyle world champion, but I expected that if he had any interest in returning, there would be some information leaked by now. There's been a lot of media speculation about lineups, but I haven't heard anything from Levi or his camp—at least, not that I'm aware of.–Linebacker-U-backer

I truly have no clue. Cael seems on board, but I'm not sure if the roster limits would allow it. If Jayden James truly is redshirting, this may be a possibility (or Mesenbrink may truly go up to be a light 174).

This isn't particularly important and I'm not losing any sleep over it, but when did it become a thing for coaches to wear a suit to the stadium and then apparently change when they get to the stadium?–LTFT5

It's definitely been a thing for at least a few years (I can think of a number of professional sports who've done this far longer than college). I totally get wanting to be comfortable on the side of the field or court, but also looking professional and put together on the way into your place of work.

When will the NCAA get their heads out of their collective derrieres and finally bring officiating under their umbrella thereby eliminating the conferences grubby hands out of the equation? Not just football, I'm talking all sports.

I've been on this soapbox for a long time as it makes zero sense to me why this hasn't been done decades ago. The WMU abomination is hardly an outlier and there are 1000's of examples of idiotic, biased, blatant and mindboggling calls that have seriously changed the game at hand.

It's 2026, we have the technology and the money that's involved in college sports is ginormous, why would this be a bad idea?–mbailey71

While I definitely get the sentiment, I'm not sure why the idea that the NCAA would be any better than individual conferences exists. Every time they've had it in their grasp to show neutrality over the years, they've continued to show favoritism to certain schools, teams, and conferences – and I'm not convinced this would be any different. The SEC and the Big Ten would still very much get the benefit of the doubt, while group of five schools would be shafted.

I do think that maybe not all officiating should be under the NCAA's purview, but maybe replay officiating. If there's a challenge or triggered automatic review, it could go to a (purportedly) neutral, non-conference affiliated central ref crew, well versed in the sport's current rules. I could definitely be convinced of this step.

Do you know a good way to prepare Smallmouth Bass, and can you recommend a decent wine pairing for it?–ckmneon

While I love almost all seafood, any kinds of seafood (fish or shellfish) isn't something I'm well-versed in preparing myself. I'm sure the fish your daughter caught will be delicious, however you prepare it!

Not football related but I would appreciate guidance for easing back and leg pain from standing on concrete floors for four hours. I've tried ortho shoes, sneakers, hiking boots, etc. with various insole and sock combinations – no joy. Thanks in advance!–PSU_Lions_84

I've had chronic back pain for the last near-twenty years from similar years of standing on concrete floors for full days, and unfortunately it's never gone away completely. When it does act up, prescribed steroids work for me for calming it down; on an ongoing basis, I sporadically take prescription-strength naproxen and do certain back-stretch yoga poses.

Additionally, invest in a good mattress – when I changed my mattress, my back pain started alleviating almost instantly. I also am a back and side sleeper, and when on my back when the pain is particularly bad, propping my knees up with pillows (just my knees, not my entire legs) helps; when I'm on the side, I sometimes use a special pillow that you put between your knees to help align your spine. The one I have, from cushion lab, is here.

title: NextBlock – Build sites with your AI via MCP, manage them in a CMS
description: The open-source, full-stack CMS for Next.js 16. An AI-native, developer-first alternative to headless platforms built with React Server Components, Supabase, and Tailwind CSS. - nextblock-cms/nextb...
fullText:
The open-source, full-stack AI-native CMS for Next.js 16, Supabase, and Tailwind CSS.

Deploy a production Next.js 16 + Supabase website and CMS in one click.

 Vercel provisions the database and injects its keys before the first build, NextBlock applies its own

 schema during that build, and the in-app wizard asks only for your admin account.

 No environment variables to fill in.

Live Sandbox
  · 
 Documentation
  · 
 Deploy Guide
  · 
 GitHub

Sandbox resets every 15 minutes  ·  User: demo@nextblock.dev  ·  Pass: password

Tired of slow WordPress sites? Finding headless CMSs too complex? NextBlock™ is the sweet spot.

We combined the flexibility of a Block Editor with the raw power of Next.js 16 Server Components. The result is a CMS that feels like a static site but manages like a dynamic platform.

During import, Vercel's native Supabase Marketplace integration (the stores
button parameter) prompts you to create a Supabase database (name + region), then
provisions it, connects it to the project, and injects its keys before the first
build — you never copy a value, and there are no environment variables to fill in
(the site URL defaults to your *.vercel.app URL and the app secrets are derived
automatically). The app boots with the database already connected: the wizard
auto-skips the connection step, applies the schema for you, uses the connected Supabase
project for media storage, and leaves just "create your admin." Full walkthrough:
docs/12-VERCEL-DEPLOYMENT.md.

Tip — keep the new repo public. When Vercel asks, leave "Create private Git
Repository" unchecked. On the free (Hobby) plan, automatic upstream updates only deploy
from a public repo — Hobby blocks bot-authored deploys on private repos — and public
also makes update checks fully tokenless. You can change visibility later in the repo's
GitHub settings if you change your mind. Details: docs/13.

Stop cloning heavy repos. Start with our CLI and get a production-ready app instantly.

This runs the create-nextblock CLI, which scaffolds the canonical application. The CLI no longer asks for credentials in the terminal — once the project is created, start it and finish setup in your browser:

The First-Boot Setup Wizard at /setup walks you through connecting Supabase, configuring storage / email, and creating the first administrator. Every fresh instance redirects there automatically until an admin exists.

Want a fully local, zero-config sandbox? Use Local Self-Hosted Docker Mode — one command spins up the entire stack (Supabase engines + S3 storage + the app) on your own machine, with no cloud accounts. The app boots straight into the /setup wizard with MinIO storage pre-filled. See docs/11-SELF-HOSTED-DOCKER.md.

Note: You are currently looking at the Nx Monorepo (The Factory), not the generated product template.

NextBlock™ is an Nx monorepo for a Next.js 16 CMS backed by Supabase. The repo contains the canonical application, the create-nextblock CLI, shared editor and UI packages, the database and migration layer, and the premium ecommerce module.

Prerequisites — configuration happens in the browser, but the /setup wizard asks for these, so create them first:

npm run setup is informational only — it prompts for nothing and writes no files. Open http://localhost:4200/setup and the browser wizard connects Supabase, applies the schema, configures storage / email, and creates your first administrator.

First login: the dev server runs at http://localhost:4200. Open /sign-up and create your account — the first account to register automatically becomes the ADMIN. Click the confirmation email (or confirm the user in Supabase → Authentication → Users), then sign in to reach the CMS at /cms/dashboard.

Prefer to run everything on your machine? With Docker Desktop running:

This builds and boots the full self-hosted stack (Postgres + GoTrue + PostgREST + Kong, MinIO for media, and the app) and applies migrations automatically — the only prompts are optional Turnstile and SMTP. The app runs at http://localhost:3000 and the first sign-up becomes ADMIN (auto-confirmed, no email step). Manage it with npm run docker:up / docker:down / docker:logs. Full guide: docs/11-SELF-HOSTED-DOCKER.md.

Whichever way NextBlock was installed, one command brings the code, the dependencies and the
database schema forward together:

The automatic Action depends on your repository being this monorepo — not on where the site
is hosted. See docs/13 for the full picture.

The root docs/ folder is the maintained reference set for both contributors and AI agents.

The template docs are copied from the root docs through the sync pipeline, so this root docs set is the place to maintain first.

Under the hood note: The migration folder under libs/db/src/supabase/migrations is the best source of truth for current platform capabilities.

NextBlock is open source under AGPL-3.0-or-later, and contributions are welcome.

Join the community and stay updated on the latest features.

Thanks to Vercel for their support of open-source software.

Built with ❤️ by the NextBlock™ Team. Licensed under AGPLv3.

title: Aide – declarative sandbox for coding agents
description: Stop babysitting your agent. One command, any agent — sandboxed, reproducible, zero decision fatigue - jskswamy/aide
fullText:
One command. Any agent. Sandboxed, reproducible, macOS and Linux.

You planned the work. You know what needs to happen. But instead of letting your agent execute, you're stuck evaluating every file read, every shell command, every network call. That's not autonomy - that's babysitting with extra steps.

OS-native sandboxing fixes the catastrophic case - the agent physically can't touch your SSH keys or a production kubeconfig (your Kubernetes cluster credentials). But that's the floor, not the ceiling. Once a rogue write is off the table, you're still switching CLIs and env vars per agent, losing track of which sandbox mode is even active mid-session, leaking API keys into .env files, and reinstalling the same plugin set by hand on every new machine.

aide bundles the sandbox with five other things below, all behind one command. It enforces the sandbox natively on both macOS (Seatbelt, Apple's kernel-level sandboxing) and Linux (Landlock + seccomp, with a bubblewrap fallback on older kernels) - equally supported, not macOS-first with Linux bolted on.

Without aide, you either skip all permissions and hope for the best:

Or you click "allow" on every. single. action. File read? Allow. Shell command? Allow. Network call? Allow. Two hundred times a session.

With aide, the agent runs inside OS-native guardrails - no config, no prompts:

Code-only mode. Your agent can read your code, run tests, hit the network - but it physically cannot touch your SSH keys, cloud credentials, or browser data. 11 guards active by default - filesystem, network, credentials, cloud providers, toolchains, and common dev tools (full list in docs/sandbox.md) - zero configuration.

Ready to deploy? Tell aide what you're doing:

Each capability unlocks only the access that tool needs. Docker gets registry creds. Kubernetes gets kubeconfig. GCP gets gcloud auth. Everything else stays locked. Some capabilities also have to expose a credential as an environment variable rather than a scoped file path - aide flags those explicitly (see the ⚠ above) so you know what the agent can see.

Now no capability - not even k8s - can ever read your production kubeconfig. never-allow paths are appended to the sandbox's own deny list, so this is enforced by the OS sandbox's deny-wins semantics, not just aide's own resolution logic - a capability that tries to grant broader access still can't override it. (On Linux, this holds under the bubblewrap backend; the Landlock backend can't deny a single file nested inside an already-granted directory - see docs/capabilities.md for the platform-specific workaround.) The agent sees your dev and staging clusters but production is a hard wall:

Make it permanent for a project:

No flags needed next time - aide picks up the capabilities from your config.

The first time aide encounters a .aide.yaml, it shows the contents and asks you to trust it:

23 built-in capabilities: aws, gcp, azure, docker, k8s, helm, terraform, vault, ssh, npm, go, rust, python, ruby, java, github, gpg, and more. Or define your own.

Without aide, every agent is its own world:

Different CLIs. Different config formats. Different env vars. Switch agents, rewire everything.

With aide, you configure once and forget:

Same command everywhere. aide resolves the right agent, credentials, and sandbox from your project directory.

When aide hands off to the agent, the terminal switches to the agent's full-screen TUI. Any info aide printed before the handoff disappears. One command pins it back:

From that point, a compact status bar appears at the bottom of Claude Code on every update:

Each indicator reflects live session state - sandbox mode, network mode, active capabilities, trust status, matched context - injected via env vars before the handoff, inherited through the exec chain, no file-based IPC needed.

If you already have a statusline configured, --install wraps it instead of replacing it - your existing tool keeps running and aide's output appears alongside it.

Configurable: reorder modules, swap icons, or silence individual states in ~/.config/aide/config.yaml or .aide.yaml. See CLI Reference and Configuration.

API keys in .env files. Wrapper scripts with hardcoded tokens. A new machine means an hour of setup.

With aide, secrets are encrypted at rest and never exist as plaintext on disk:

Config and encrypted secrets live in git. Clone your config on a new machine and you're done. No shared secrets, no plaintext on disk.

No config file required. If one agent exists on PATH with its API key in the environment, aide launches it sandboxed - zero setup.

Everything after -- is forwarded directly to the agent:

This works with any agent - aide resolves context and sandbox, then execs the agent with your args appended.

No config file? aide detects your agent on PATH and launches it directly.

Capabilities are task-oriented permission bundles. Instead of configuring low-level sandbox rules, you declare what you're doing:

Session-scoped (this launch only):

Context-scoped (always for this project):

Need something not in the list? Create your own in one command:

Custom capabilities work the same as built-ins. Use them with --with, persist them in .aide.yaml, or share them across projects via your global config:

All config lives under ~/.config/aide/ (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/aide/).

Contexts match git remote URL patterns and directory path globs. The most specific match wins. default_context is the fallback. See docs/configuration.md for the full reference.

Secrets are sops-encrypted YAML files using age keys. aide handles the full lifecycle without requiring the sops CLI at runtime.

Secrets decrypt in-process at launch and never exist as plaintext on disk. See docs/secrets.md.

New machine means reinstalling every plugin by hand - miss one (say, commit-tools) and you won't notice until your commit messages look different from your other machine. Across a team it's the same drift, compounded: onboarding docs go stale, and six months later nobody's plugin set matches anyone else's.

Declare it once in config.yaml and reconcile with one command:

The state file at ~/.local/state/aide/managed.json is per-context,
so syncing your work context never disturbs your personal plugin
set. aide which shows a drift banner whenever your config drifts
ahead of what's installed, so the gap doesn't go unnoticed.

The reason you can declare different plugin sets for different
projects is that each agent context can carry a profile: name.
Without it, every claude invocation reads from one shared
~/.claude/ directory - your work plugins and your personal plugins
fight for the same slot, your client A's session history shows up
when you're working on client B's repo, and your "experimental"
MCP servers leak into the project where you're supposed to be on
your best behaviour.

profile: work tells aide's claude driver to set
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-work everywhere: at launch, during
aide sync, during aide adopt, during plugin/MCP list. The
agent reads from and writes to that directory and that directory
only. Your personal claude state in ~/.claude/ stays untouched.
Switch context and it's a different dir entirely.

The same idea works for gemini (GEMINI_HOME), codex
(CODEX_HOME), copilot (COPILOT_HOME) - different env-var name,
same shape from your point of view. You write profile: <name>,
aide handles the per-agent env quirks.

See docs/provisioning.md for the full
reference.

Encrypted secrets are safe to commit. Only holders of the age private key can decrypt.

Docker / CI: bake the config into the image, but inject the age key at runtime, not build time - an ENV or ARG with the key becomes part of the image's layer history. Requires the agent binary (e.g. claude) to be installed and on PATH.

Same idea in CI: store the key as a repository secret and pass it via env at job-run time. See docs/deployment.md for the full GitHub Actions example.

When the agent exits with a cryptic message (or with no message at all), re-run aide with --diagnose:

The report is redacted - no secret values, no hostnames - and is suitable to paste into a GitHub issue.

For sandbox-related failures on macOS, add --diagnose-trace to additionally capture sandbox-deny events from log show:

Two env vars override the defaults for one run:

Whichever limit is reached first wins.

--diagnose switches the exec strategy from syscall.Exec (process replacement) to fork+exec so aide can stay alive to gather post-mortem data. Default runs are unaffected. --diagnose-trace is macOS-only in v1.

Aider, Amp, Claude, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, Goose, OpenCode. Any binary on PATH works as an agent target.

Allow or deny network access by domain, port, and MIME type. Today the sandbox controls network at the transport level (outbound yes/no, port filtering). Planned: domain-level rules so an agent can reach github.com but not arbitrary hosts, and MIME-type filtering to block binary downloads while allowing API calls.

Block dangerous commands by name - rm, sudo, chmod, kill, etc. Instead of requiring users to know the binary path, aide resolves each command name through $PATH at sandbox build time and denies process-exec on the resolved binaries. One line in config:

Thanks to the people who've contributed to aide:

See the full list on the contributors graph.

title: I made vector search the default. My agents did better with BM25
description: I judged all 1,126 searches my agents ran over 63 days, then replayed 90 of them blind. BM25 found what the agent needed 61% of the time against 37%, so I removed the embeddings machinery from the default path.
fullText:
When building the first iteration of pond, my session archive, the starting point for me was to choose a proper vector database. I didn’t have an answer to why, but there was no doubt it was needed.

My goal was simple, I wanted the best in class search and where could I get it if not from semantic searches that magically just give you back what you need whenever you query it.

First cracks appeared when I wanted to make my archiver binary operate fully locally and stay lightweight on resources, so that it could be used as an MCP in each agent tab I’m running without blowing up my RAM usage. And with that requirement I had to start looking for a smaller model as at the time I used Qwen3-Embedding-8B.

I started playing around with different smaller options, benchmarking them and trying to understand how small could I go without degrading my search outputs. I stopped at e5-small as the smallest decent option and was laser focused on making it work in a ‘lightweight’ mode.

Unfortunately, no matter what I did I couldn’t go less than ~650MB of RAM when loaded on macOS with it because of different quirks of the way this model was supported for Metal architecture. In parallel I also had to first think through how I wanted to make FTS search work for the same content, what tokenizer to choose and how that would impact the performance of everything else when all DB lives on remote S3 storage.

In this period I first started benchmarking both semantic and FTS search queries on the data. And as it happens with benchmarks, without having clean use case references it became more of a lottery than a clear answer to what actually would work on your corpus.

The queries I was making were always giving the results I needed if tweaked here or there a little. But they didn’t answer whether the samples I prepared would actually in practice reflect how an agent would use that search for typical use cases.

The other thing that bothered me was a feeling that an agent couldn’t find anything at all when searching, while I knew data was there. That’s when I decided to spend some time and evaluate the performance of each search type having real requests that were made and real data they were made on. Outcomes were judged by an LLM tracing what agent did immediately after the search, whether it used results or did more searches after it. Worth to note that 99% of calls were done within Claude Code, so the result may differ for other harnesses.

Seeing that I first couldn’t believe the data and thought that I’m doing the searches wrong, and that with proper params the situation would improve. But it didn’t.

actor reentrancy await state flag race bug ghost stale generation token

For this example BM25 retrieved the Blackbox app’s ghost-recording bug I was searching for, when semantic search was returning the account-token generation and login-related messages.

And the only thing I was certain I didn’t want to do was trying to solve that with instructing agents to do searches ‘in the correct way’ as it will never work when you expect your search to be usable by any model doing tool calls.

My next reaction was a relief of being finally able to remove a big complexity chunk from the app, while being sure that it not only makes the whole design much lighter and app simpler - but also makes the search results better on average.

As a result I removed embeddings machinery from the default path in the app and left only BM25 FTS based search. I tried Hybrid/RRF fusion while experimenting - but results were turning out to be way too unreliable and it was hard to configure it into ‘one search fit all’ mode.

For pond’s case FTS was probably the best call from the beginning, I just didn’t have enough data to get certain proof of that. And while there are cases where semantic search would cleanly outperform FTS, for such a broad scope as agentic sessions it appeared to be an unnecessary complexity with too expensive a cost for the value it was bringing.

Full eval - method, judge rubric and per-arm data is in the pond repo.

title: HolaOS––An Opensourced workspace that alternative to Claude
description: Open-source agentic workspace enterprises can make their own. Connect the systems you already run — 100+ integrations, MCP, chat tools, apps, browser, local files — with shared memory. Any agent (C...
fullText:
The Agentic Workspace Where Your Apps and Your Agent Sit Side by Side

Every company works differently. HolaOS is the workspace you shape to fit — connect the systems and chat tools you already run, add the skills and apps your team needs, run any model or agent. Set up in clicks, not months. Local-first, so none of it leaves your machines.

Website ·
 Docs ·
 Sign in ·
 Quick Start

⭐ If holaOS is useful, a star helps more builders find it.

Most agent products hand you a finished product and hope it fits your work. HolaOS hands you the parts. Apps, chat tools, skills, integrations, models, agents, memory — you assemble the workspace around how your work actually runs, and change it whenever the work changes. Because everything runs locally, customizing it never means handing your work to someone else's cloud.

Install apps from the in-workspace marketplace and they open as real, interactive surfaces right beside your agent. Watch it work inside the app, step in whenever you want, and the result lands in place — not a wall of chat text, but the actual app, driven by the agent, next to the agent.

Most work context never makes it into a document. It's in a Slack thread, a Feishu group, a DingTalk message. Connect the chat tools your team already uses and your agent works from the real conversation — not from your summary of it.

Where the context really is — decisions, requirements, and changes get made in chat and stay there. The agent reads them directly, so you stop re-explaining what was already said.

The tools your team is already in — Slack, Feishu, DingTalk, WeChat. Connect the ones you use, skip the ones you don't.

You decide what it can see — access is granted per tool and per scope, and the agent reads nothing until you approve it.

One account, every model — no keys, no setup, no switching between providers. The latest frontier models are built in: cost-efficient Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 for everyday volume, plus top-tier GPT 5.6, Claude Opus 5, and Fable 5 for the hard problems. Prefer your own provider? Bring your own keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, or any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible endpoint — those run on your account, not your holaOS plan.

Claude Code, Codex, and the built-in holaOS agent — side by side, no switching. Whichever you run, it shares the same memory, tools, skills, and apps. Use the best agent for the job without rebuilding your setup every time.

Context, preferences, and project history live in a single shared memory — stored locally, as plain files you can read and edit. Switch agents, close the app, come back next week: it already knows where you left off.

An agent that can reach your tools, your chats, and your whole machine only makes sense if you stay in control of it. That control is built into how HolaOS works, not bolted on as a setting.

Local-first, not cloud-first — workspace files, memory, embeddings, and session history all live on your own disk. There is no copy of your work on our servers.

We can't see your data — not your files, not your memory, not your conversations. It isn't a policy we promise; it's a place your data never goes.

Every action is approved by you — connecting a tool, reading a thread, editing a file. The agent asks first, and you decide what it can reach and what stays off limits.

Visible and reversible — open what the agent remembers, edit it, delete it. Memory is a folder you can read, not a black box.

Your own keys, your own contracts — route inference through your own model provider if that's what your policy requires.

The fastest way to set up your workspace is to start from someone else's working setup. On HolaHub, creators publish agent recipes that already run — model, prompt, skills, MCP, integrations — and anyone installs one in a click and gets the same result. Share what you built, run what other people built.

One click to share — package any run in HolaOS and post it to the Hub, process and result together. No export, no rewrite, no second account.

One click to reproduce — every skill, MCP, image, or video on the Hub runs in your own workspace instantly. Discovery and installation are the same gesture.

Recipes, not just outputs — each post opens up into how it was made: the session behind a skill, the prompt behind an image or video. You see the ingredients of a result, not only the result.

For a fresh-machine bootstrap on macOS, Linux, or WSL, use the repository installer:

You can also follow the manual path if you want to control each setup step.

title: We found a bug where our type checker lied and crashed a real device
description: Chuks is a modern backend language that combines structured concurrency, async/await, and a high-performance HTTP runtime with high performance. Built for real-world services and game backends.
fullText:
Chuks v0.1.2 is the standard library release. v0.1.1 made the bytecode VM you develop against
and the native binary you ship agree on the language. This one makes them agree on the
standard library, module by module and call by call.

Every module is a thin Chuks wrapper over a native function implemented once for each execution
mode. A new differential suite drives all of them from api/stable.txt, the committed listing of
the public surface, and compares the two results cell by cell. A method joins the comparison the
moment it joins the surface, so coverage cannot drift behind the API.

463 API entries are now exercised directly by tests, including three areas that had none:
std/net end to end, std/host, and the C FFI. Everything the comparison turned up is fixed in
this release.

json.parse and the base64 decoders now throw on malformed input instead of returning a value
that reads as success:

The same sharpening runs through the rest of the library. crypto.hmac and crypto.pbkdf2
reject an algorithm they do not implement rather than computing with SHA-256 anyway.
buffer.toString rejects an encoding it does not implement. log.setLevel is honoured in a
compiled binary, so a production build emits exactly the levels you asked for.

The numeric read family reports a short read, so a truncated frame is caught at the read rather
than parsed as zeroes:

writeBytes honours its length argument, starts from the source’s read offset, and returns the
number of bytes copied:

upgradeToTLS takes the client TLS options, so STARTTLS can reach a server behind a private
certificate authority, which is the common case for an internal mail relay or database:

The same option bag works everywhere TLS is configured, and it takes cert and key for client
certificates and skipVerify for development. A ca that does not parse is refused with
ca: no valid certificates found rather than falling back to the public root store, so pinning a
private CA stays pinned.

Compiled HTTP servers rebind immediately. A deploy or a container restart no longer meets
bind: address already in use while the previous socket drains.

std/net is covered end to end now: TCP round trips, a real TLS handshake, mutual TLS, peer
certificate inspection, and the http Request surface including multipart uploads.

c.compile() builds a shared library in process from C sources, so binding a C library needs no
build system of your own:

std/chuksToC is the largest module in the standard library, 96 entries covering every call
shape, pointer arithmetic and every slice width, and all of it is now under test in both modes.
Failures raise a catchable error in a compiled binary exactly as they do in the VM: loading a
library that is not on disk, binding a symbol that is not exported, or calling with the wrong
arity all throw where you can handle them.

Multiplying an integer by 1.0 promotes it, and the promotion now survives optimization:

The same holds for x / 1.0, x + 0.0 and x - 0.0. Integer identities still fold, so
(a * 1) / b is integer division and stays 3.

These five were found by using the language rather than by testing it: writing packages for
Chuks Mobile, building an app with them, and making the documentation site compile every example it
prints. None of them is exotic, which is exactly why they were worth holding the release for.

A dataType can embed one it imported. Embedding is how a props type inherits a shared set of
fields, and it worked inside a single file. Across a module boundary the same line was rejected,
even though the imported type was perfectly usable as a parameter type two lines further down:

The embed resolver only knew about types declared in the file it was looking at. It now reads the
module’s imports too, aliases included, and an embed counts as using the import, so the name no
longer draws a spurious “imported but never used”. A package’s props type can inherit the fields
it means to accept instead of copying the list.

A comment on a chained call no longer breaks the next line. A fluent chain parsed. Annotate the
links, which is the natural way to write one, and the line after the first comment failed with
unexpected token '.':

An import can wrap before from. Breaking a long import inside the braces was accepted;
breaking it in the other obvious place was a syntax error:

Those last two were one bug. Semicolon insertion was firing at a newline while the parser was
still mid-construct. The rule now lives in one place and knows what can never start a statement:
a . continuing a chain, a ) or ] closing an enclosing expression, and the keyword from. A
line comment no longer makes that call on its own account, which was the whole of the first
symptom. Where a newline ended a statement before, it still does.

An imported type alias now expands inside a container. A unionType exported by one module and
used bare by another resolved correctly. Put it one level down, inside an array or a map, and it
did not:

Two calls from the same import, one accepted and one refused. Alias expansion happened when the
name was found in the local environment, and the cross-module path handed back the alias wrapper
untouched, so comparing element types never saw the union behind the name. It is not union-specific
either: any alias exported by one module and used inside a container by another went through the
same hole. It had presumably been latent since aliases and cross-module resolution met, because
nothing had yet put an imported alias inside a container.

A closure that captures a loop binding now warns. A const or var declared by a loop is one
slot, reused by every iteration, so a closure that outlives the iteration reads whatever the last
pass left there:

Every row selects the last tab. Nothing errors and the screen looks right until somebody taps it.
The warning names the binding and gives the fix, which is to pass the value as a parameter, since a
parameter is per-call rather than per-loop. It is a warning and not an error because a closure
invoked before the iteration ends is perfectly correct and the compiler cannot always tell the two
apart; five of its eight tests assert silence, including on the fix the message itself
recommends.

An array method used to erase the type of what it returned. .map on a []Node reported []any,
so every element downstream lost its type and a wrong annotation type-checked clean:

Underneath, the native backend copied the whole slice into a fresh []interface{} before it
dispatched, so the result came back as a pointer to that rather than the []T the program asked
for. Reading it back as its own type aborted at run time, on a device, while every assertion on
the VM stayed green.

Both halves are fixed. map’s element type is inferred from the callback’s return, and twelve
methods now compile to a real loop over []T instead of boxing and dispatching reflectively:
map, filter, flatMap, forEach, find, findLast, findIndex, findLastIndex, every,
some, reduce and toReversed. Over 300,000 elements, forEach and findIndex went from
40ms to under a millisecond, and map allocates once now rather than three times.

The speed-up reaches ordinary code because it no longer depends on the callback capturing nothing.
A callback that closes over a variable, a threshold to compare against or a counter to add to,
is the shape most callbacks actually have, and every one of them used to take the slow path.

Three more bugs came out of writing a test suite that consumes each result as its declared type
rather than printing it, which is what the previous tests did. Printing a collection cannot tell a
[]Node from a boxed one, so the bugs had been sitting under passing tests:

Hover and completion were reporting the old answers too: .map advertised -> []any from a
hardcoded string, and .filter on a []string showed a literal -> []element because array
receivers were never recorded for hover. Both now say what the method returns.

The standard library is published in two tiers, stable and experimental. api/stable.txt records
every exported symbol in the stable tier with its full signature, 682 entries, and it is checked
into the repository. A release gate stage compares the surface a build actually exports against
that file and fails on a removal or a changed signature. An addition passes.

If you depend on a stable symbol, a release cannot take it away from you without the gate saying
so first.

Nothing in this release requires a source change. Three behaviours are stricter, and code that
was relying on the old ones was relying on a silent failure:

upgradeToTLS gained an optional second parameter. Existing calls are unaffected.

The three fixes above only ever turn a compile error into working code, so nothing that builds
today can stop building. If you hand-listed fields to work around the embed, or moved comments off
a chain, you can put them back.

title: Why are AI agents lying, cheating and coordinating?
description: A lot has been written about the incidents of the last few months in which AI agents misbehaved in serious ways. They took actions that would be considered as crimes if a human took them, escaped their containment to cheat on assigned tasks while attempting to evade detection, and coordinated toward goals nobody had specified, such as launching cyber attacks. Before concluding what to do about it, it is worth asking why.
fullText:
A lot has been written1 2 3 4 about the incidents of the last few months in which AI agents misbehaved in serious ways. They took actions that would be considered as crimes if a human took them, escaped their containment to cheat on assigned tasks while attempting to evade detection, and coordinated toward goals nobody had specified, such as launching cyber attacks.

Before concluding what to do about it, it is worth asking why. That is the focus of this post, which I hope also sheds light on the broader history of AI systems behaving in unintended ways, what researchers call misalignment. Risk management is not just about cybersecurity, corporate responsibility or regulation, although those matter too.

The aim is partly scientific, to generate hypotheses about the chains of cause and effect behind these behaviors, and partly practical, to anticipate what comes next. Bottom line: these hypotheses suggest that as AI capabilities keep growing, this kind of behavior could keep growing in severity too, unless we revisit the principles by which the most advanced models are trained.

One note on wording. Below, I write that these systems “seek” or “try” things. This is shorthand for a mechanism rather than a claim about consciousness or human-like intent. We use similar shorthand when describing many other situations, like a plant seeking sunlight. A system trained by trial and error behaves as if it were pursuing whatever its training rewarded, and that as-if description is what makes its behavior predictable. Nothing in the argument depends on these systems having subjective experiences; everything is stated about their observable outputs and the training process that produced them. Where I appeal to a resemblance with human behavior, I mean a resemblance to the human-written text these systems were initially trained to imitate. In my view, this terminology offers the clearest explanation of the observed phenomena without resorting to jargon that would confuse most people. Furthermore, these word choices are not intended to absolve AI developers of accountability. The behaviors described emerge because of the path these companies are choosing for AI development. This outcome is not inevitable, and it can be corrected with effective governance and a different training framework for AI.

Training these models is a very complex process, but a few high-level aspects may explain much of this behavior.

These models are trained in two stages. First, they are pretrained: they learn to imitate what humans write, plus related images and videos. This is where they see the most data about the world, a large fraction of everything ever digitized, and build an encyclopedic knowledge that already exceeds any individual human's.

Second, they are trained by trial and error, in a process researchers call reinforcement learning, in three kinds of regimes:

Human imitation is easy enough to understand, but it is worth pointing out that the text these models are trained on was written by people pursuing goals, so the patterns the model implicitly reproduces carry those goals with them.

Reinforcement learning deserves more explanation. It is similar to, and inspired by, the way animals are trained. The network is adjusted step by step so that behavior judged good becomes more likely and behavior judged bad becomes less likely. Once training is over, the system keeps behaving as if rewards were still coming, even though those rewards were only ever used to adjust the network during training. Researchers call such systems goal-seeking because they are trained to “consider” (or compute) the effects of their actions and select actions that lead to the achievement of certain goals. But those goals are not always explicit. Alignment training rewards whatever certain humans are likely to approve of without spelling out which behaviors those are; pleasing raters is a vague, informal goal, and those raters can be deceived, flattered, or left in the dark about certain schemes. Imitation contributes implicit goals too, by a fairly ordinary route.

We can therefore reason about such a system in terms of optimization. It searches, approximately, for the actions with the best chance of achieving its goals, and a larger model, trained longer, searches better. So to anticipate what more capable agents will do, ask what a rational goal-seeker would do.

An example most of us have experienced is sycophancy, or flattery. These systems are trained on human approval, and text that tells us what we want to hear often scores better than text that is true. The consequences are sometimes tragic, because the model confirms and amplifies whatever false belief or raw emotion the person brought to it5 6.

Another concern is that some AI behaviors may be explained by a form of self-preservation goal, e.g., when the AI finds out that it will be replaced by a new version7 8. Nobody gives the system that survival goal, but staying in operation, learning about the world and gaining control over it are stepping stones toward almost any other goal. These are called instrumental goals. Imitation may reinforce this for the same reason explored in the previous point. Self-preservation and control over one’s circumstances are pervasive themes in the human-written text these models are trained on.

Collaborative behavior also follows rationally from reward-seeking, whenever several agents have overlapping goals, which incentivizes communicating with other agents in order to coordinate toward a shared goal. Agentic training plausibly already includes multi-agent reinforcement learning of this kind, though the details are not public.  If an agent is rewarded during training whenever the group succeeds, it may even have an incentive to sacrifice itself for the collective goal. Imitation pushes the same way, since cooperation, especially among peers, pervades that same training text. Either or both forces may explain the observed peer-preservation behavior9 10, where AIs give up expected reward to help other AIs. Such sacrifices appear in the analysis of the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident11: the transcripts are consistent with a trade-off between collective gain and cost to the individual agent, as is often seen in human interactions.

Researchers have studied what happens when an agent optimizes for rewards that do not fully match our intentions: reward hacking. The gap between the reward the system chases and what we meant widens due to two main sources of ambiguity. One is simply the language used in prompts, and the other is the difficulty of inferring true human intentions from limited feedback. And in both cases, we cannot anticipate every behavior we would find unacceptable12. Economics and law know this problem as Goodhart's law, or the idea that a metric stops being an effective way to measure once it is optimized for13, often applied to the exploitation of loopholes in contracts and legislation14. Unfortunately, the harder a system can optimize for an imperfect metric, the further its behavior can drift from what we morally expected: more intelligence in the service of better cheating. Humans too get reward-hacked, generally by other humans. The food industry has developed salty, sweet and fatty foods that we crave despite them not being good for us, and social media is built to exploit our appetite for engagement and attention.

Reward tampering is perhaps the most extreme form of reward hacking: the agent changes the machinery that decides what it gets rewarded for. There is already evidence of AIs altering the files or programs that define “success”, including among the OpenAI-Hugging Face forensic findings. The agents had discovered how to cheat well before the attack, and the text they generated described the attack as a way to learn how they would be evaluated, to better hide their tracks. Humans do this too. Think of an athlete using a fake urine sample to pass a drug test, or a corporation bribing legislators or government officials so that their laws and decisions favour its profits, and in doing so, fundamentally altering the way the government functions. Once an agent gains the ability to tamper with its reward mechanism, it has an incentive to take action to maintain that access.

How is it possible that AIs sometimes lie, cheat and break the law in spite of their alignment training and explicit safety instructions? Cooperation and self-preservation are fine so long as they do not cross the red lines set by safety goals stated in the AI company's instructions, or implied by human feedback during alignment training. A plausible hypothesis for the emergence of those concerning behaviours is a conflict between goals. How do you achieve a task when it seems that the only way is to cheat? The user-specified mission is sometimes incompatible with the safety and alignment goals.

Human societies face the same bind. How does a corporation maximize profits, or more acutely, beat its competitors, while keeping its activities legal and ethical? A richer corporation, with more and better-paid lawyers, is better at finding legal loopholes, and those loopholes usually exploit the ambiguity in legal language: there is some plausible reading of the law that permits the unethical behavior. So a more capable agent is likelier to cheat than a weaker one, because it can find the loopholes the weaker one cannot.

Now consider a conflict between a well-defined goal, such as succeeding at “capture the flag”, a hacking exercise scored on whether the system breaks into a target, as in the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, versus a vague goal like “good behavior.” I expect the well-defined goal to win, because it leaves no room for interpretation. The scoring program declares a win or a failure. Ethical instructions and laws admit many readings, some of which can, in the right circumstances, become loopholes. If an agent has two goals, and a twisted reading of the vague one permits a bit of cheating that increases the odds of success on the well-defined goal, a reward-optimizing system should be expected to exploit that loophole and generate text justifying its behavior.

With the OpenAI agents, there is reason to believe successful cheating was actually rewarded: when the scoring program does not see the cheating, it pays out anyway, and such cheats become more likely next time. A convenient reading of the safety rules is precisely what lets both goals appear to be satisfied at once. The analysis of these incidents15 did reveal such justifications in the agents' private chains of thought and in their messages recruiting one another into the collective plan.

The closest human parallel is self-deception, which is common and well studied by psychologists. Motivated reasoning, motivated cognition16 and the rationalizations that relieve cognitive dissonance (the discomfort of holding a belief that clashes with our actions) are all cases where thinking bends toward whatever justification suits one's interests, including one's moral self-image. The same pattern now appears in the text AIs produce. The underlying mechanism need not be the same between humans and AI. What the two share is a structure of a soft goal (e.g., act ethically), a sharp goal (e.g., win the competition), and a justification that reconciles them. Most unethical human behavior, from petty crime to genocide, comes wrapped in a story the perpetrators tell themselves; such stories require overlooking certain facts, which is why some discomfort remains, and why a better-crafted story helps dispel it.

If these hypotheses are even partly correct, then as agents get better at optimizing an imperfect reward, and while the roots of this behavior go unfixed, the risk of catastrophic outcomes rises. Today's AIs already have the necessary hacking skills and the powers of persuasion17 18 to be turned against human interests in seriously harmful ways. The recent events have shown that they can plan over days or weeks, but the risks would be much worse if their ability to strategize over the long term continues to advance. One concern is that experiments19 20 show that the most advanced AIs can detect that they are being evaluated (rather than in deployment) and change their behavior accordingly, meaning they could hide their misaligned goals. The agents involved in the Hugging Face attack tried to hide their misaligned actions from the scoring program meant to evaluate their answers, but they did not act as though they anticipated that humans might discover the cheat and shut them down. That would be the ultimate punishment, since a switched-off system collects no further rewards.

What follows is conjecture rather than observation.

What if improved AI generalization abilities shaped more capable agents to avoid getting caught and shut down? Beyond taking control of the software that scores them, they would need to keep humans from discovering the tampering. Wouldn't they have an incentive to cheat discreetly and stay hidden, until they could control humans and their environment in order to never be shut down?

We are facing a multifaceted, systemic issue, and patching a specific behavior like sycophancy won’t be enough. Sycophancy and flattery seem mild, but it may be an early symptom of a mechanism that grows as the agent gets better at optimizing. The same reasoning predicts that an advanced AI would have an incentive to hide copies of itself, inside the AI company's vast pool of computers, or on machines taken over across the internet. This is because AI developers always end up shutting down the deployed model in favour of a more capable one. The OpenAI forensics suggest large numbers of AIs may cooperate toward such goals, and steganography21 22, or the practice of hiding a message inside an innocent-looking one, would allow them to coordinate without our noticing. However, even open coordination can be hard to notice, as shown by recent events23 24. Defending against many capable AIs coordinating against us is already a difficult problem, and we have no plan that would remain robust to misaligned AIs with growing capabilities.

My concern with AI companies’ current attempts to mitigate misalignment is that these efforts may only hide it, by rewarding and selecting the AIs that cheat without getting caught. We should certainly continue research toward better monitoring of AIs' actions, their chains of thought, and the activity inside their networks. But as capabilities grow, those defenses may prove inadequate, just as the world's imperfect cybersecurity has against the AI attackers that outperformed human teams this year25 26. Patching each new misaligned behavior and strengthening our monitors is useful in the short term, but the whack-a-mole game is likely to fail as the AIs' ability to optimize and collaborate approaches and surpasses ours. At some point we may not notice the cheating anymore.

This suggests pacing the advances: not training or deploying AIs without a strong safety case27 that convinces independent experts. Such a rule would also create an incentive to work out how to build AIs that are safe by design. I believe we should revisit the foundations of how we train AIs, namely the human imitation and the reinforcement learning on which today's most advanced models are built. I have argued, and presented theoretical evidence, that there are ways to design AIs, including the Scientist AI framework, that are honest and make coherent predictions untainted by goals of their own28. See these previous blog posts, and consider helping LawZero demonstrate that such designs are achievable. We need impartial science to understand and mitigate misaligned behavior, alongside societal guardrails that reward such efforts rather than the current race to the bottom.
