title: House Democrat urges US action over sleeping Tesla drivers
description: A Democratic lawmaker called on a U.S. auto safety agency on Thursday to take action to address misuse of Tesla’s Autopilot and Full Self-Driving
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 10 (Reuters) - A Democratic lawmaker called on a U.S. auto safety agency on Thursday to take action to address misuse of Tesla's Autopilot and ‌Full Self-Driving systems, citing dozens of videos that appear to show drivers asleep or ‌disengaged from driving.

In a letter to U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois cited an NBC News ​report that identified 43 videos appearing to show individuals asleep in the driver's seat of moving Teslas, including 17 this year.

Krishnamoorthi said the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration "must ensure that manufacturers have adequate safeguards to prevent foreseeable misuse and that drivers are not encouraged to place dangerous levels of reliance on ‌systems

that still require their full ⁠attention."

Many Tesla drivers say the systems allow them to take their hands off the wheel for extended periods and some have posted videos suggesting they can ⁠perform other tasks while behind the wheel.

Tesla, the DOT and NHTSA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"Is NHTSA aware of the growing body of publicly available videos showing Tesla drivers apparently asleep or ​otherwise ​disengaged from the driving task while Autopilot or FSD ​is operating?" Krishnamoorthi asked.

He said he wants ‌to know if NHTSA has evaluated Tesla safeguards when the cabin camera is obstructed, visibility impaired, or drivers use sunglasses or hats to interfere with detection.

In 2023, Tesla recalled about 2 million vehicles, nearly all of its electric vehicles on U.S. roads, to better ensure that drivers pay attention when using Autopilot.

Tesla has said Autopilot enables vehicles to steer, accelerate and brake within their lanes, ‌while Full Self-Driving vehicles can obey traffic signals and ​change lanes. The automaker has also said both technologies require "fully ​attentive" drivers whose hands are on the ​wheel.

In March, the NHTSA escalated its probe into 3.2 million Teslas equipped ‌with Full Self-Driving, concerned the system may fail ​to detect issues or ​warn drivers in poor visibility.

In October, NHTSA opened a separate probe into 2.9 million Tesla vehicles equipped with its FSD system over more than 50 reports of traffic-safety violations and ​a series of crashes. The ‌auto safety agency said FSD — an assistance system that requires drivers to pay attention ​and intervene if needed — has "induced vehicle behavior that violated traffic safety laws."

title: Critics of AR-15 Bans Urge SCOTUS To Reject the 7th Circuit's Distinction Between Civilian and Military Arms
description: The Second Amendment does not cover "military-grade weapons," the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit averred last year, when it upheld an AR-15 ban enacted by Cook County, Illinois. The ruling ...
fullText:
The Second Amendment does not cover "military-grade weapons," the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit averred last year, when it upheld an AR-15 ban enacted by Cook County, Illinois. The ruling reaffirmed the reasoning of a 2023 decision in which the 7th Circuit distinguished between civilian and military arms, saying the "assault weapons" that Illinois had banned "lie on the military side of that line."

That distinction is misguided and ahistorical, Solicitor General D. John Sauer argues in a brief urging the Supreme Court to reject Cook County's rifle restrictions. "The founders would have been astonished at the claim that legislatures may ban arms in common use if those arms can also be used for military purposes," he writes.

Several briefs in that case, Viramontes v. Cook County, elaborate on Sauer's point, highlighting the Second Amendment's connection to "a well regulated militia," which implies that a weapon's usefulness in that context counts in favor of concluding that Americans have a constitutional right to possess it. Relatedly, the briefs note that the Second Amendment's purposes include common defense against invaders, insurrectionists, and tyrants as well as individual self-defense against criminal predators.

The Supreme Court is considering Viramontes along with Grant v. Higgins, which involves a similar Connecticut law. Both laws target "assault weapons," which they define to include AR-15s and similar semi-automatic rifles. Those rifles, the petitioners argue, are plainly covered by the Second Amendment because they are "in common use" for "lawful purposes like self-defense"—the test that the Supreme Court applied when it overturned the District of Columbia's handgun ban in 2008.

The Court's decision in District of Columbia v. Heller focused on the use of handguns "in defense of hearth and home." But as Sauer notes, Heller acknowledged that the Second Amendment also "protects the right to possess arms so that they are available for the common defense—i.e., for 'repelling invasions,' 'suppressing insurrections,' and 'resist[ing] tyranny.'"

The Second Amendment's prefatory clause, which describes "a well regulated militia" as "necessary to the security of a free state," indicates that "the founders codified the right precisely because it would promote 'the security of a free State' by enabling armed common defense," Sauer writes. "The founding generation understood that the individual right to keep and bear arms 'helped to secure the ideal of a citizen militia, which might be necessary to oppose an oppressive military force if the constitutional order broke down.'"

The Cato Institute's brief in Viramontes emphasizes that theme. "Although Heller's holding [regarding] guns in 'common use' for self-defense resolves this case," Cato attorneys Matthew Cavedon, Clark Neily, and Dan Greenberg say, "the Second Amendment protects AR-15s for a further reason: they are suited to the reserve militia"—i.e., "the entire population of 'citizens capable of bearing arms.'"

At the Founding, the "well regulated militia," which was viewed as a safeguard against the dangers posed by a standing army and a potentially oppressive national government, included all able-bodied men, who "were expected to appear bearing arms supplied by themselves and of the kind in common use," as the Supreme Court explained in the 1939 case United States v. Miller. Although Miller upheld the federal ban on short-barreled shotguns, its rationale was that the petitioner had failed to show that such weapons were "part of the ordinary military equipment or that [their] use could contribute to the common defense."

The implication was that arms are covered by the Second Amendment if they meet that test. Cavedon et al. argue that the AR-15 does, as the 7th Circuit implicitly conceded. The features of the AR-15 "align with those of the small arms historically used by the reserve militia," they say, and that counts as "an independent reason for constitutional protection."

In declaring the militia "necessary to the security of a free state," the Framers were not talking merely about repelling invasions or maintaining law and order. "A 'free state' meant a republic or constitutional monarchy, not despotic rule," Cavedon et al. note. "The Amendment checked military power and would deter tyranny."

The Second Amendment "was enacted so 'the people could resist oppression' as well as private violence," Cavedon et al. say, citing a 2014 Indiana Law Journal article by Robert Leider, now a professor at George Mason University's Antonin Scalia Law School. "William Blackstone wrote that the right to keep arms was a way to combat 'the violence of oppression.' Blackstone was alluding to the people's remedy against tyranny: armed resistance."

The Founders were "suspicious of standing armies," Cavedon et al. note. "The reserve militia would reduce 'civil-military tensions' and deter the prospect of devolution into tyranny that was thought to be inherent in democracy. This cultural outlook was a pillar of civic republicanism, and it was meant to ensure that the people 'could readily resist' any government oppression."

Historically, that background guided courts in deciding which arms are covered by the Second Amendment and state analogs. "Even for courts with a relatively narrow understanding of the right to keep and bear arms," Cavedon et al. say, "the suitability of arms for militia use weighed in favor of their protection. Courts consistently protected 'rifles, muskets, and army pistols.'"

The upshot: "Arms suited for militia service are not outside the Second Amendment's protection. Historically, they are at its core. Although the features triggering the bans
at issue here focus more on comfort than on martial effectiveness, the usefulness of such arms for militia service should weigh in favor of Second Amendment protection."

The Cato brief addresses concerns about the potentially "absurd" implications of that principle, such as the possibility that Second Amendment could be construed to protect "the private ownership of nuclear weaponry, warplanes, or ballistic rocketry." Since Heller restricts the Second Amendment to "bearable arms," that scenario seems implausible.

As understood in Heller, the Second Amendment was "not meant to equalize the strength of the reserve militia compared with that of the nation's military," Cavedon et al. write. "Rather, Heller protects Americans by preserving access to 'the sorts of lawful weapons that they possessed at home' for use in militia duty." Although "it may be true that no amount of small arms could be useful against modern-day bombers and tanks," the Supreme Court said in that case, "the fact that modern developments have limited the degree of fit between the prefatory clause and the protected right cannot change our interpretation of the right."

Cavedon et al. add that "semiautomatic rifles using the AR-15 platform," which fire just one round per trigger pull, are "easily distinguishable" from machine guns, which fire continuously. "A restriction on fully automatic firing 'narrowly regulates' a potential use without banning 'an entire class of weapons,'" the brief says. "To recognize constitutional protection for AR-15s is hardly to authorize private armies."

The National Association for Gun Rights (NAGR) likewise argues that the right to arms "secures defense against public violence as well as private violence." And "because deterring tyranny is a purpose of the codified right," the NAGR says, "suitability for militia service places an arm at the Amendment's core."

The Second Amendment Institute (SAI) joins Sauer, Cato, and the NAGR in disputing the distinction drawn by the 7th Circuit. The appeals court mistakenly read Heller as saying "the sole purpose of the Second Amendment was to protect armed self-defense," the SAI's attorney, George L. Lyon Jr., says in the organization's brief. "And it drew a distinction between 'civilian' weapons on one side and weapons 'reserved for military use' on the other."

That analysis turns Miller "upside down," Lyon writes. While Miller "asked whether
the weapon has militia utility as a reason for coverage," he says, the 7th Circuit "treated military utility as a reason for exclusion."

All this talk about the militia as a safeguard against tyranny "may seem quaint," Cavedon et al. concede. "Nonetheless, it is historically true that a people can expect to be disarmed 'when a country is overborne by force.'"

The Cato brief quotes the North Carolina Supreme Court's 1921 decision in State v. Kerner. "The constitutional provision which forbids any prohibition upon the people to bear arms and use them effectively by being accustomed to their use should be strictly and stoutly maintained," the court said, "for we know not when the occasion may again require the assertion of that doctrine which was once familiar throughout this country that 'resistance to tyranny is obedience to God.'"

AR-15s "are the sort of small arms that the Founders expected the American reserve militia to have in the event of such an evil," Cavedon et al. conclude. "In the interim, they have proven an extremely popular choice for other lawful purposes. They are protected by the Second Amendment."

The post Critics of AR-15 Bans Urge SCOTUS To Reject the 7th Circuit's Distinction Between Civilian and Military Arms appeared first on Reason Magazine.

title: Israel says it destroyed Hezbollah underground complex at Lebanon's Ali al-Taher
description: Sept 10 (Reuters) - The Israeli military destroyed Hezbollah underground infrastructure at the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel
fullText:
Sept 10 (Reuters) - The Israeli military destroyed Hezbollah underground infrastructure at the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister ‌Israel Katz said on Thursday, adding that the operation completed the consolidation ‌of a security zone in the area.

Israeli forces would remain in the area to prevent the Iran-aligned Hezbollah ​militant group from re-establishing its presence and rebuilding its capabilities, the two officials said in a joint statement.

The Ali al-Taher ridge, about 15 km (10 miles) from the Israeli border, has become one of the most contested areas of the war between Israel and Hezbollah. Hezbollah ‌is believed to have built ⁠an underground command centre and weapons stores there, according to Lebanese security sources who spoke to Reuters in July.

Lebanon's state news agency ⁠NNA said the Israeli military carried out a powerful blast at the ridge, with tremors and the sound of the explosion felt across Nabatieh and surrounding areas.

The Israeli military said its ​forces had ​established "operational control" over the ridge, both above ​and below ground, before dismantling the ‌infrastructure. The network extended for more than 2 km (1.24 miles) and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and drones, as well as anti-tank missiles, mines and explosive devices, it said.

The military said a central command complex belonging to Hezbollah's Badr unit was located within the underground infrastructure. The complex contained command centres, weapons storage rooms and living quarters that ‌allowed fighters to remain underground for extended periods, ​it said.

Israel has pushed into southern Lebanon and seized ​several strategic positions since the ​conflict erupted on March 2.

The ridge has been one of Israel's main ‌operational focuses and lies within an ​expanded, self-declared Israeli buffer ​zone in southern Lebanon.

A U.S.-brokered framework agreed after a June ceasefire called for Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from southern Lebanon while Lebanese troops disarm Hezbollah. ​The process has stalled, however, ‌with Hezbollah refusing to give up its weapons and Israel saying it will ​not withdraw until the group disarms.

title: President Trump's Republican convention speech draws 2.5 million viewers on Fox News
description: U.S.
fullText:
Sept 11 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump's speech on the opening night of the ‌Republican midterm convention drew about 2.5 million viewers on ‌Fox News, according to Nielsen data, potentially undercutting his claim the ​event "beat the NFL" opening night.

Fox News was the only major cable network to carry Trump's roughly two-hour address in full. The Murdoch family-controlled network averaged 2.5 million viewers during ‌the speech, ahead ⁠of MS NOW's 1 million and CNN's 441,000 in the same window.

Trump used the convention ⁠to appeal to voters to treat November's midterm elections as a referendum on him.

He urged voters to "pretend I'm on ​the ballot" ​during the two-day gathering that ​kicked off what Republicans ‌hope will be a Trump-focused campaign aimed at galvanizing the party's base and recreating the turnout that powered his 2016 and 2024 election victories.

In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump said the gathering was "far bigger, better, ‌and more important than anyone thought ​possible" and that "the overall numbers ​beat the NFL," without ​specifying figures or methodology.

The convention coincided with ‌the NFL season opener between ​the Seattle Seahawks ​and New England Patriots.

Ratings for the game are not yet available, but the NFL averaged about 18 ​million viewers per ‌game last season, and last year's opener drew ​close to 28 million.

title: Fisherman who found Mica Miller’s belongings describes scene to NewsNation
description: Fisherman Johnnie Jacobs died in a car crash less than a year after Mica Miller's death.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — A fisherman who heard crying and a gunshot near the area where Mica Miller died described his experience to NewsNation.

Miller's death was officially ruled a suicide, but her family and friends have called for more investigation, calling attention to her estranged husband, JP Miller, and alleged abuse in the relationship. They say JP Miller also stalked and harassed his wife once they separated.

A new Netflix docuseries has drawn increased attention to the case.

NewsNation's Rich McHugh spoke to Johnnie Jacobs, who was at Lumber River State Park in North Carolina when Mica Miller died, not long after her death.

Jacobs himself was killed in a car accident less than a year later.

"I heard a cry," he told NewsNation. "Then I heard a gunshot, maybe probably bout two minutes or so after, I started hearing the crying."

Jacobs showed NewsNation the area of the river he was fishing on when he heard the crying and gunshot.

"There's a path that comes in there, there's a path that comes into here, there's a path leading straight to where her belongings were laid at," he said, describing how Miller might have reached the area where she died.

Jacobs picked up Miller's belongings, which he said included a driver's license, bank card, keys and about $500, all of which he turned over to law enforcement.

"I never seen nothing," he said, of Miller herself.

When he spoke to NewsNation, Jacobs also addressed theories from people who tried to link him to Miller's death.

"Quit trying to be investigators. I did not do this," he said. "There is no way in this world I would harm anybody like that, not even my worst enemy would I do anything like that. I was just here fishing."

title: Winter festival move criticised as sneaky
description: Organisers say they hope to return to Penrith, where disappointment greets a late move to Carlisle.
fullText:
A decision to change the location of an annual winter festival at just over a month's notice has been criticised as "sneaky" by a business group.

The Winter Droving has been held in Penrith for more than a decade, but this year the live music, outdoor performances and twilight procession will take place 20 miles away in Carlisle on 24 October.

Eden Arts director Adrian Lochhead said organisers had been working "until the last minute" to keep the event in Penrith but it had not been possible for financial reasons.

However, Penrith Business Improvement District (Bid) accused Eden Arts of "sneakily organising" the move for some time, while the local council said it was "disappointed" at the news.

Lochhead told BBC Radio Cumbria the announcement did not happen earlier because they were "still trying" to stay in Penrith, but "it was becoming more and more impossible".

He said the charity lost £20,000 last year when windy weather saw the festival cancelled at less than 24 hours notice.

The parade portion of the event was eventually held in November.

Lochhead said: "Can we get back to Penrith next year? Please, let's be able to do that.

"But for this year it's about making another event in another part of the north of the county that everyone says needs more, so that's what we're trying to do."

Penrith Bid chair Dan Harding said he did not think the festival would return to the town and his group would look to do something "away from Eden Arts".

"We think Eden Arts have been sneakily organising this in the background for some time and they've been very poor in the communication," he said.

Westmorland and Furness Council said it had been a "long-standing" supporter, Eden Arts, which was one of the groups "receiving the highest amount of cultural grant from the council".

"We are very disappointed by this news and the short notice given," a spokesperson for the local authority said.

The council was seeking assurances from the charity that core funding provided this year would be used to deliver activities in the Eden area "in line with the funding agreement".

title: Former NYPD pilot reveals unseen aerial photos of 9/11
description: Retired NYPD Detective Greg Semendinger was a helicopter pilot who took some of the only aerial photos of the Twin Towers' destruction 25 years ago.
fullText:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Greg Semendinger's aerial photos still transport him back to that fateful day.

Semendinger, a detective and helicopter pilot for the New York City police, had been dispatched to the World Trade Center right after the first plane attack that morning in 2001. As his chopper approached, he could see the giant gash where an airliner had sliced through seven floors near the top of the north tower, and black smoke was billowing out.

Semendinger wasn't an official photographer for the NYPD, but he always carried a camera to document his squad's rescues and had one in the chopper that morning as an unthinkable horror unfolded before him.

He grabbed it and started snapping away.

The images he captured over the next 90 minutes were astonishing, among the only aerial photos of the Twin Towers as they burned and then collapsed, one after the other. With his copilot at the controls and hovering above, Semendinger trained his lens as the second tower vaporized in a plunging cascade of debris, and an immense grey cloud mushroomed across Lower Manhattan.

Some of the photos he took 25 years ago have emerged into public view in various ways: appropriated by other people for their books; displayed in news articles in 2010; mounted in the 9/11 museum at Ground Zero with his permission. But many have remained unseen until recently, when he shared his trove with the USA TODAY Network for 9/11 anniversary coverage.

Semendinger, now 77 and retired from the NYPD Aviation Unit since 2002, toggled through those stunning images on his laptop one August afternoon at the Long Island airport where he works. He recounted his fateful flight as he clicked from one photo to the next, the horrific scenes he witnessed and preserved for history.

"This was taken right after the second plane hit," he said as he lingered on an image and thought back to that moment. "We saw the initial explosion, the explosion went away. But the papers that were blown out of the building was unbelievable. The compression from the second plane hitting was just tremendous."

Semendinger was already at work that morning when the first startling reports came in.

It was 8:46 a.m. on Sept. 11, 2001. A plane had crashed into one of the towers, in what people first thought was an accident involving a small private aircraft. Because how else could a plane fly into the paired peaks of the Manhattan skyline on a clear day?

Semendiger, who was readying police helicopters for that day's flights at Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn, stepped outside the hangar and gazed toward the tip of Manhattan. The late summer sky was azure blue, absolutely cloudless, offering a clear view of the tops of the nearly 1,400-foot-tall buildings.

"I look at the towers and I see the amount of smoke coming from it," Semendinger recalled in the recent interview. "And I said, 'That does not look like a small plane.'"

It was, in fact, a Boeing 767, an American Airlines jet with 92 people aboard that five terrorists had hijacked and flown into the north tower, striking it between the 93rd and 99th floors. Semendinger soon had a close view of the damage. He and his partner, Jim Ciccone, raced over Brooklyn in their helicopter and got to the scene eight minutes after the impact.

They flew an L-shaped pattern around the burning tower to see if any people emerged on the roof, where a larger chopper might scoop them up. No one came out (a rooftop rescue may have been impossible anyway, since landing there was ruled out as too dangerous).

Then the second plane hit at 9:03 a.m. His view blocked by the buildings, Semendinger hadn't seen it speeding north over Staten Island before slamming into the south tower. He didn't even hear the crash over the noise of the helicopter and the radio noise on his headphones. But the sight of the explosion was unmistakable and he realized then what was happening.

"Well, now we know it's a terrorist attack," Semendinger recalled. "And now we know that there are other planes that are a possibility of being in the area."

With the second tower now burning, too, Semendinger and Ciccone were summoned away from the scene to pick up a commanding officer in the Bronx. They had delivered him to Floyd Bennett Field and were returning to the towers when the next stage of the day's horror took place.

They were crossing over Brooklyn's Prospect Park when the south tower came down at 9:59 a.m.

Semendinger captured that first collapse from a distance, now using a Canon digital camera instead of his film camera. He had grabbed his latest gear while their helicopter was refueling at Floyd Bennett Field. In those early years of advancing digital photography, it was one of the first cameras with built-in image stabilization.

"That's why the pictures came out so good," Semendinger recalled. "Because when you're bouncing around in a helicopter, stabilization was very important."

As they flew near the burning north tower, Semendinger could see one edge buckling, an ominous sign after what had just happened. He got on the police radio to deliver a warning that was later quoted in the book "102 Minutes," a Sept. 11 account by Jim Dwyer and Kevin Flynn.

"I don't think this has too much longer to go," Semendinger said in their account, taken from a recording of the radio transmission. "I would evacuate all of the people within the area of that second building."

Recalling that moment years later, Semendinger said, "We knew the writing was on the wall." He pointed out a detail in the photos that he took at that time: scattered streams of smoke pouring from spots between the vertical steel columns that framed the tower.

Places where people had broken windows to breathe and signal for help. Or climb outside.

"All those gaps in the channels are people," he said. "They're people waving sheets and flags and stuff like that. Whatever they had, tablecloths. Those are all people."

Those were his final, wrenching images of the north tower before its collapse. It fell at 10:28 a.m.

That awful moment and its aftermath are vividly frozen in time in Semendinger's digital archive, totaling about 150 images. They are grim scenes, laid out in full from the air. Lower Manhattan engulfed in smoke and debris. The bustling financial district shrouded in dust, looking like the soot-covered ruins of Pompeii.

Semendinger retired a year later, having served 18 years in the Aviation Unit and 35 years in all with the NYPD. By that time, several of his images had been spirited into a trio of books, including memoirs by the commissioners who led New York City's police and fire departments on Sept. 11.

Chris McKenna covers government and politics for The Journal News and USA TODAY Network. Reach him at CMcKenna@usatodayco.com.

This article originally appeared on Rockland/Westchester Journal News: Former NYPD pilot reveals unseen aerial photos of 9/11

title: Mamdani heads to 9/11 memorial despite 110,000-signature push from victims’ families to stay away
description: Scores of New Yorkers and 9/11 families signed a petition urging Zohran Mamdani to skip the Ground Zero memorial over his Ramzi Kassem pick.
fullText:
Scores of New Yorkers, including some families victimized by the Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the World Trade Center, are asking New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to skip the annual memorial service at Ground Zero — a call he is not heeding.

Mamdani is set to attend the annual remembrance ceremony on Friday at Ground Zero, which is an invitation-only event attended by victims' families, dignitaries and other invited guests. Hosted by the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, the event begins at 8:30 a.m. Vice President JD Vance and former presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and George W. Bush are also expected to attend.

A petition launched by relatives of 9/11 victims, which has since garnered roughly 110,000 signatures, asks Mamdani to stay home on Friday, citing his appointment of Ramzi Kassem as the city's chief legal counsel. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, an al Qaeda operative who pleaded guilty to war-crimes charges.

"For 9/11 families, this is not simply a public ceremony—it is a deeply personal day of mourning. The presence of individuals whose words or associations are perceived as conflicting with the solemn purpose of the event risks detracting from that focus and causing additional pain," the petition reads.

9/11 Families Push To Ban Mamdani From 25Th Anniversary Remembrance Over 'Hostile' Record

"The 25th anniversary should remain centered on remembrance, unity, and an unambiguous rejection of the violence and extremism that defined that day. Ensuring that all participants reflect these principles is essential to preserving the integrity of the commemoration."

The controversy intensified after Mamdani handed a ceremonial pen used to sign 9/11-related executive orders to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and asked her to pass it to Kassem. Critics on social media characterized the hand-off as a slap in the face to relatives of those who died in the attacks.

The mayor has defended his decision to attend the 9/11 memorial despite the criticisms levied against him.

"I'm proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country. And what I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers," Mamdani said in response to the criticisms.

Mamdani Under Fire After Symbolic 9/11 Pen Goes To Former Al Qaeda Defense Lawyer

Former New York Gov. George Pataki and one-time New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, both Republicans, have echoed calls for Mamdani to stay away from the ceremony.

"Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he's coming," the former mayor said.

​In addition to his appointment of Kassem, Mamdani has also caught flak from critics in the lead-up to Sept. 11 for his past failure to denounce the phrase "globalize the intifada," his praise for an unindicted co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, his endorsement of candidates who have made controversial statements about the attack and his continued association with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who stated that America "deserved 9/11."

Hasan Piker Stands By 'Intentionally Provocative' Claims That Hamas Is 'A Thousand Times Better' Than Israel

The mayor later called Piker's comments "objectionable and reprehensible," though has not disavowed him as a figure. He has also since stated that he would "discourage" people from saying "globalize the intifada."

The mayor's office did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

title: More than 500,000 Russian troops killed in Ukraine, UK defense chief says
description: More than half a million Russian troops have been killed in Ukraine since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, a senior British defense official said Friday.  The dead are part ...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — More than half a million Russian troops have been killed in Ukraine since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, a senior British defense official said Friday.

The dead are part of 1.5 million Russian casualties in Ukraine, Air Chief Marshall Sir Richard Knighton, Chief of the U.K's Defense Staff, said.

The U.K. figures roughly coincide with those published by the Ukrainian military. There was no immediate comment from Russian officials.

Moscow's bigger army is struggling to make headway on the battlefield. Western officials and analysts say the Russian rate of advance has slowed significantly this year.

Russia's armed forces have also lost an "enormous" amount of military materiel, Knighton told reporters. That includes more than 10,000 armored and protected vehicles, close to 3,000 air defense and artillery systems, and over 370 aircraft and helicopters, Knighton said.

He didn't say what Ukraine's losses were.

Neither Moscow nor Kyiv give regular updates on their battlefield losses.

Russian drones targeted roadside gas stations in Kyiv for a second straight day Friday, as Moscow broadened its air war in what Ukrainian officials say is an effort to rattle civilians.

The attacks struck two Ukrnafta gas stations, killing two people and wounding six at one of them, the prosecutor's office said.

Russian strikes on urban gas stations have intensified in recent months, mostly in regions near the front line in eastern and southern Ukraine. It is part of a campaign to disrupt civilian life and weaken morale that has also included attacks on food distribution hubs, sporadically leaving some supermarket shelves bare in the Ukrainian capital.

"Russia is systematically attacking places where it knows people will be spending their time going about their daily lives, seeking to maximize casualties, spread fear, and put pressure on Ukrainian society," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X late Thursday.

Authorities have urged residents not to linger near gas stations and other exposed infrastructure during air raid alerts.

Ukraine is urgently trying to improve its air defenses as Russia's invasion stretches into its fifth year, and on Thursday won pledges of more support from Canada.

Pavlohrad, a city in central Ukraine, observed an official day of mourning Friday for five residents killed near shopping malls in broad daylight by Russian drones the previous day.

The attack also wounded 67 people, Sybiha said on X.

In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, a 32-year-old woman and her 10-year-old son were wounded in an overnight Russian drone attack, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The drones struck a nine-story apartment block and a shopping mall, it said.

Efforts to put out the blazes were slowed by the constant threat of repeat strikes, forcing firefighters to stop working and take shelter, it added.

In Dnipro, a city in central Ukraine, a Russian daylight attack Friday wounded 12 people, according to local officials.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has extended its own long-range drone campaign deep into Russia, straining air defenses across its bigger neighbor's vast territory. On Thursday, its military reported hitting a refinery more than 3,000 kilometers (1,800 miles) away in Siberia as Kyiv tries to hurt Russia's vital oil sector. Its strikes have caused fuel shortages in Russia, one of the world's biggest energy producers.

Russia's oil product exports hit record lows in August, and Moscow is importing fuel from South Korea and India, the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air said in a report.

"Ukrainian strikes on Russia's refining capacity have turned tables on the world's once largest oil product exporter to see them start importing fuels, with imports surging to a record 172,000 metric tons (189,600 tons) in August — more than seven times the previous monthly high," the Finland-registered nonprofit said Thursday.

Ukraine launched a major barrage overnight from Thursday to Friday, with the Russian Defense Ministry saying air defenses intercepted 777 Ukrainian drones over 16 Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the waters of the Azov and the Caspian seas.

Two people were killed and three others wounded overnight in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Tula region south of Moscow, local officials said Friday.

A Ukrainian drone strike during the night started a fire at the Saratov oil refinery in southwestern Russia, Russian independent online outlet Astra said Friday. Kyiv has repeatedly targeted that refinery, which was last hit in early August.

Major online retailer Ozon said its logistics facility in the same city was struck and set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone, though no casualties were reported. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said long-range strikes overnight hit eight Russian regions, including a business and an oil industry facility in the Saratov region.

The attacks were "aimed at reducing Russia's capacity to wage war," he said on X Friday.

Burrows reported from London and Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.

title: Trump announces $500 checks for Americans for alleged overcharge under Obamacare
description: Trump announced the administration would refund $500 to nearly 1 million people who were allegedly overcharged for health insurance under Obamacare.
fullText:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump announced his administration would refund $500 million that he said people allegedly were overcharged through the Affordable Care Act's federal exchange for buying health insurance.

Trump said in a video statement posted by the White House that $500 checks would be mailed in October to 1 million people in 30 states that used Healthcare.gov, the federal marketplace where people 

"Our Administration is doing the right thing and giving the money back to the people who were wrongly ripped off," Trump said.

The health-insurance refund is different from the $5,000 dividends to all American adults that Trump pledged Sept. 9 at the Republican National Convention. Critics including Democratic lawmakers have called the proposed dividends "blatantly illegal" and unlikely to pass Congress.

For the health insurance refunds, the White House said the Biden Administration collected user fees from health insurance companies that consumers paid for in the form of higher premiums. Trump argued the premiums exceeded what was needed to run the exchange.

Trump said the excess fees would be refunded to Americans who didn't receive premium assistance under the Affordable Care Act in the 30 states that use the federal exchange. The expiration of the enhanced ACA subsidies at the end of 2025 made insurance more expensive for millions of consumers.

The 30 states are: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Under the ACA, health insurance companies are required to rebate consumers when insurers don't spend at least 80% of premium dollars on health care. KFF, a health policy nonprofit, estimates ACA insurers will refund more than $500 million to consumers and more than $200 million to consumers under the rebate.

title: 'You can't break the fundamental laws of physics': T-Mobile CFO says he's not worried about Elon Musk's cellular ambitions
description: T-Mobile CFO Peter Osvaldik said "everybody in the know" is "laughing at" Starlink's plans to use lots of small cell stations in cities.
fullText:
SpaceX wants a piece of the cellphone market, but T-Mobile's CFO is far from concerned.

Peter Osvaldik said "everybody in the know" is "laughing" at parts of Starlink's plans.

While Starlink satellites provide coverage in remote areas, it faces different challenges in cities.

Elon Musk thinks Starlink can shake up the mobile industry, but a T-Mobile exec said its strategy should be laughed out of the room.

"It's not a competitive threat from a wireless perspective at all," T-Mobile CFO Peter Osvaldik said Wednesday at Citi's 2026 Global TMT Conference.

"If we, as a management team, over the course of two months, changed the strategy to how we're going to roll out a wireless network like a dozen times, it would laugh us out of the room and kick me out of the management team appropriately."

Musk and SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell outlined their goals for Starlink Mobile in the company's first earnings call in early August.

The Big Three telecoms firms — AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile — make about $600 billion a year in revenue. "I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers because I think our service will be better," Shotwell said.

She pointed to Starlink's ability to "eliminate dead zones" and provide coverage in remote areas through its satellites.

It has 650 direct-to-cell satellites in orbit, as well as its flagship constellation of over 10,000 satellites for broadband internet.

However, for urban areas, satellites aren't as useful as cell towers.

Starlink's satellites operate in low Earth orbit, a few hundred miles above the planet, which means their signals reach cellphones quickly — though these signals can be blocked by typical city infrastructure.

"You can't get through buildings, walls. You can't even get through a Tesla windscreen," Osvaldik said. "You can have 1 million satellites up there with all the spectrum in the world, you can't break the fundamental laws of physics."

SpaceX isn't planning to rely only on satellites for Starlink Mobile.

Instead of using cell towers, which are expensive and difficult to install, SpaceX wants to use a huge number of small cell stations, called femtocells.

"Essentially, they're really just Starlink dishes that also provide connectivity in the mobile spectrum bands, and have them be all over the place," Musk told investors. "The Starlink antennas are located on the roofs of houses and businesses, so they've got a clear view for providing connectivity directly to cellphones on the ground."

Osvaldik ridiculed this idea, saying "everybody in the know" is "laughing at" it because potentially 1 billion femtocells would be required to match the coverage of cell towers.

"I mean, it's just not fathomable," he added.

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Police investigate death of Tasia Fortune, found hanging from tree, as a homicide
description: Jackson, Mississippi, police are investigating the death of Tasia Fortune as a homicide after the 29-year-old Black woman was found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned house last month, the city’...
fullText:
Jackson, Mississippi, police are investigating the death of Tasia Fortune as a homicide after the 29-year-old Black woman was found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned house last month, the city's police chief said Tuesday.

"Jackson Police Department has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide, until we hear otherwise from the medical examiner's office," Chief RaShall Brackney said at a city council meeting.

Police had previously categorized the case as a "death pending investigation."

With the autopsy results pending, Fortune's family is demanding answers and local officials are questioning the circumstances surrounding the case.

The scrutiny is unfolding against Mississippi's long history of racial violence involving hangings and follows other recent hanging deaths in the state that authorities ruled were suicides.

"We need to pursue (Fortune's) investigation to its final conclusion and whatever the results, we need to address those results," Jackson City Council President Vernon Hartley said.

The police chief addressed the city council after a letter written by Christy Spivey, Fortune's mother, was read aloud at the meeting.

"I have no more answers from one day of this investigation," Spivey wrote. "The detectives are like they are on a prerecorded message, just saying the same thing over and over. And now it's gone to silence."

On Thursday, Spivey said in a post on the family's GoFundMe page that she had asked Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes for help "because of the silence and rudeness of Jackson Police Department."

"Thanks to him putting Tasia's case on for the council meeting Jackson Police department finally came out and admitted that they were treating this as a homicide which I had already known that but the public didn't personally know," Spivey wrote.

Investigators have remained in regular contact with Spivey and her husband, but are awaiting the ruling from the medical examiner's office, Brackney said.

CNN has reached out to Spivey for comment.

The Mississippi State Medical Examiner's Office conducted an autopsy on Fortune on August 11, but police have not yet received the results, Brackney told the council.

The chief said she had been in contact with the director of the medical examiner's office as well as the commissioner who oversees it but has not been able to get a ruling on the cause and manner of Fortune's death.

"Autopsy reports are not considered outstanding or backlogged until they have exceeded 90 days," and the average turnaround time for the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, which oversees the state medical examiner's office, is less than that, spokesperson Alex Gibert told CNN on Thursday.

CNN has reached out to the medical examiner's office 

There have been no arrests made in relation to Fortune's death, police told CNN in August, but the father of one of Fortune's children was arrested shortly after the discovery of her body on unrelated weapons charges. He is still in custody, jail records show.

Fortune's "children have their future secured" as the family continues "working on justice," Spivey said in the GoFundMe post.

Brackney warned people not to jump to conclusions before all the results are in.

"There is a lot of misinformation out there about this case and other ones," she said.

Stokes called for answers, especially considering the violent history of race relations in Mississippi and several other hangings in the state.

He said people in his ward are worried and want to know what happened to Fortune.

"They're concerned because they're saying no answers have been given as to what happened, who did what, or anything else, and everybody wants to know what happened," Stokes told CNN affiliate WAPT.

The investigation into Fortune's death comes less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg, according to The Associated Press. Both deaths were determined by authorities to be suicides.

"Hanging is an ugly, ugly part of our past that we never, ever want to come back again," Stokes said at the city council meeting.

The council member also told CNN affiliate WLBT the delay in answers about Fortune's death raises questions about the investigation.

"It sends the message that you're trying to hide something, and we do not need to hide anything in the state of Mississippi. We want the world to know we're open and above board," he said.

CNN's Cindy Von Quednow and Leah Thomeer contributed to this report.

title: How the iPhone Duo Stacks Up to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8
description: How does Apple's new foldable compare to the rest?
fullText:
After years of rumors, Apple finally made a foldable: the iPhone Duo. The initial reaction online has been mostly positive—particularly how iOS adapts to the phone and that cool transition wallpaper effect—but it begs the question: How does Apple's new device compare to the folding phones already on the market?

The iPhone Duo is now competing against the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which I'll focus on here rather than the Z Fold 8 Ultra). There are key similarities and differences between the three handsets that suggest whether or not the iPhone Duo will be a success. And having used both Google and Samsung foldables in the past, I have some ideas about what the iPhone Duo needs to get right.

Google and Samsung have been doing this longer than Apple has, and their phones are thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo. That might make a difference once Apple's handset gets out into the world, with preorders set to start on Friday, Oct. 16. You can also see here that Apple and Samsung have gone for the "passport" style approach: Displays that are shorter and wider, which means a more tablet-style main display. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold has the aspect ratio of a standard smartphone when closed, with a main display that's more square.

You can see how the passport-style foldable compares to the more traditional foldable form factor in the display dimensions too: There's a lot more vertical space on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold when all of these foldables are closed shut, which is quite a consideration. If you're like me, you'll end up using your foldable closed more often than unfolded, in which case the outer display becomes very important. (But more on that later.) It's worth knowing that both Apple and Google rely on Samsung to supply their phone displays, as per industry sources.

If you'd like a foldable phone, it's going to cost you, whichever brand you favor. The iPhone Duo starts a little higher than the competition and goes up to 2TB of storage—something Google and Samsung don't do. It's worth mentioning RAM here too: The iPhone Duo has 12GB, the Google phone comes with 16GB, and Samsung offers either 12GB or 16GB in the Galaxy Z Fold 8, depending on the amount of storage you buy. But it's not an even comparison: The Duo runs iOS, which has different RAM requirements than Android devices.

Cameras abound on foldable phones—you need a selfie camera for the inner display and the outer display—and it's notable that Apple isn't telling anyone the specs of its inner selfie cameras. Google's foldable is the only one with a telephoto camera. In the modern era, software processing is just as important as hardware specs, so how the handsets compare on this front is to some extent subjective. It'll be interesting to see how photos from the iPhone Duo stand up against those on the iPhone 18 Pro, which has a more advanced camera system.

The iPhone Duo doesn't have face unlock as the Google and Samsung phones do, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 doesn't have the IP68 waterproofing of the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold (though this doesn't last). Battery life is a key consideration when picking a smartphone, but the capacity numbers here can only tell us so much. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 4,806 mAh battery, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a 4,800 mAh battery, and Apple isn't revealing the battery capacity on the iPhone Duo—though it does say you can get up to 44 hours of video playback between charges on the outer display. Software optimization and other factors play a role too, so some real-world testing will be needed for a proper comparison.

Speaking of software, there's the iOS and Android divide, of course. From what we've seen of iOS on the iPhone Duo, it looks like an elegant and thoughtful adaptation, with shifting buttons, split keyboards, a dual pane mode, and some other nice touches—no doubt helped by Apple's iPad experience. To my eye, it seems like a more fluid experience than what you get on an Android foldable, though that's not to say you get a bad experience on Google and Samsung phones.

Spec sheets can only get you so far, and while the iPhone Duo has made a bold impression based on what we've seen from Apple so far, no one has properly used one yet. The true test for whether the foldable iPhone is a hit or not is going to depend on how well it works through all the moments of day-to-day life.

I've spent several years using foldable phones from Samsung and Google, and aside from the rather prohibitive cost, the main issue that makes me still prefer standard phone form factors is that, for most of the time, there's no reason to open up the full display—which means you're left with a device that's chunky and heavy, with no real upside. Checking messages on the go, making contactless payments, taking photos: the majority of phone tasks don't need or suit a tablet-sized screen. That's what all of these foldables are fighting against. Would you use an iPad to take a photo at a gig, call your parents, or find your way around in an unfamiliar city?

Apple seems to have the software experience right, and the iPhone Duo looks as well crafted as you would expect a foldable iPhone to be—but even if you can foot the bill for one of these, you might find that the cost of using a thicker, heavier, smaller phone isn't worth it, just so you can occasionally have a bigger screen available. The iPhone Duo actually stacks up pretty well against the foldables from Samsung and Google, but its real competition is going to come from other iPhones.

title: Trump administration lends $100M to US-owned cell phone network in Africa to expand American tech
description: The Trump administration has provided a $99.6 million loan to a U.S.-owned cell phone network operator in Africa to expand American tech presence on a continent where China's Huawei is a leading playe...
fullText:
CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — The Trump administration has provided a $99.6 million loan to a U.S.-owned cell phone network operator in Africa to expand American tech presence on a continent where China's Huawei is a leading player.

The loan from the U.S. government's Export-Import Bank was announced by the operator Africell on Friday. It is the only U.S.-owned cell network operator in Africa.

Africell said in a statement the loan would "boost U.S.-based employment in the telecommunications sector and strengthen American technology leadership abroad." It said the money would allow it to invest specifically in American and European technology for its operations in the southern African country of Angola.

Africell also operates in Congo, Sierra Leone and Gambia, it said.

Huawei is the world's biggest supplier of telecommunications network equipment and is estimated to have supplied more than half the 4G and 5G network infrastructure in Africa.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration raised national security concerns about Huawei in his first term and has moved to counter its global expansion.

The U.S. has lobbied Western allies to avoid using the Chinese company's products in their high-speed wireless networks, while U.S. prosecutors have accused Huawei of stealing technology, plotting to steal U.S. trade secrets and committing wire and bank fraud, among other crimes.

A criminal racketeering trial against Huawei opened in New York this week. Huawei said the U.S. allegations are "demonstrably false."

The Trump administration has also moved to counter China's large influence in other areas in Africa, including in the extraction of critical minerals and rare earth elements that are key in the production of electronics, other new technologies and defense systems.

title: Durham beat Middlesex to seal Championship promotion
description: Durham seal promotion from Championship Division Two with two games to spare as they beat Middlesex by 93 runs.
fullText:
Rothesay County Championship, Division Two, Banks Homes Riverside (day four)

Durham 252 & 374 McKinney 184, Ackermann 48; Higgins 4-79

Middlesex 203 & 330: Duke 100*, Geddes 50; Parkinson 4-45, Carse 4-116

Durham (20pts) beat Middlesex (3pts) by 93 runs

Durham secured promotion back to County Championship Division One at the first time of asking as Callum Parkinson and Brydon Carse bowled them to a 93-run victory Middlesex.

Having set a distant target of 424 and taken two wickets last evening at the Riverside, they bowled the visitors out for 330, despite Harry Duke's unbeaten 100.

Durham made a dream start as Kasey Aldridge picked up a wicket with the first ball of the day and another fell soon after, but a stand of 64 from Ben Geddes and Ryan Higgins held up their charge towards victory.

But Parkinson accounted for both, only for the ninth-wicket pair of Tom Helm and Duke to offer further prolonged resistance.

However, Parkinson who broke the 79-run partnership between the pair and while Yorkshire loanee Duke displayed great defiance with a brilliant maiden first-class century, Carse took the final wicket to seal promotion for the hosts.

Durham on course for promotion against Middlesex

Carse & McKinney put Durham on top against Middlesex

Morgan stars as Middlesex bowl out battling Durham

Resuming on 55-2, Middlesex's aim was to keep their wickets intact and delay Durham's promotion party for a few days at least.

However, that plan was dealt a blow almost immediately when Nathan Fernandes after the Middlesex man edged Aldridge to third slip.

Will Rhodes came into the attack for Durham and picked up the scalp of Middlesex captain Max Holden, caught at first slip, and nearly had their fifth wicket when Carse found the edge of Geddes' bat, but Aldridge could not cling on to a regulation chance.

Higgins picked up two boundaries off Rhodes to relieve some of the pressure on the visitors and Geddes then joined in with a lovely shot down the ground off the bowling of Aldridge.

Their partnership passed 50, but Higginsn was dismissed soon after as he slapped a Parkinson delivery straight to backward point.

Geddes continued his good morning with the bat as he passed 50 for the third time this season, but he then holed out to Mayank Agarwal who took an excellent catch running in from the long-on boundary.

Parkinson bowled Zafar Gohar after lunch with a beauty as Durham closed in on victory and Carse then got Seb Morgan lbw, but Duke and Helm combined to stem the flow of wickets.

Helm was finally lbw for a valiant 32 but Ben McKinney dropped Duke on 95 after the Middlesex man went for a big shot and he reached three figures for the first time in his career from the next ball.

Carse then took the decisive wicket one ball later as he got Naavya Sharma caught behind.

ECB Reporters' Network supported by Rothesay.

Quite simply, Durham have been far, far too good for Division Two. With the players they have been able to use this season, they would be more than a match for every single side in the division above.

A shocking batting collapse at Headingley on the final day of last season sent Durham back into Division Two after two years in the top flight, and they have played all season with a determination to erase that painful memory.

David Bedingham was the leading run-scorer in the division with 1,029 runs before he had to leave early to prepare for South Africa's Test series with Australia next month.

That included five centuries, two more than Emilio Gay, who hit three hundreds in six matches in early season to catapult him into the England Test team.

Matthew Potts has not featured for that side since the Ashes last winter, but England's loss has been Durham's gain with 58 wickets - the leading wicket-taker in the Championship this summer.

Throw in other strong contributions from captain Alex Lees and fellow opening batter Ben McKinney and the evergreen Ben Raine as Potts' new-ball partner and it's clear to see why the north east county have sailed to promotion.

And that's before we even mention Ben Stokes. Durham were already top at the time of his fallout with England in June, but Stokes has thrown himself wholeheartedly into Championship cricket since announcing stepping down as England captain and announcing his retirement from Tests.

Stokes has contributed with bat and ball and to add arguably world cricket's finest player from the last decade to Durham's side has made them untouchable.

Look at the margin of their victories, two by an innings, 10 wickets, nine wickets, eight wickets, 338 runs, they have usually been far too good for their opponents.

The title is only a matter of time as they must surely go down as the strongest second-tier team since two divisions were introduced in 2000.

title: Ex-West Ham striker Antonio joins Watford
description: Watford announce the signing of former West Ham United striker Michail Antonio on a free transfer.
fullText:
Watford have announced the signing of former West Ham United striker Michail Antonio on a free transfer.

The 36-year-old made his final senior appearance for the Hammers in their 3-1 defeat by Leicester City on 3 December 2024, suffering a broken leg four days later in a car crash.

Antonio last played in April for Qatari side Al-Sailiya and made a total of four appearances for the club. He had been training with Alessio Dionisi's Hornets for the past month and has joined on a one-year deal.

"Watford is a big club and hopefully I can come in and bring success and help wherever I can." Antonio told the club's website., external

The deal for the Jamaican international has been announced pending international clearance that would allow him to be part of the squad for Saturday's Championship home match with Stoke City.

After being released by the Hammers in June 2025 following a 10-year spell, Antonio returned to the club as part of his rehabilitation and played two games for the under-21 side in Premier League 2.

He trained with Leicester City last December and had also been close to a move to Brentford but sustained a torn calf muscle the day before he was set to sign for the Bees, which scuppered the deal.

Prior to his move to West Ham in September 2015, Antonio played in the EFL for clubs including Reading, Sheffield Wednesday and Nottingham Forest.

Antonio, who will wear the number 18 shirt at Vicarage Road, is Watford's 12th signing of the summer.

title: No northern Ashes Test a result of 2023 switch
description: The decision not to host a men's Ashes Test in the north next year is a result of the reallocation from Southampton to Headingley in the previous series in 2023.
fullText:
The absence of a men's Ashes Test in the north of England in 2027 is a direct result of the decision to switch a match from Hampshire to Headingley for Australia's last visit in 2023.

Next year, Hampshire's home in Southampton will host an Ashes Test for the first time, with both Old Trafford in Manchester and Headingley in Leeds missing out.

As first reported by the Guardian, Southampton was due to host the Australians in 2023, only for the match to be changed.

Hampshire were awarded more than £1m in compensation by the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB), then subsequently given an Ashes Test in 2027.

Neither Hampshire nor the ECB have commented.

The Ashes venues for 2023 were announced in 2018, when the ECB was chaired by Colin Graves.

Graves, the current Yorkshire chair, held the same position at Headingley prior to his time with the ECB.

He told the Guardian he was not involved in the allocation of matches.

"I always left the room when their recommendations were discussed by the board. I was not involved," he said.

The method for allocating matches in the 2023 series was under the ECB's old, 'competitive tender' process, where venues essentially made financial bids to host fixtures.

The governing body has since moved to a rotation system, which it believes is fairer.

The rotation system was backed by the 18 first-class counties and Marylebone Cricket Club, and was used to allocate major matches up to 2031.

From 2031, the ECB plans to host at least one men's Ashes Test in the north of England, with Southampton receiving a men's Test in every other Ashes series.

Both Headingley and Old Trafford have hosted a men's Test in the two previous home Ashes series.

Next year, the most northerly men's Ashes Test will take place at Trent Bridge in Nottingham, while Headingley will host the sole women's Ashes Test.

title: Teams need to adapt to fixture scheduling - Maresca
description: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says teams "need to adapt" to the fixture scheduling as his side head into Sunday's derby with two days extra rest over rivals Manchester United.
fullText:
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says teams "need to adapt" to the fixture scheduling as his side head into Sunday's Premier League derby with two days extra rest over rivals Manchester United.

City won 2-0 at Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday evening, with United thrashing Sabah 4-0 a full 48 hours later - meaning Michael Carrick's side have less recovery and preparation time than their opponents.

But Maresca pointed to City's own situation from last September before facing Arsenal - when the Gunners played in the early kick-off at Athletic Club on Tuesday, while City faced Napoli in the 20:00 BST game on Thursday.

Last season, former boss Pep Guardiola joked he was taking his players "hiking in the mountains" in preparation for the game at Emirates Stadium.

When asked about the scheduling, Maresca told BBC Sport: "To be honest, the club mentioned to me that it happened exactly the same last year when the club played Napoli and then, after two days, played Arsenal.

"Sometimes it happens in football. I don't have any doubt that Man United are going to be ready for that. It just matters to adapt."

The expanded Champions League means teams now play two extra games in the group phase before the end of January, while English teams also have to contend with participating in the Carabao Cup.

City host Norwich in the third round next Thursday, while United play Brighton at Old Trafford the day before.

"I think that happens and you need to adapt," said Maresca, when asked if the scheduling equals itself out. "It happened last year with us, this season with them, next season it will happen with a different team."

Quizzed on how Carrick would be feeling, Maresca replied: "That's a question for Michael. The only thing I can say is it happened and you need to adapt."

Maresca takes charge of his first Manchester derby and has started the season with City in superb fashion, winning all three league games so far, while United have only managed to collect four points from their opening three games.

"It is very important for different reasons," said the Italian." We know how important a derby is, especially here. It is a special game.

"The most important thing we can do is try to be ourselves and then we see the final result."

title: I disrupted pre-season travel plans to prepare players - Arteta
description: Mikel Arteta says Arsenal were ready for their midweek Champions League flight delay - because he deliberately disrupted their training and travel plans in pre-season to prepare them.
fullText:
Mikel Arteta says Arsenal were ready for their midweek Champions League flight delay - because he deliberately disrupted their training and travel plans in pre-season to prepare them.

The Premier League champions were affected by air traffic control issues as they travelled to Italy to face Napoli on Wednesday.

They eventually arrived three hours behind their schedule but manager Arteta said his team were ready because of his methods.

"I love those challenges, I try to create them in pre-season," Arteta said at his news conference on Friday, before Saturday's Premier League trip to Sunderland (20:00 BST).

"So when they happen, we have already experienced them and we are ready.

"Get to the stadium very late, change the routine so the players have to do something else. When it happens, and it can - the flight can be cancelled, or the train is delayed, there is so much traffic, I don't want the players and staff panicking.

"When that happens, adapt to it. We have two or three hours on the plane - can we use it? Play together, spend some time together, sleep.

"But don't complain or use it as an excuse because it's not helpful at all."

Arteta went on to add that his methods also include delaying meals or transport, take different routes to grounds and making the dressing room hotter and more uncomfortable for players.

He said that it reduces the amount of stress and surprise on a matchday when such disruptions occur.

It is not the first instance of Arteta using unusual methods in his team's preparation.

The Spaniard once brought a light bulb into the dressing room while asking his players to be energetic and shine.

On another occasion, he even hired professional pickpockets to attend a team dinner to take phones and wallets from players, which was used as a lesson to teach them to stay alert.

In 2023, he brought a dog named Win into the training ground to boost morale, saying that it was used to represent the team as a family.

He is not opposed to others in the squad using his methods, either - in April, a fire was lit at the club's training ground before they hosted Sporting in the Champions League.

title: Pacesetter Russell says Madrid 'has less margin than Monaco'
description: George Russell goes quickest in first practice for the Spanish Grand Prix - hours after saying the circuit has little margin for error.
fullText:
George Russell says Formula 1's new circuit in Madrid "has less margin than Monaco" as the sport races there for the first time at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver set the pace in first practice at the Madring - a street-circuit style track built around an exhibition centre near the Spanish capital's airport.

Russell was 0.286 seconds faster than team-mate Kimi Antonelli in second place.

"In Monaco, the walls are closer, but because you're going far slower, if you make a mistake, you're not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes, a small lock-up," he said.

Russell was speaking a couple of hours before a practice session that ran incident-free.

A few drivers brushed the wall, including Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso, but no-one damaged their car.

Russell said: "There's a lot of really fast corners, but the barrier is kind of like coming back onto the track. So, if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you're not hitting it kind of at the same angle as the car is going. The wall is sort of coming in at you."

Recap: Mercedes duo quickest in Spanish Grand Prix first practice

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid

Russell singled out Turns Five, Seven and 17, where Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc went off into the run-off area during practice.

"Another element of the challenge here, which probably won't cause major crashes, but I think there'll be a lot of lock-ups," said Russell.

"You've got three corners where you're turning and braking, and if you lock up, the wall is right in front of you, which is very reminiscent of the corner in Baku - Turn 15."

There is also a section of high-speed swerves, Russell said, which is similar to the fast Jeddah street track in Saudi Arabia.

Ferrari set the pace on the medium tyres in the first part of Friday's opening session but they could not match the pace of the Mercedes on the soft compound.

Leclerc was third fastest - 0.459secs off Russell and just ahead of Hamilton - with Red Bull's Max Verstappen fifth and McLaren's Lando Norris' sixth.

Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, Mclaren's Oscar Piastri, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Red Bull's Liam Lawson completed the top 10.

title: Celtic given 'timely' police reminder before derby
description: Celtic players had a visit from Police Scotland on Friday to give them "a timely reminder" about their "general behaviour" in Sunday's Premier Sport Cup quarter-final against city rivals Rangers, manager Martin O'Neill reveals.
fullText:
Manager Martin O'Neill says Celtic had a visit from Police Scotland on Friday to give them "a timely reminder" about their "general behaviour" in Sunday's Premier Sport Cup quarter-final against city rivals Rangers.

Both Glasgow clubs were last month ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup matches behind closed doors after last season's quarter-final - won by Celtic after a penalty shootout at Ibrox - was marred by fan disorder.

It will be the first time Celtic have returned there since, although the Scottish champions did host a Scottish Premiership encounter in May, beating Rangers 3-1.

The Scottish Professional Football League recently announced no away fans will attend Old Firm derbies in the league or League Cup this season.

"We had the police come in today, just a little 15-minute meeting to remind us of our behaviour, which I think is a timely reminder," O'Neill revealed.

O'Neill on Baur fitness, police visit & 'strange' setting

Will fan factor work for or against Rangers?

Celtic take confidence & momentum into 'special' derby - Baur

Asked what had been said, the Northern Irishman said: "They didn't mention this, but I would have assumed that one of the things that would be considered is what happens in the field of play, because these things can be taken further.

"You don't want any sort of punch-ups for a start. Secondly, you don't want excessive celebrations, stuff like that.

"But I think it's just the behaviour in the light of what has happened in recent fixtures. I think that the conversation with the police wouldn't have taken place had not recent events been brought up to us."

Celtic have won the latest three derbies since Rangers beat them 3-1 at Celtic Park in the league in January - and are five points ahead in the Premiership after just six games of the new season.

Asked how having no away fans might impact the match, O'Neill added: "I think the games themselves almost take care of themselves in that sense.

"It'll be strange in many aspects not to have any away fans in our area. I always felt as if it would give you a crumb of comfort in some description.

"Nervously looking forward to it, excitedly looking forward to it."

Rangers have come in for some criticism from their own fans for a poor start to the season under new manager Derek McInnes, although the hosts are on a run of four successive victories.

"I suppose if you get in front in the game, that makes them anxious," O'Neill suggested.

"Talking about getting in front and getting in front are two different things. The crowd will be right behind their team, which you would expect.

"We just do our best. We know that we're up against a very fine side. We're up against a crowd that can make a difference. I'd be delighted to be celebrating something in the game."

title: Hull fined £30k & bans issued over Chelsea chant
description: Hull City have been fined £30,000 over discriminatory chanting with the club issuing three supporter bans following their FA Cup defeat by Chelsea in February.
fullText:
Hull City have been fined £30,000 over discriminatory chanting during their 4-0 FA Cup defeat by Chelsea in February.

The club is now urging supporters not to engage in the same chant when they face the Blues in the Premier League on Saturday.

And it revealed three supporters had been banned for "a minimum of three years" following February's game at the MKM Stadium.

Three people were arrested for allegedly engaging in homophobic chanting at the match, in which spectators were repeatedly warned to stop the chants over the PA system and messages were displayed on screens.

The chanting was condemned by one fan group as a "stain on our game".

The Football Association later charged the club with failing "to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters) do not use words or behave in an improper, offensive, abusive, indecent or insulting way with a reference - whether express or implied - to sexual orientation" and on Friday announced the club had accepted the charge and received a £30,000 fine.

"Hull City condemns, in the strongest possible terms, the offensive and inappropriate language used by the supporters responsible," the club said, saying the "chant in question is recognised as a homophobic slur and its use may constitute a hate crime".

It warned those using the chant faced arrest and criminal charges.

"Ahead of Saturday's trip to Stamford Bridge, the club reminds all supporters that discrimination of any kind is wholly unacceptable and will not be tolerated," it added.

title: Hull's Thomas unhurt after car crash
description: Premier League winger Sorba Thomas's Land Rover overturns in Cottingham.
fullText:
Premier League winger Sorba Thomas has been involved in a car crash close to Hull City's training ground, the club has confirmed.

The 27-year-old walked away from the crash, which happened on Millhouse Woods Lane in Cottingham on Friday morning. His vehicle, a grey Land Rover Defender, was pictured on its roof, with broken windows.

Humberside Police said emergency services remained at the scene and asked people to avoid the area.

In a statement, the club said it was "relieved" to hear its player, who joined the Tigers from Championship side Stoke City earlier this month, was unharmed.

The club added: "The club is aware of images of Sorba's car circulating on social media and can reassure supporters that he has sustained no injuries and emerged from his vehicle completely unscathed."

A woman who lives at the scene said the crash, which happened at about 08:30 BST, woke her up.

"I was laid in bed [and] heard a noise – crash, bang," she said.

"I got up, come down and the car is in my hedge."

An NHS worker who lives on the road said the incident had left him unable to go to work as the road was blocked.

"There will be patients who will miss appointments because of this," he said.

"It's one road in and one road out. It was an accident waiting to happen."

Thomas signed for an undisclosed fee at the end of the transfer window until summer 2030.

He represented Wales at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.
