title: Sutton's predictions v Dorking Wanderers manager Marc White
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on Dorking Wanderers manager Marc White, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
New Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has made a table-topping start, but will his 100% Premier League record survive Sunday's short trip to Old Trafford?

"Marcus Rashford is fit and has looked a threat when I've seen him play," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton. "Because of that, I can see Manchester United scoring.

"But United have conceded twice against Hull, Ipswich and Everton, so why wouldn't they ship goals against City too?"

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week four, he takes on Dorking Wanderers manager Marc White.

White's story as founder, player and manager of his own club was the subject of a docuseries,, external which racked up more than half a billion views by the end of 2025. You can also follow his strategies and insights on TikTok., external

Do you agree with Sutton and White's scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

Seeing his club win a place in the Football League remains the aim for White, but reaching the Premier League feels a far more distant dream.

"For me the gulf in football is between the Premier League and some Championship clubs, and the rest," White told BBC Sport.

"The Premier League is still the elite place to be, and it's like being part of a financial institution when you are there, but you need to spend your money wisely.

"One big theory I have, if you flip it around the other way, is you would not want to get relegated from the Premier League.

"There are clubs in there, like Fulham or Bournemouth and Brentford, where arguably there are much bigger clubs than them in the Championship.

"That next manager is always so important for clubs of that size because, if they get it wrong and go down, some of them may never come back.

"The Championship is a little bit divided too. We do a lot of business with Charlton Athletic, and their finances, compared to the majority of that division, are nothing. There's no comparison between them and West Ham, for example. They are miles apart.

"Beyond that, there is not such a gap, but you can definitely put a thick border between the Championship and League One.

"I think that's why you see the likes of Bromley and Stockport go on the same journey from non-league that we are trying to make, and go up from League Two too. But then they get to League One and it is like the next bit is the tough bit."

Chris Sutton and Marc White were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

This is a hard one to start with because, while Aston Villa still haven't won or scored in the Premier League, they got a good win over Club Brugge in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Nicolas Jackson got off the mark in that game and, although his finishing can be erratic, he's the kind of player who will mature and get better every season. I think he will do well for them.

Forest are also yet to win. I know there was controversy over Neco Williams' disallowed goal in their draw against Spurs last time out but I do think they got the decision right in the end.

This is going to be close and I am tempted to go for another Forest draw, but Villa are obviously going to score in the Premier League at some point so I'll be brave and say they will edge it.

Marc's prediction: Villa have been turned inside-out over the summer, but they fall into that category of having a great manager and Unai Emery will stabilise them. 1-1

To say Bournemouth keep on throwing it away is a bit harsh, but they have been ahead in all three of their league games so far and have not won any of them.

Will they see this one through? I am not sure, but I like the way Cherries boss Marco Rose talks when he has been interviewed after games. He is a bright guy and he will get things right.

I was spot on with my prediction for Brentford's 1-1 draw with Sunderland last week, but the Bees were actually lucky to get a point in the end.

Brentford will play on the counter-attack here and Bournemouth will have a go at them, so this smells like a draw to me.

Marc's prediction: It's mad to think this was a League Two fixture in 2009, when Bournemouth almost went out of the Football League. With Brentford, it could be just a matter of time before Keith Andrews is seen as a manager who is desired by the big clubs. If he has another good season, someone will be in for him. 1-2

I have happy memories of this fixture because one of my three goals for Chelsea came against Hull, in the FA Cup.

Hull haven't conceded yet and they are the team I have been most wrong about so far this season.

With every passing week, they are putting more egg on my face [see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page] but it can't keep happening, can it?

It probably can, but I am still going for Chelsea to win this. The Tigers have defended brilliantly so far, but they are not going to keep out Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro.

Hull will defend ferociously but, as Chelsea showed in the Carabao Cup against Leeds on Wednesday, they have enough quality to play through teams who sit in; and, if they score first, then Hull will have to open up - that's my theory anyway.

The only thing I was unsure about was whether Hull would score too. Chelsea still seem to be a bit chaotic with the way they defend, and they have leaked a few goals, but I have given them a clean sheet. They need one.

Marc's prediction: It's a bit like Beauty and the Beast, this. Hull will be quite happy to be the beast, but there are some games where that won't work. With Chelsea's front-line, this is one of them. 4-0

Crystal Palace picked up their first win under Pierre Sage last weekend, which was really important for them.

They have still got goals in their team, as they showed against Fulham, but it was quite an open game and they always look like they will concede a few too.

I covered Ipswich's defeat by Liverpool and what worries me a little bit is the way their manager Gary O'Neil saw that game.

He was overly positive about his team's performance and, while I know why he is doing it, you can't mask that they didn't match Liverpool and they were not creative enough in the final third either - I don't remember Alisson having to make a save of note.

This feels like an important game for Ipswich after two successive defeats but I don't know why I am thinking they will get a point because that's not going to happen, is it?

My first thought was that they will grind out a draw, but I've changed my mind and am going with Palace to take the points at home.

Marc's prediction: Palace are in the bracket of clubs who might be in trouble this year, but I have put this down as a draw because they have got that Selhurst Park thing going on. 1-1

I am covering this game for 5 Live and will be co-commentating with Ian Dennis.

For Fulham, the big talking point is their manager, and whether they will sink any lower under Alvaro Arbeloa. He will be under pressure until he gets his first Premier League win.

Fulham look a little bit lightweight to me and, while Cesar Palacios in midfield and Gonzalo Garcia up front have clearly got something about them, it is always going to be hard for any young player to hit the ground running when they are thrown into the Premier League, especially under a manager who is new too.

If you don't get off to a good start, you are going to be scrutinised. It is the same for every manager and, while Fulham have got some good attacking players, they are shipping goals at the other end.

To lead twice against Palace, who had also started the season poorly, and still lose makes this game even bigger for Arbeloa.

He is trying to play a high pressing game, and he also wants to dominate the ball, but at the highest level, which the Premier League is, if you are not on point with your press then teams will play through you.

Arbeloa needs a result to kickstart his season, or at least something to grab hold of, and I don't think it's impossible for them to get something at Anfield.

I certainly don't think Liverpool have cracked it after watching them win at Ipswich, and they will give up some chances with their high defensive line too.

Fulham will score, but the problem for Arbeloa is that Liverpool will score more.

Marc on why he follows Fulham: I went to watch Fulham as a really small kid, which was my first memory of 'big' football, standing on the terrace at Craven Cottage, and I still go there now whenever we're not playing. I am friends with the captain, Tom Cairney, so luckily I get to watch them quite a lot. They are quite a unique family club at that level and I really enjoy it, plus it's a good chance to watch Premier League football.

Marc's prediction: Fulham have done the opposite of what Brentford did when Thomas Frank left. They don't just have a new manager to replace Marco Silva, they have a new system and with new players. It's a big gamble. 3-1

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 17:30

This is absolutely massive for Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi. First and foremost, though, he needs to take a bit of responsibility for his side's poor results.

He blamed the Spurs strikers after their 0-0 draw with Nottingham Forest, but at least he has got some in his squad.

I just find it wild that in a billion-dollar industry, which football is now, Everton got themselves in a position where they let Beto leave, knowing there was a possibility that Folarin Balogun might fail his medical and without having anyone else lined up.

Could they still go to Spurs and nick something? Absolutely. I am still not sure whether Tottenham being at home counts as an advantage.

But this game has a draw written all over it, and is actually an easy game to predict.

Spurs are a 'law of averages' team, or at least that's the way I see it. Eventually they have to score and eventually they have to win too, but I don't see both things happening this weekend.

Marc's prediction: Spurs have a new team but continue to frustrate their fans, while Everton just seem to go about their business. 2-2

This was a cracking game last season, which finished 2-2, and is arguably Arsenal's toughest test so far in this campaign.

I really like Sunderland and their European campaign has not started yet so those extra games won't affect them here.

I feel like being brave and giving them a draw because they are well capable of taking a point off Arsenal, but the Gunners just have the ability to shut up shop when they need to, and they can get physical again if they need to.

Thinking about it, I can't really go against an Arsenal victory, because of the players they were able to bring on in last weekend's comeback win against Chelsea.

They have got A-list replacements everywhere they look and, if they need a goal against Sunderland, I can see them bringing someone on to get them one.

Marc's prediction: I'm a bit worried about Sunderland this season. They had a lot of momentum last year, and they also made a really good start. 1-3

Coventry Building Society Arena, 14:00

Coventry played well against Manchester City and should have got something from the game, but didn't.

I can see them going toe-to-toe with Brighton, but it's dangerous to think they will get something this week just because they troubled Man City.

Brighton are a naturally attacking side, with some very good players. It will be hard to keep them out.

Marc's prediction: Clubs like Brighton are very astute. They know that these are the games to win - that's where their points come from. 0-2

I have got this result really badly wrong over the past couple of seasons, when I have tended to go for City, but I am not sure this time.

City are more methodical under Enzo Maresca, with the way that he builds play from the back - they won't be swashbuckling, put it that way.

I don't think he has changed much about his way of playing from when he was in charge at Chelsea, and United will be ready for that.

I really like United boss Michael Carrick and the way he does not get too carried away, win or lose.

Everton's late equaliser would have felt like a loss last weekend, but United still haven't clicked in attack yet, and that's part of the problem for them.

Then I look at the goals they are shipping too, and wonder if they are really good enough to keep City out?

I am not so sure they are, but I also think they can hurt City.

City have made a brilliant start, with four wins out of four in all competitions since the Premier League got under way, but if they looked a little vulnerable against Coventry then United are going to cause them more problems.

Marc's prediction: I think I know the way this is going for United. Carrick has had that natural bounce that a former player is going to get but, long term, sustaining that is tough. For me, he could become a manager under pressure this year.

With City, it's a sign of a good manager for them to start like this under Maresca. I have them down as clear winners here. 0-2

Newcastle are the new counter-attack kings and I am expecting more of the same from them here.

It will be interesting to see how Leeds boss Daniel Farke tries to deal with that. He has been quite versatile with the way he has set his side up this season.

Leeds have shown a bit more steel in their league games too, and look well organised, but at the same time I don't know if they carry as much of an attacking threat as they did previously.

I probably still fancy Leeds more to win this because they are at home, but Newcastle showed plenty of fight against Bournemouth last week and this will probably end up in a draw too.

Marc's prediction: A Monday night thriller. 2-3

As Chris said after a successful week two, "it's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it".

It was the final few fixtures which decided the outcome this time too - only it wasn't Chris who took the victory in week three.

He was leading on Saturday night after eight of the weekend's 10 games had been played, but his guest, Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, enjoyed a 'Super Sunday' with exact scores in both remaining games to snatch the overall win.

Chris ended up with six correct results, including one exact score, for a total of 90 points.

That was enough to beat the BBC readers, who managed four correct results with one exact score for a tally of 70 points, and also AI, which got three correct results and one exact score, giving it 60 points.

It was Serge who surged to victory, however, after correctly predicting Everton's 2-2 draw with Manchester United and Arsenal's 2-1 win over Chelsea.

He got four correct results but those two exact scores proved decisive, giving him a winning total of 100 points.

Everyone was right about only two of the fixtures - Liverpool's win at Ipswich and Manchester City's victory over Coventry.

There were three fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - the draws in Newcastle-Bournemouth and Brighton-Leeds, and Crystal Palace's 3-2 win at Fulham.

From more than 37,000 predictions, only around 5,000 (14%) went for any sort of Palace win, and only 79 of you got the correct scoreline.

title: $10m on line at inaugural Ultimate Championship
description: The inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship begins on Friday. From the global stars competing to how it all works - here is everything you need to know.
fullText:
One trophy, no medals. Ten million dollars. A red carpet. A black infield. Noah Lyles as MC. Armand Duplantis singing before eyeing another world record.

This athletics season was set to be the first since the pandemic which did not culminate in an Olympic Games or World Championships.

To bridge that gap, the sport's governing body has devised a new competition.

Introducing: The World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

Across three days of competition in Budapest, live on the BBC from 11-13 September, the world's top athletes will compete for record prize money and a new title.

A new event pitching the best against the best, with increased financial commitments. You may be thinking: 'Haven't we been here before?'

Last year, Michael Johnson's inaugural Grand Slam Track league attempted to maintain focus on the sport following Paris 2024 while offering lucrative prize money, but ended after encountering serious financial issues.

This innovative, biennial format is bankrolled by World Athletics - and president Sebastian Coe has said he hopes to use it as an "incubator for change" which will shape the future of the sport's established World Championships.

So, how does the Ultimate Championship work, what do the athletes think, and is it needed? Here is everything you need to know.

The sport has long grappled with the issue of retaining the attention and excitement it generates at the Olympics throughout those four-year cycles.

Because of the disruption caused by the pandemic, and subsequent postponement of the Tokyo 2020 Games, each of the past five years have provided a pinnacle event which gathered the biggest stars in front of a global audience.

For many top British athletes, a 2026 season centred around a Commonwealth Games and European Championship on home soil would probably have finished at the Diamond League Final.

Coe and World Athletics have planned for three years to fill that perceived void.

"It is an attempt to just start experimenting a bit and innovating, with an event that will determine who really is the best of the best," Coe told BBC Sport.

"There's no guarantee we're going get everything right, and no guarantee that everything is going to work. In two years, we might look at a slightly different format.

"I also want to be able to put some of the things we're doing into the World Championship format. We have a responsibility to try and engage new young audiences."

World Athletics Ultimate Championship

Day one coverage: Friday, 11 September 18:00-21:00 - BBC Two, BBC iPlayer, BBC Sport website & app

The Ultimate features a condensed three-night schedule, held as three-hour sessions.

It is reserved for reigning Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, plus athletes who have qualified by world ranking.

However, a few star names who did not qualify have been granted exceptional invitations, including Great Britain's Josh Kerr and Norwegian rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen into the men's 1500m.

There will be a total of 28 finals, including straight finals in all field events and both the 1500m and the 5,000m. The 800m and shorter distances will have semi-finals.

Not every discipline has been included, however. World Athletics says those decisions were taken based on the popularity of each event and data it gathered on viewer behaviour, including sweat response and pulse rate.

As a result, long distance events such as the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, and field events such as the shot put and discus, have been left out.

World Athletics is providing "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport" with a total of $10m (£7.4m) to be won.

Each individual event winner will pocket $150,000 (£110,000) - more than double the offering at last year's World Championships - with $75,000 (£55,000) for the runner-up and $40,000 (£29,500) for third.

World Athletics has introduced several innovations for the inaugural event in an attempt to develop both the fan and athlete experience. They include:

The day before: The eve of the championship will include a red carpet entrance for athletes, with a designated media day featuring press conferences and photoshoots.

The lane draft: Athletes contesting the 200m will take part in a lane draft, selecting their preferred semi-final heat and lane in world rankings order.

No medals: Only the Ultimate champions will receive a trophy, which will be waiting for them to collect on a plinth at the end of their event.

Adapted for TV: There will be the use of augmented reality, athlete headshots, win probabilities and projected finishing positions to develop viewer experience.

Entertainment: Pole vault star Duplantis will perform the official song of the championship among the live acts, while American sprinter Lyles - ruled out by injury - will act as host. Centre-court style interviews will follow events.

Attention-grabbing look: The black infield is designed to steer focus to the ongoing action, with only the active competition areas highlighted in contrast.

Great Britain have confirmed a team of 22 athletes for the championship, including Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson.

Hodgkinson will be reunited with rivals Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol in the women's 800m, having taken European silver behind Werro in August.

Training partner Georgia Hunter Bell contests the 1500m seeking a fourth major title of 2026 following European, Commonwealth and world indoor success.

After winning a remarkable four European titles, Amy Hunt will race against global champions including Julien Alfred, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and Gabby Thomas in the 100m and 200m, while the mixed 4x100m relay is also included in the schedule.

European gold and silver medallists Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu contest the men's 100m alongside world champion Oblique Seville, while Matthew Hudson-Smith is in the 400m after his triumph in Birmingham.

Mile world record holder Kerr, world champion in 2023, is joined by 2022 world champion Jake Wightman in a stacked men's 1500m featuring Ingebrigtsen, Olympic champion Cole Hocker and world champion Isaac Nader.

Ingebrigtsen is also entered in the 5,000m, having returned from long-term injury to win European gold in that event last month.

'I'm not a robot' - Kerr responds to criticism before Ingebrigtsen reunion

Many of the sport's biggest names have voiced their support for athletics' new global event.

Pole vault world record holder Duplantis was named as the inaugural 'Ultimate Star' last summer and has collaborated on the official anthem for the championship, Gold, which he has written and performed.

"It's super exciting. I think it was time to try something new and innovate within athletics," Duplantis said.

"It's tough for athletes when we have years without a championship. I think this fills the gap perfectly, you want to have some sort of climax to build towards."

Kerr, set for a first race against rival Ingebrigtsen for two years, said the substantial increase in prize money showed how "serious" World Athletics are about the event.

However, while the 2023 world champion agrees that a global championship was needed, he accepts there is "probably going to be some confusion from the outside world about what this is".

"If that's what they're willing to put forward in prize money, it means that they're willing to put that effort into marketing and media," said Kerr.

"We're seeing progress. Obviously, $150,000 is a lot of money. It's not as much as other big sports, but they've earned that through years of pushing their marketing."

Hurdles star Karsten Warholm has voiced his concern regarding the impact on the calendar, describing this year's late-season schedule as "chaos".

"I think the Diamond League is a fantastic concept that should be cultivated. It will take a long time before people understand what an Ultimate Champion is," Warholm told Norwegian media outlet VG.

"It's pretty much the same athletes who participate but there could be two different winners at the Diamond League final and the Ultimate Championship.

"In terms of storytelling, it's going to be difficult. I don't think even athletics people are keeping up."

There is also the matter of the excluded athletes and events.

World triple jump champion Pedro Pichardo responded on social media to the decision to exclude his discipline: "I really don't understand what your problem is, and even less so making this decision without any explanation.

"This isn't track and field and it's not good for our sport."

After ending her season with victory in the Diamond League Final, world shot put champion Chase Jackson told Citius Mag: "My body is saying 'yes' but my pockets are saying 'why the hell am I not at the Ultimate?'

"How [do] you have track and field and just skip events? How does that make any sense?"

Hunt 'not afraid of anyone' after 100m second-place finish

title: Bed at 6:45am - US Open semi-finalists fight effects of late-night finishes
description: New York is known as the city that never sleeps. But that comes at a price for US Open stars - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev.
fullText:
New York is known as the city that never sleeps - and so it has been at this year's US Open.

A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal.

But when some players - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev - are heading to bed as Manhattan commuters are waking up for work, it raises questions about fairness.

Three of top seed Zverev's five matches over the past fortnight have finished past 1am.

"I've been to bed as late as 6:45am in the past week so I'm kind of a bit jet-lagged," Zverev said.

"I feel like I'm playing the Australian Open in New York right now."

Friday's semi-final against Karen Khachanov - not before 15:00 local time/20:00 BST - will be the first time the German has played in the day at this year's US Open.

American eighth seed Shelton did not complete his last-eight victory over Carlos Alcaraz until 3:34am on Wednesday.

Shelton faces 11th seed Frances Tiafoe, who wrapped up his quarter-final about 19:00 on Tuesday after beating US compatriot Alex Michelsen in a five-set epic.

"The advantage of the opponent who has played earlier in the day will be big - they've had that full evening's rest and a good night's sleep," Matt Little, who was Andy Murray's long-time strength and conditioning coach, told BBC Sport.

"We can all relate to it - if you have one really bad night's sleep, you have the knock-on effect of that for the coming days."

Little saw the effects first hand when Murray infamously finished a match at 4am at the 2023 Australian Open, with the former world number one managing only three hours sleep before returning to Melbourne Park about 11am the following day.

Zverev did not go to bed until gone 5am following his opening three victories at Flushing Meadows and stayed up to watch Shelton beat Alcaraz on his night off.

Shelton, who meets Tiafoe in Friday's night session (19:00 local time/00:00 BST, Sat), insisted he would pull up "all right" after two days off court.

"He'll have to be napping to catch up some sleep," said Little.

"On the nutritional side, he'll be making sure he gets as many carbs and as much protein as he can in for that next match, and trying to get back to a bit of a routine.

"It's about making sure you can optimise the hydration and get as much sleep as possible without completely going into a full slumber."

Murray described the situation in Melbourne - where he beat Thanasi Kokkinakis in the second-latest finish in Grand Slam history - as a "farce".

Few disagreed, and slight tweaks have been made in an attempt to limit matches finishing at the crack of dawn.

In response to Murray's match, the Australian Open cut the number of day-session matches on the main courts from three to two to reduce the risk of night sessions being delayed.

In early 2024, the ATP and WTA created new rules which prevented tour matches - played over three sets and not five like the Slams - starting after 23:00. These rules, however, do not apply at the majors.

Last week, former world number one Venus Williams and her opponent Sofia Kenin began their first-round match at 12:13am - the latest start in US Open history.

It was one of three matches which finished post-2am in the first seven nights, with three others ending after 1am, while Shelton's victory over Alcaraz was the latest finish in US Open history.

"Something has got to give," said 18-time Grand Slam singles champion Martina Navratilova. "This is not OK and it is not normal."

Some argue these occasions are the essence of the US Open - and a raucous sporting representation of the city which never sleeps.

The volume of early-morning matches has increased at Flushing Meadows this fortnight, although Tuesday's play finishing at 3:34am on Wednesday was the product of unusual circumstances.

All three preceding quarter-finals on Arthur Ashe Stadium - Aryna Sabalenka beating Linda Noskova and Jessica Pegula overcoming Emma Navarro, with Tiafoe's win sandwiched in the middle - went the full distance.

Data shows matches are becoming longer - so what is the solution?

Starting the US Open night sessions earlier is the most common proposal.

That is met by a resistance from television executives and the practicality of New York life, with many fans unlikely to arrive at Flushing Meadows much before 7pm.

There is a more extreme suggestion - cutting back on the best-of-five sets format at the Slams.

That idea gained further traction after Andrew Abdo - Tennis Australia's recently-appointed chief executive - suggested the Australian Open could look to reduce men's matches to three sets in the future.

Abdo's comments provoked a backlash, with Tiafoe among those defending the traditional way.

"Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not," Tiafoe said.

"But it's tennis, man. I grew up watching so many incredible five-setters.

"Novak-Rafa, Federer-Rafa, epic five-setters that go on for hours and hours. That's the history of the game."

title: Raiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of Atlantis
description:
We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?
We join Lara Croft in St Francis’ Folly – inspired by the Unesco-listed monasteries of Meteora in Greece – as the light shines through the cracked ceiling and a flock of bats glide across the vast ruins below. When Lara leaps down to the monastery’s crumbling pillared courtyard, it becomes clear that these screeching, leathery creatures aren’t just set dressing. As they lurch towards her with unpredictable movements, she dispatches the swarm with a flurry of gun fire and panicked punches.
fullText:
We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?

We join Lara Croft in St Francis’ Folly – inspired by the Unesco-listed monasteries of Meteora in Greece – as the light shines through the cracked ceiling and a flock of bats glide across the vast ruins below. When Lara leaps down to the monastery’s crumbling pillared courtyard, it becomes clear that these screeching, leathery creatures aren’t just set dressing. As they lurch towards her with unpredictable movements, she dispatches the swarm with a flurry of gun fire and panicked punches.

It’s a suitably cinematic reintroduction to our heroine and her very first adventure. Co-developed by longtime Lara custodians Crystal Dynamics and Polish studio Flying Wild Hog, Legacy of Atlantis is a reimagining of the classic 1996 game Tomb Raider, and this familiar cliffside location is now brimming with new life and believable detail. Yet while our reunion gets off to an auspicious start, I have my concerns. It feels like reconnecting with an old friend at the pub, only for them to begin spouting conspiracy theories two pints in.

Where the ’96 original forced players to rely on their wits – or a pricey strategy guide – to figure out what to do, Lara can now straight-up cheat. She’s equipped with an environmental scanner, so a button tap reveals extra environmental lore or simply the solution to a puzzle. It’s a change that feels somewhat sacrilegious, and may detract from the eerily isolating atmosphere that made the original so beloved.

“If the devs from 1996 had the technology that we have today, what choices would they make?” asks Raul Siqueira, game director at Crystal Dynamics. “The sense of isolation in the original game was largely due to the technological limitations of that time,” says Arek Tomaszewski, art director at Flying Wild Hog, likening it to the fog in Silent Hill which was both an artistic decision and a way to cover up empty environments on the PlayStation 1. “The darkness and the feeling of being alone created an emotion that you remember. When I replayed Tomb Raider, my initial memory was the exact same. What we are trying to do now is build environments – like the spaces in Greece – where you feel as if you are the first person discovering them in centuries, entering places that have been left untouched.”

Lara now crafts balms from a menu rather than finding anachronous first aid kits in centuries-old untouched tombs. Somewhat less believably, she can also pause her adventure to whip up stat-boosting stews, Breath of the Wild-style. These additions are among a slew of modern flourishes that I feel unsure about. Is the original really improved by giving Lara a grappling hook, RPG-esque stats, skill trees and quick time events?

One area that Flying Wild Hog – the maker of Hard Reset and Shadow Warrior – knows well is combat. As Lara delves deeper into the dingy ruins of the Damocles chamber, she is ambushed by a familiar foe: a leopard. But this roaring beast now moves with convincing agility. As well as swiping at Lara, leopards now hide from her, retreating through holes in the walls before returning with an emboldened counterattack. Luckily Lara is fiercer too. As the beast lunges toward her, she draws her shotgun and blasts, causing the creature to crumple to the floor in Max Payne-esque slo-mo. The newly dynamic combat is the gameplay overhaul that looks most promising – a world away from the stationary shooting and “dog scooting across the carpet” backsteps of yesteryear.

Narratively, the remake promises a deeper story and some fan-pleasing easter eggs. For this iteration, Lara is played by Dragon Age: Inquisition and Cyberpunk 2077 actor Alix Wilton Regan. “Hearing her voice in the game now, she is Lara Croft,” says Tomaszewski. “The sheer amount of character and depth she brought to Lara is unbelievable.” The game’s publisher, Amazon, is also the custodian of a forthcoming Phoebe Waller-Bridge-produced Tomb Raider TV show, and the developers suggest there will be some connective tissue between the two projects. After hopping across falling swords and solving Damocles’s puzzles, Lara emerges from the darkened tomb into a burst of sunshine, and my demo culminates with the tease of a vast, ancient civilisation.

“I think this game changed our DNA as a studio,” says Tomaszewski. “In our previous games, like Shadow Warrior, every second was filled with nonstop action. Here we wanted to master pacing, and we learned a lot from Crystal Dynamics.”

Gaming as a whole has undoubtedly transformed since Lara’s first adventure. Tomb Raider’s dodgy camera controls and questionable Playboy collaborations are thankfully now dusty historical relics themselves. Yet as visually impressive as Legacy of Atlantis looks, I can’t help but wonder if a touch of Lara’s brilliance lay in her original simplicity. By encumbering her with modern game mechanics, a bit of her soul may be lost. If Legacy of Atlantis offers the option to disable all of that for a purer Tomb-raiding experience, it could still be a winner.

Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis is scheduled for release in February

This interview took place at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by Gamescom.

title: UK economy unexpectedly grows 0.4% in July boosted by AI
description:
Welcome boost for chancellor with unexpected rise put down to rapid growth of AI in services sector outweighing Iran war fallout 
The UK economy grew in July as the rapid expansion of AI appeared to outweigh the economic damage from the Iran war, in a welcome boost for John Healey.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product (GDP), compared with 0.3% growth in June. City economists had forecast zero growth.
fullText:
Welcome boost for chancellor with unexpected rise put down to rapid growth of AI in services sector outweighing Iran war fallout

The UK economy grew in July as the rapid expansion of AI appeared to outweigh the economic damage from the Iran war, in a welcome boost for John Healey.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product (GDP), compared with 0.3% growth in June. City economists had forecast zero growth.

The figures suggested the economy continued to be robust despite the fallout from the Iran war, which has raised energy costs and led to higher interest rates than were expected at the start of the year.

The ONS said the expansion in July was driven by growth of 0.4% in the services sector, particularly admin services, and computer programming and consulting. Within the latter sector, it said: “Many of the businesses reporting the largest turnover in July 2026 are involved in activities related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing.”

Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “At a time when many traditional parts of the economy remain subdued, this is exactly the kind of productivity-enhancing spending the UK needs more of.”

PWC’s chief economist, Barret Kupelian said: “Artificial intelligence continues to have imprints across the UK economy, with AI exposed sectors – professional services, information technology, administrative services – recording strong growth.”

The ONS said industrial production was also up in July, by 0.2%, with a rise in manufacturing output offsetting falls in mining, and electricity and gas supply.

Over the three months to July – a period the ONS says is more representative of economic conditions – GDP growth was also 0.4%, the same pace as in the three months to June.

Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “The UK growth story is becoming harder to ignore. Households and businesses are still spending – despite the unfolding energy shock impacting disposable incomes.”

The economy’s continued strength is good news for Healey, the chancellor, as he prepares for his first budget on 28 October, though experts have warned that the longer-term picture for the economy is less positive.

Healey said: “Britain’s economy is demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty. Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year. But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home – from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing.”

Economists fear the latest rise in the global oil price – to well above $100 a barrel – is likely to stoke higher inflation worldwide, prompting rising borrowing costs.

Higher interest rates on the UK’s debt are expected to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom Healey’s predecessor had built up against the fiscal rules – potentially forcing him to increase taxes or cut spending at the budget.

Since the recent jump in oil prices, markets have raised their expectations for future interest rates and now expect the Bank of England’s policymakers to make four quarter-point rises over the next twelve months.

Rates are still expected to remain on hold, at 3.75%, when the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee meets next week, however, despite the stronger-than-expected growth figures.

Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the accountancy body the ICAEW, said: “While these figures may strengthen the hawkish mood among rate-setters, a September rate rise still looks unlikely as most policymakers remain hopeful that a sluggish economy will ultimately help bring inflation under control, despite escalating US-Iran tensions.”

As well as strong growth in AI-related sectors, the ONS highlighted the economic impact of the summer heat, and the World Cup, which culminated in mid-July.

Its director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, said: “some businesses reported that the warm weather and Fifa World Cup had affected their activity, although effects differed across industries, benefiting some businesses while creating challenges for others.”

The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith said: “Nobody in this Labour government should be high-fiving themselves. Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we’ve got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years.”

title: China’s Huawei branded a criminal enterprise as tech firm’s US trial opens
description:
The defense says: ‘It’s about competition, not conspiracy’ 
A US prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from US companies to build its telecommunications empire, as ⁠the trial against the tech company kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.
“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the US Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies ⁠and abused the American financial system, all ⁠in an effort to dominate the telecommunications ​industry around the world.”
 Continue reading...
fullText:
The defense says: ‘It’s about competition, not conspiracy’

A US prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from US companies to build its telecommunications empire, as ⁠the trial against the tech company kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.

“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the US Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies ⁠and abused the American financial system, all ⁠in an effort to dominate the telecommunications ​industry around the world.”

Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from five US companies, including operating system source code for internet routers from Cisco Systems and a robotic arm to test phones from T-Mobile, to gain an unfair competitive advantage and grow its business, ⁠the prosecutor told jurors.

“We’ll hear from people who caught Huawei red-handed trying to steal American tech,” Stout said, adding there was video of an employee stealing the robotic arm.

The defense painted a very different picture of the company and its success in court.

“It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, ⁠not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct,” Brian Heberlig, one of a team of lawyers representing Huawei, said in his opening. “Huawei earned its success ... There was no blueprint for crime.”

Huawei is known ​for its telecommunications equipment, mobile phones and, in recent years, AI chips. It does ‌business globally but its networking gear is restricted in ‌the US and suppliers are banned from exporting US goods and technology to the company without approval from the Department of Commerce.

On Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said “the Chinese ‌government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” when asked about the case and the US prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.

China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular press conference.

The case against Huawei began in 2018 with an indictment charging the company and its chief financial officer with bank fraud and sanctions violations for allegedly misrepresenting its business in Iran to get around US sanctions and move millions of dollars through the US financial system.

In the ensuing years, it grew into a sprawling indictment that includes racketeering, a pattern of illegal activity conducted by an enterprise to generate profit.

Heberlig, defending Huawei, told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities ‌by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.

He said the incidents involving Cisco and T-mobile were “actions by individual employees” and that ​management worked to make things right after learning of them.

The prosecutor also accused the company of keeping the nature of its work in Iran secret so it could launder US dollars through the financial system and could help the Iranian government spy on its own citizens. The defense said there was no evidence Huawei knew the dollar-clearing would violate US sanctions law.

In 2018, Huawei’s chief financial officer, ​Meng Wanzhou, was detained in Vancouver after being picked up on ​a US warrant as a part of the original indictment. She fought extradition for nearly three years before being freed to return to China ​in a diplomatic agreement between the US, China ‌and Canada.

The charges against her ​were dismissed in 2022 as part ​of a deferred prosecution agreement but admissions she made are set to be introduced as evidence at the trial, which is expected to last three months.

title: Hundreds rally at Israeli embassy in Bangkok to demand foreigners respect Thai laws
description: Hundreds of people demonstrated outside Israel's embassy in Bangkok on Thursday to demand foreigners show more respect for Thailand's laws and culture as public discontent over bad behavior by visitor...
fullText:
BANGKOK (AP) — Hundreds of people demonstrated outside Israel's embassy in Bangkok on Thursday to demand foreigners show more respect for Thailand's laws and culture as public discontent over bad behavior by visitors has increasingly focused on Israeli tourists.

"The era of gentle diplomatic pleasantries and calculated silence, which has been misinterpreted as tacit consent, has come to an end," protest leader Sondhi Limthongkul, a media mogul and political activist, told the crowd while reading from an open letter to Israel's ambassador to Thailand, Alona Fisher-Kamm.

Recent incidents drawing public scrutiny in Thailand have involved tourists of several nationalities, but one of the highest profile cases was of an Israeli tourist who was convicted of threatening a zoo owner and then deported.

Fisher-Kamm met Tuesday with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow to address concerns and discuss possible solutions.

Sondhi said the embassy and Israeli government should understand "generosity must never be mistaken for weakness, hospitality does not equate to submission to exploitation and courtesy is not an open license for anyone to act with impunity on our sovereign soil."

In a video message posted to Facebook on Thursday following the morning protest, Israeli embassy Deputy Chief of Mission Rami Teplitskiy said they are not ignoring news and negative sentiments about Israeli tourists in Thailand.

"The embassy will continue to work hard to foster sustainable friendship and ensure everyone enjoys Thailand with mutual respect," he said in a message delivered in Hebrew with English and Thai subtitles.

The relevant agencies in both countries are working to resolve the issues together and Israeli visitors to Thailand will receive official travel guidance asking them to respect Thai laws and culture, Teplitskiy said.

Sondhi, who founded a protest movement that led to the 2006 ouster of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, voiced a litany of complaints against Israelis in Thailand, including violations of domestic laws, creating public disturbances and showing disrespect for local traditions and cultures.

Thailand's economy is heavily dependent on tourism, but also has implemented new measures to ensure visitors respect the country's norms. The government also has cracked down on foreigners who overstay visas or seek to circumvent property-ownership regulations, while also shortening visa-free stays.

Israeli visitors last year generated about $1.2 billion of Thailand's $48 billion in income derived from tourism. More than 277,000 Israelis visited Thailand in the first eight months of 2026, up about 7% over the same period last year, according to Thailand's Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul last week ordered the deportation of an Israeli man who was convicted of threatening a zoo owner on the resort island of Koh Samui. The zoo had displayed a Palestinian flag.

The case was the first use of new regulations designed to ease the deportation of foreigners who break Thai laws or show "undesirable behavior."

The French citizen who owned the zoo also had been accused of causing several other unrelated disturbances and was ordered to be deported days later.

While there has been a focus on Israelis, a confrontation in July between a Thai woman and a group of boisterous Italian students on a Bangkok train was caught on video and went viral, sparking widespread anger against the visitors. The Italian embassy intervened and posted an apology video from the group.

The Jerusalem Post reported that Fisher-Kamm, the Israeli ambassador, acknowledged the concerns during the meeting with Sihasak and proposed issuing a "do's and don'ts" document for Israeli travelers, which was a demand by protesters on Thursday.

The Thai foreign minister said after the meeting that Thailand felt it could not "stand idly by" if visitors are acting detrimentally toward the country or people.

"Thailand is a country that welcomes tourists, but at the same time, our hospitality doesn't mean that tourists, regardless of their nationality, can do whatever they want in Thailand," Sihasak told reporters in Bangkok.

The Israeli embassy told The Associated Press on Wednesday it takes the concerns seriously and has provided practical guidance about Thailand to Israeli communities, adding that those who violate the laws should face appropriate consequences.

Public attention, however, may be disproportionate to the scale of incidents involving Israeli citizens and should not be taken as a representation of all Israelis in Thailand, the embassy said.

Chabad of Thailand, the country's branch of an Orthodox Jewish movement that was mentioned by name in the open letter by protesters, said it had no immediate comment on the demonstration or the letter.

David Rising in Bangkok and Natalie Melzer in Nahariya, Israel, contributed to this report.

As Trump squeezes the International Criminal Court, more countries are leaving
description: As the United States ratchets up the pressure on the International Criminal Court, sanctioning two more high-ranking staff members in recent weeks, a small but growing number of the global tribunal’s ...
fullText:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — As the United States ratchets up the pressure on the International Criminal Court, sanctioning two more high-ranking staff members in recent weeks, a small but growing number of the global tribunal's member states have announced they will quit the institution.

The recent departure of Venezuela and Chad brings the number of countries to pull out of the court in the past year to five, joining Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The surge in withdrawals comes as the ICC faces hostility from Washington and a leadership crisis after ousting its own chief prosecutor.

"Five countries so far have announced plans to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and we welcome more announcements in the future," a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told The Associated Press.

The Rome Statute established the ICC in 2002 as the court of last resort to prosecute individuals responsible for the world's most heinous atrocities: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression. Based in The Hague, it takes on cases when nations are unable or unwilling to prosecute crimes on their own territory.

"The ICC regrets any decision to depart from the collective effort to end impunity for the most serious international crimes," the court's spokesperson Oriane Maillet told the AP.

In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty."

Rubio said he will pressure the court's 125 member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organizations that work with the court and ban staff from traveling to the United States. Trump's administration already has sanctioned a dozen ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials over the war in Gaza and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.

The Central African country of Chad specifically cited the United States in its decision to withdraw. Its Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul said in a statement that in a phone call with a U.S. official on July 23, "the American side expressed its concerns regarding the functioning of this institution and requested that Chad reconsider" its membership.

Four days later, Chad said it would leave the ICC.

Iva Vukušić, a researcher at Utrecht University, told the AP that the U.S. campaign will lay bare just how committed countries are to the court. "Are they willing to defend it if it costs them something real?" she said.

The State Department told AP the U.S. would call upon nations that "enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella" to reject the ICC.

It's not just pressure from Trump that is sending ICC members toward the exit door.

The ruling military juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger blamed selective justice. The ICC has become an "instrument of neocolonial repression in the hands of imperialism," the trio said when they announced their departures last year.

A coup ousted Niger's democratically elected government in 2023. Since then, a military junta has abandoned longtime partners and has formed new alliances instead, including with Russia, where President Vladimir Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant linked to the war in Ukraine. Mali and Burkina Faso have undergone similar transformations.

"These countries are ruled by authoritarian leaders who want to avoid accountability for the harms they are inflicting on their own people," Mel O'Brien, an associate professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, told the AP.

Burundi similarly accused the court of focusing too much on conflicts in Africa when, in 2017, it became the first country to leave the ICC. The court had opened an investigation into the East African nation earlier that year.

Most of the court's initial investigations were into African countries, though most requested the involvement of the ICC.

South Africa and Gambia also announced in 2017 that they would leave but later changed course.

A change of government can also bring a country back into the fold. Hungary announced it would quit the court in 2025 but following the election of a new government, the country's parliament voted to stay.

The court also had an active investigation in the Philippines when then-President Rodrigo Duterte said his country would leave the ICC. In 2019 the Southeast Asian country became the second country to leave but as withdrawal from the court is not retroactive, the investigation continued.

Duterte is now in ICC detention in the Netherlands awaiting trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deadly anti-drug crackdowns he allegedly oversaw while in office. Opening statements are set for November.

An investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro will continue despite the country's announcement last month that it will also leave the ICC.

In a statement, the country's Foreign Minister Félix Plasencia said the court had been "instrumentalized to deepen inequalities among peoples and disregard their right to self-determination and sovereignty."

Venezuela is currently in the middle of U.S.-backed talks between the ruling party and the opposition following Maduro's capture in January by U.S. forces.

Ukraine is the court's most recent addition. The country joined in 2025 and previously had signed an agreement to give the court jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, following the outbreak of hostilities with Russia in 2014.

Joining the court was "Ukraine's way of saying that accountability for the gravest crimes cannot be optional, and that we intend to help build that system of justice," the country's ambassador to the Netherlands, Andriy Kostin, told AP.

title: Iran-backed terror group’s latest territorial grab threatens second global shipping chokepoint
description: Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen's Mocha port and advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb, threatening Red Sea shipping as Brent crude surged past $106.
fullText:
Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen's strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday and pushed toward positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opening a potentially dangerous new front for global trade as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely constrained.

The advance threatens the southern gateway to the Red Sea just as Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on that route to bypass Hormuz — putting pressure on critical shipping lanes on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula and raising the risk of further disruptions to oil and commercial traffic through a key global trade choke point.

"Now you have Iran on one side of the Arabian Peninsula controlling Hormuz, and now the Houthis controlling Bab el-Mandeb on the other side of the peninsula," Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen advisor at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital. "Which basically is going to drive prices — oil prices, goods and everything else — up exponentially."

Iran-backed Terror Proxy Houthis Threaten Fresh Attacks After Yemen Airport Strike

On background, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

Yemeni government sources said Thursay the Houthis captured Mocha and reached the Hanish Islands, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces withdrew south toward Dhubab, which sits directly on the Bab el-Mandeb opposite the strategic island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and Perim would be critical to gaining a stronger hold over the strait, Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Sept. 10.

Bab el-Mandeb is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and connects the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, farther north, the Suez Canal. It is a major artery for goods moving between Asia and Europe as well as energy shipments.

Its importance has grown dramatically during the Iran conflict.

Who Controls The Strait Of Hormuz Right Now? Here's What The Ship Traffic Actually Shows

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported Sept. 9 that crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through Bab el-Mandeb averaged 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.4 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025. At the same time, flows through Hormuz plunged from 21.6 million barrels per day to just 4.9 million. The EIA attributed the increase at Bab el-Mandeb in part to Saudi Arabia rerouting crude through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to avoid Hormuz.

Al-Omeisy said the danger extends beyond the Houthis' geographical gains. He said retreating government forces left behind military materiel that could strengthen Houthi forces on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."

Rubio AccU.S.Es Iran Of Flying Irgc Personnel Into Yemen As Houthi Threat Escalates

The seizure comes amid what conflict-monitoring organization ACLED described Sept. 9 as the most serious escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed camp since hostilities resumed in mid-July.

ACLED recorded at least 276 fatalities between Sept. 3 and 7 as clashes spread across al-Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwa, al-Jawf, al-Hudayda and Taizz, according to an analysis published Sept. 9.

Sherwan Hindreen Ali, ACLED's Middle East research manager, said fighting along the Red Sea coast had become particularly intense as both sides sought control over territory with direct strategic importance to Bab el-Mandeb.

"Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in al-Hudaydah and Taizz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia/IRG have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab el-Mandab," Ali said in an analysis.

Saudi Arabia itself has also become more deeply involved.

Expert Warns Of 'General Escalation' Of Fighting If Houthis Resume Red Sea Campaign

Ali said Saudi forces launched at least 15 strikes against the Houthis between Sept. 3 and 7, mostly around Taizz, marking the highest number of Saudi strikes since Riyadh resumed military engagement against the Houthis in July.

The Houthis responded Sept. 8 with what Ali described as their largest wave of direct attacks on Saudi territory since March 2022, launching dozens of drones and ballistic missiles toward Abha, Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait. Ali said the attacks injured 73 people.

The widening fighting is now posing an early test for a new joint defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.

Al-Omeisy said the international response allowed the Houthis to exploit divisions among their opponents.

"The Houthis are also good in exploiting divisions and delays, they move rapidly on the ground to force a status quo while the international community debates merits, responsibilities and costs of an intervention."

The escalation also raises questions about Saudi Arabia's newly signed defense agreement with Pakistan and Turkey.

Iran-backed Houthi Threat In Red Sea Could Lead To Major Us Policy Shift, Analysts Say

The agreement, signed last month in Mecca, states that an armed attack against one member will be considered an attack against all three, Reuters reported Sept. 10. But after Houthi drones and ballistic missiles struck Saudi cities and energy infrastructure this week, Pakistan said Thursday that no military response under the pact was currently being discussed.

"There is no such thing under discussion right now," Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said, according to Reuters. "When time comes [we] will act under the agreement."

The Houthis, meanwhile, have said international navigation through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remains safe, while maintaining that Saudi vessels are subject to their previously announced blockade, Reuters reported Thursday.

Al-Omeisy warned that reversing the Houthis' latest territorial gains could become increasingly difficult.

"The Houthis are really good at capturing a position, they entrench really well," he said. "They send these massive reinforcements, and then it's going to be extremely difficult to push them out of those areas."

Oil markets were already responding to the widening regional threat Thursday. Brent crude jumped more than 5% to $106.60 a barrel by late Thursday morning, while U.S. crude climbed above $100 for the first time since May, according to Reuters.

title: Billionaire Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong says most charities are ‘net negative’—and that he has no plans to make his own foundation
description: The crypto billionaire says he has a donor-advised fund but no plans to start a foundation, joining Elon Musk in casting doubt on traditional giving.
fullText:
Elon Musk isn't the only billionaire who has a contrarian view of philanthropy. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong admitted on a recently published episode of the Katie Miller Pod he doesn't think charities have much of a positive impact on the world.

"The common view is that philanthropy is like this noble cause," said Armstrong, who is worth nearly $10 billion. "I guess I have sort of a contrarian view, which is like a lot of charities and philanthropies are actually net negative on the world, and they get captured."

He went on to argue it's "remarkably hard to find" a philanthropic organization that hasn't gotten captured by ideology and hasn't had unintended consequences on the world. Armstrong, the CEO of the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, gave the example of a hypothetical nonprofit organization focused on criminal justice reform that ultimately "just increased crime."

Armstrong said his main fear about setting up a foundation is "that it just gets captured by some ideology [and] that I lose control of it." He drew a comparison to Henry Ford, who he argued would be "turning over in his grave" if he knew what the Ford Foundation was doing. That organization awards grants to reduce poverty, stop injustice, and advance human welfare and has awarded about $4 billion across thousands of grants.

Armstrong said, though, he does have a donor advised fund (DAF), "and I just try to put money toward things that I think are helping civilization advance," although he didn't mention exactly what those causes are. DAFs essentially serve as a personal charitable savings account allowing people to set aside money for charity, get an immediate tax break, and choose where the money goes later.

While he didn't say he would never form a foundation, he said it would be "crazy" to do so now.

While some billionaires, such as MacKenzie Scott (who has given away more than $26 billion) and Melinda French Gates, have been on a giving spree, other ultrawealthy people don't see the same ease or value in making philanthropic donations.

Musk, the world's richest man, has infamously lamented how difficult it is to give away money effectively. He also made a direct jab at Scott, arguing her philanthropy was making the world a "worse place."

Peter Thiel, the venture capitalist and PayPal cofounder, also said the Giving Pledge—the campaign urging the ultrawealthy to give away most of their fortunes—has "really run out of energy," adding he's nudged fellow signatories to walk it back.

Trump rejected the request, and U.S. officials said the ​administration does not intend to take direct military action against the Houthis at this time, the report said.

According to Axios, the U.S. is increasingly concerned about the ⁠rapidly escalating conflict in Yemen and is stepping up support for Saudi Arabia while seeking to avoid direct military involvement.

Admiral Brad ​Cooper, commander ​of the U.S. Central Command, traveled ​to Saudi Arabia on Thursday ‌for urgent coordination talks, according to the report.

U.S. military and civilian officials have also told their Saudi counterparts in recent weeks that Trump's directive is to keep American forces focused on Iran and safeguarding the Strait of Hormuz, while avoiding the opening ‌of another military front, Axios added.

title: Hiker in Georgia makes disturbing discovery on mountain
description: White County Sheriff Rick Kelley says more details are forthcoming after the remains of two people were found on Mount Yonah, a popular northeast Georgia hiking spot.
fullText:
A hiker made a grim discovery on a Georgia mountain Wednesday, finding the remains of two people in a case that has drawn state investigators and left key questions about the deaths unanswered.

The remains were found on Mount Yonah in White County at about 11:20 a.m. on Sept. 9, according to the White County Sheriff's Office.

Sheriff's investigators and the Georgia Department of Natural Resources responded to the mountain after the discovery.

Hiker Stumbles On Human Skull In Iconic Desert As Mystery Grows And Detectives Open Homicide Probe

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation's Region 8 Crime Scene Unit was later called to help examine the scene.

Few other details have been released.

The sheriff's office has not identified the two people or said how they died. Their ages and genders also have not been released, and it is unclear how long their remains had been on the mountain.

The sheriff's office has not said whether foul play is suspected.

Cold Case Takes Grim Turn After Remains Identified As Runaway Teen; Homicide Investigation Underway

The investigation remained ongoing Wednesday, with Sheriff Rick Kelley saying his office would provide more information as it becomes available.

"The human remains located on Mt. Yonah have been sent to the GBI crime lab for an autopsy to determine cause of death and for identification purpose," the sheriff said in a press release Thursday afternoon. "Investigators are working on trying to identify the two deceased persons. The investigation is active and ongoing."

Mount Yonah is in northeast Georgia, near the cities of Helen and Cleveland, and is a popular destination for hikers.

title: Republican sounds alarm on rising Dem star: 'This guy’s going to be a problem'
description: Mike Collins claims Jon Ossoff is using the Georgia Senate race as a Democratic Party springboard for a 2028 presidential run as a DSA candidate.
fullText:
DALLAS — There's a rising star in the Democratic Party that is generating buzz for a possible presidential run, but one Republican argues he's the only thing standing in the way of a future "DSA candidate" in 2028.

Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., is running to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., in one of the most closely watched contests of this midterm election cycle. Ossoff has sought to nationalize their battle, focusing more on President Donald Trump and leaning into viral clips on social media to sell his message.

But Collins told Fox News Digital during the GOP's midterm convention that Ossoff's intentions extended beyond a second term representing the Peach State. Instead, Collins charged that Ossoff is eyeing the White House and using this cycle as a springboard to get there.

Trump-backed Candidate Survives Grueling Runoff, Advances To High-stakes Senate Race

"This guy is nothing but a trust fund kid who's never had a real job in his life," Collins said. "And at the end of the day, and I think the whole puzzle has been put together now, you can put the pieces of this thing so easy."

"He caters to that far-left base, and at the end of the day, we've got to stop him in Georgia," he continued. "If we don't stop him in Georgia, this guy's going to be a problem for the entire country in 2028."

Those puzzle pieces were scattered throughout his voting record, which Collins said aligned over 90% of the time with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., through his support of progressives, like former Maine Senate Democratic nominee Graham Platner and Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and because the bulk of his campaign donations are from out-of-state.

'Jesus Was A Radical': Progressives Invoke Christ To Sell Left-wing Agenda On Campaign Trail

Collins contended that the final piece was when the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) opened their first permanent field office in Atlanta last month. The organization has not endorsed Ossoff.

"That just tells you, yes, Jon Ossoff is really running for president," Collins said. "He's going to be the DSA candidate. He uses Georgia as a platform to raise money."

Ossoff's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Obama Strategist Turns On Rising Dem Star Over Viral Trump Attack: 'Gratuitous And Unnecessary'

He has previously thrown cold water on the notion that he was chasing the White House and told MSNOW last month, "I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and, frankly, zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now."

The first-term senator is considered one of the most vulnerable incumbents on the Democrats' Senate map this cycle, running in a state that Trump won in 2024 over former Vice President Kamala Harris by nearly three points.

Still, he has gained national attention over the summer for his speeches on the campaign trail, particularly when he needled Trump in a viral social media clip bringing into question his relationship with his executive assistant, Natalie Harp.

"He doesn't want to do the job," Ossoff said. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar."

That remark stoked a news cycle and earned him accolades from the likes of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who noted that Ossoff was one of the top communicators on the trail when it came to targeting Trump.

title: Shouts of ‘he should be shot’ heard during GOP midterm convention speech criticizing Democratic candidates
description: Shouts of “he should be shot” could be heard multiple times Thursday night at the Republican midterm convention as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz was criticizing prominent Democratic politicians by name.
fullText:
Shouts of "he should be shot" could be heard multiple times Thursday night at the Republican midterm convention as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz was criticizing prominent Democratic politicians by name.

Cruz mentioned three Democrats — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. After each name, there were shouts audible on the broadcast of "He should be shot!"

It was unclear if Cruz heard the shouts, and representatives for the senator and the Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

But the shouts came on the same day that many Republicans denounced political violence on the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Vice President JD Vance, who was friends with Kirk, reflected on his killing in a headlining speech.

El-Sayed responded during an interview on CNN's "The Source with Kaitlan Collins."

"I'm a dad with two daughters and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad," he told Collins. "This is what has become norm in our politics. I mean, literally calls to violence."

He added that "everybody who heard" the shouts should condemn them.

Kirk, the co-founder of Turning Point USA, was shot and killed on a Utah college campus a year ago. He was 31.

"Charlie was killed one year ago today," RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said as the second day of convention speeches kicked off. "He believed in America and freedom and young people's courage to stand up and fight for the country they love."

Many of Thursday's speeches were otherwise devoted to attacking Democrats as ideologically radical. The shouts of "He should be shot!" could be heard while Cruz was telling Republicans to take seriously the past comments and positions of Mamdani, El-Sayed and Talarico.

"A simple truth: When people tell you who they are, believe them," Cruz said. "When Mamdani says he wants to seize the means of production, he means it."

"When Abdul El-Sayed says he has a, quote, 'obligation,' to comply with Sharia law, he means it," the Texas senator said.

"And when James Talarico says he wants to dismantle capitalism, he means it," Cruz said.

Mamdani, a democratic socialist, spoke about "the end goal of seizing the means of production" during a 2021 speech discussing his political beliefs, according to Politifact. When the comment came up during his 2025 mayoral campaign, a spokesperson said his platform did not include seizing the means of production.

Cruz's criticism of El-Sayed stems from a 2009 interview with The New York Times where El-Sayed, then a medical student, said he felt an "obligation" to follow Sharia law in buying his first home. Muslims are discouraged from paying interest on loans, which can make seeking out a mortgage more complicated.

And Cruz was calling out Talarico over a recent CNN report that he said in 2020 that capitalism needed to be "dismantl(ed)" along with White supremacy and climate change. Talarico's campaign said the Democrat was a "proud capitalist" in response to the CNN story.

Cruz brought up Kirk's killing during his speech while denouncing what he described as a rising tide of extremism in politics, one day before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

"The hate that killed Charlie Kirk, that knocked down the Twin Towers, that led to two assassination attempts on President Trump, it just gets keeping getting worse and worse," Cruz said.

El-Sayed agreed in the CNN interview that politics was becoming too consumed by hate.

"When you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us," he said. "I hope that everybody who heard that is going to call it out for what it is: a call for violence that ought to be condemned across the board."

Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, the second highest-ranking Democrat in the House, condemned the shouts in an X post, saying "every single Republican" should as well. And Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, also weighed in, calling them "clear hate."
